notes.title: Automobile Engineering 2/12 — The Engine, Part 2: Power, Torque and Mileage
notes.summary: Power is how fast an engine works and torque is how hard it pushes. This part shows how to read a spec sheet, pick a car by torque spread and power-to-weight, and understand what really drives mileage, including why ARAI numbers run well above real-world city figures.
notes.body:
🔧 THE ENGINE, PART 2: POWER, TORQUE AND MILEAGE

==========

⚡ TL;DR

Power is how fast an engine can do work; torque is how hard it can push. You feel torque when pulling away or climbing, and power when overtaking at speed. To pick a car, look at the spread of torque (the rpm range where it is available) and the car's power-to-weight, not the single biggest number. Mileage is decided by how much energy it takes to move the car (weight, drag, tyres) and how efficiently the engine and gearbox turn fuel into that energy. ARAI figures are lab numbers; owners of the Creta variants report city figures roughly 17% to 46% lower.

==========

🔧 1. TORQUE AND POWER IN PLAIN WORDS

Torque is the twisting force the engine puts on the crankshaft, measured in newton-metres (Nm). Power is the rate of doing work, which is torque multiplied by how fast the engine is turning. The conversion is worth knowing once:

Power (kW) = Torque (Nm) × rpm ÷ 9,549, and bhp = kW ÷ 0.746.

Use it on the Swift's spec sheet. Peak torque is 111.7 Nm at 4,300 rpm, which works out to about 50 kW or 67 bhp at that moment. The 80.46 bhp peak arrives later, at 5,700 rpm, where torque has slipped to about 100 Nm (60 kW × 9,549 ÷ 5,700). Torque falls at high rpm because the engine has less time to fill its cylinders, but rpm keeps rising, so power keeps climbing for a while longer.

==========

🔩 2. READING THE NUMBERS ON A SPEC SHEET

A spec line such as 118.27 bhp @ 5,500 rpm, 170 Nm @ 1,750–4,000 rpm tells you three things: how much, where it peaks, and how wide the torque plateau is. The plateau matters most in daily driving.

🔹 Nexon 1.2 turbo: 170 Nm is available from just 1,750 rpm to 4,000 rpm. The car pulls without you changing gear.

🔹 Creta 1.5 diesel: 250 Nm from 1,500 to 2,750 rpm. At 2,750 rpm that is about 72 kW or 96 bhp, strong pull from barely above idle, which is why diesels feel effortless in traffic and on climbs.

🔹 Creta 1.5 MPi petrol: 143.8 Nm only at 4,500 rpm. You need to keep revs up, so expect more downshifting.

Torque at the wheels is engine torque multiplied by the gear ratio, so gearing changes how a car feels as much as the engine does. Part 3 covers that.

==========

🎯 3. HOW TO PICK A CAR BY POWER

🔹 Start with your driving. City crawl, mixed use, regular highway, hills, a full family load: each rewards a different number.

🔹 Look at the torque spread, not just the peak. A wide plateau starting below 2,000 rpm means relaxed driving.

🔹 Check power-to-weight: bhp divided by kerb weight in tonnes. The Swift's 80.46 bhp over a listed 925 kg is about 87 bhp per tonne.* As a rough guide, under 70 feels leisurely, 80 to 100 is brisk enough for most buyers, and above 120 is quick.*

🔹 Remember the gearbox. An automatic or CVT can dull a small engine's response; a turbo petrol with a DCT feels sharper.

🔹 Don't pay for power you can't use. Speed limits and traffic cap how much extra power you will ever use.

🔹 Drive in the city, 1–2 people: Light weight, easy low-rpm response, an easy automatic; Swift 1.2; Nexon 1.2 turbo (plateau from 1,750 rpm).

🔹 Drive mixed with a family of four: Torque available from about 1,500–2,000 rpm; Nexon 1.2 turbo; Creta 1.5 diesel.

🔹 Do highway runs and overtake often: Power at speed, good power-to-weight, a tall top gear; Creta 1.5 turbo (158 bhp); Skoda 1.5 TSI (150 PS).

🔹 Climb hills or carry full loads: A wide torque plateau; diesel or turbo; Creta 1.5 diesel; Thar diesel (about 300 Nm).

==========

⛽ 4. WHAT ACTUALLY MAKES MILEAGE BETTER

Mileage depends on two things: how much energy the car needs, and how well the engine and drivetrain supply it.

Energy the car needs. Three forces resist motion. Weight matters whenever you accelerate or climb: more mass, more fuel. Rolling resistance comes from the tyres and rises with weight and low tyre pressure. Aerodynamic drag grows with the square of speed, so going from 100 to 120 km/h raises drag force by 44% and the power needed to beat it by about 73%. Speed is the biggest lever a driver controls.

How well the engine converts fuel. Textbooks put the best-case thermal efficiency of a petrol engine at roughly 30–35% and a diesel at roughly 40%; the rest leaves as heat.* Real driving is worse, because city driving uses only a small fraction of the engine's capability, where friction and pumping losses take a bigger share. That is why start-stop, cylinder deactivation and hybrids help most in the city.

Drivetrain and conditions. More gear ratios keep the engine in its efficient range. Air conditioning, traffic, tyre pressure, a loaded boot and a heavy foot all change the result.

==========

🧪 5. ARAI VERSUS REAL-WORLD MILEAGE

The ARAI figure comes from a standard test on a laboratory roller, with fixed speeds, no air conditioning and no traffic. It is good for comparing cars with each other, not for predicting your fuel bill. The Hyundai Creta shows the gap clearly:

🔹 Petrol, manual: ARAI claim (km/l) 17.4; City, owner-reported 12–14; Highway, owner-reported up to about 17; City shortfall 20–31%.

🔹 Turbo petrol, DCT: ARAI claim (km/l) 18.4; City, owner-reported 10–12; Highway, owner-reported 16–17; City shortfall 35–46%.

🔹 Diesel, manual: ARAI claim (km/l) 21.8; City, owner-reported 16–18; Highway, owner-reported over 20; City shortfall 17–27%.

Note the turbo petrol: it has the best ARAI figure of the three petrols and the worst city figure. Boost helps in a gentle lab test and costs fuel when real traffic makes you use it.

==========

🔄 6. TURBO, DOWNSIZING AND HYBRIDS

Downsizing replaces a big engine with a small turbocharged one (Section 8 of Part 1: Skoda's 1.0 TSI, Tata's 1.2 Revotron). A small engine at steady cruise runs at a higher load, which is more efficient, and the turbo supplies extra pull on demand. The weakness is the one in Fig 2: when you demand the boost, the engine burns more fuel.

Cylinder deactivation shuts some cylinders at light load; Skoda's 1.5 TSI is reported to do this on two of its four.* Diesel is more efficient than petrol at the same size, but costs more to buy and to keep BS6-compliant.

Hybrids change the picture most. The Honda City e:HEV claims about 27.3 km/l and the Toyota Hyryder strong hybrid about 28.0 km/l (ARAI), roughly 57–61% more than the petrol Creta's 17.4.* These are different cars, so the comparison shows scale rather than an exact gain. Part 7 covers hybrids properly.

==========

🌱 7. BS6 AND E20: WHAT CHANGED FOR ENGINES

India moved to BS6 emission norms on 1 April 2020, and to a stricter second phase on 1 April 2023 that added real-driving emission testing and on-board diagnostics. For petrol engines this mostly meant better catalytic converters and engine tuning. For diesels it meant a particulate filter and a urea-based SCR system, which add cost, and some makers, notably Maruti Suzuki, stopped selling small diesels altogether.*

E20 petrol (20% ethanol) is now the standard pump fuel nationwide. Ethanol carries less energy per litre than petrol. The petroleum ministry's estimate (August 2025) is a mileage loss of about 1–2% for E10-designed cars calibrated for E20 and 3–6% for others; the transport minister told Parliament in July 2026 that the drop is 2–6%.

==========

📝 SUMMARY

🔹 Torque is push; power is push times speed. kW = Nm × rpm ÷ 9,549, and bhp = kW ÷ 0.746.

🔹 Peak torque comes at lower rpm than peak power. The width of the torque plateau decides how relaxed a car feels.

🔹 To pick a car, match the torque spread and power-to-weight to your driving. Do not chase the biggest number.

🔹 Mileage = energy the car needs (weight, tyres, drag that grows with speed squared) ÷ how efficiently the engine and drivetrain deliver it.

🔹 ARAI numbers compare cars; real-world city figures for the Creta variants run 17–46% lower.

🔹 Small turbos help at cruise but cost fuel when you use the boost. Hybrids give the biggest real gain.

🔹 BS6 made diesels costlier; E20 trims km/l by an official estimate of 1–6%.

==========

➡️ NEXT: Part 3 covers transmissions and the drivetrain: how torque reaches the wheels.

==========

*Unverified or approximate: Swift kerb weight (925 kg) from a listing; power-to-weight bands, thermal-efficiency percentages, Skoda cylinder deactivation and small-diesel withdrawal are textbook rules of thumb or general knowledge, not checked against an official document. Hybrid figures: Carlelo (ARAI 27.26 and 27.97 km/l). Creta ARAI claims and owner-reported mileage: Spinny's Creta mileage comparison (owner-reported, indicative only). Spec sources as in Part 1. BS6 phase dates (1 April 2020 and 1 April 2023, with real-driving emissions and on-board diagnostics in Phase 2) were cross-checked in November 2026 (Autocar India, Down To Earth). Theory: Heywood, Internal Combustion Engine Fundamentals.

The PDF above carries the diagrams (torque and power curves, ARAI versus real-world mileage).

==========

🔗 See also: Automobile Engineering 1/12 — The Engine, Part 1: How It Works.

notes.summary: The gearbox exists because an engine works well only inside a narrow band of revs, while a car must move from a standstill to highway speed. Gears trade speed for pulling force. In India you will meet five kinds of transmission: manual, AMT, torque-converter automatic, CVT and dual-clutch (DCT), plus the e-CVT in strong hybrids.
notes.body:
🔧 TRANSMISSIONS AND DRIVETRAIN

==========

⚡ TL;DR

The gearbox exists because an engine works well only inside a narrow band of revs, while a car must move from a standstill to highway speed. Gears trade speed for pulling force. In India you will meet five kinds of transmission: manual, AMT, torque-converter automatic, CVT and dual-clutch (DCT), plus the e-CVT in strong hybrids. They differ in cost, smoothness and efficiency. The drivetrain layout (front-, rear- or four-wheel drive) decides which wheels get the power. Most Indian cars are front-wheel drive; true off-roaders need four-wheel drive with a low-range gear.

==========

🔧 1. WHY A CAR NEEDS GEARS

A petrol engine delivers useful power roughly between 1,500 and 6,000 rpm. Idle is far lower, and a car's wheels turn at a few hundred rpm at city speeds. The transmission bridges the gap. Torque at the driven axle = engine torque × gear ratio × final-drive ratio, before losses. Take an engine making 100 Nm, a first gear of 3.45, a final drive of 4.3 and a fifth gear of 0.77 (illustrative figures, not a specific car): first gear delivers about 1,480 Nm to the axle and fifth about 330 Nm. First gear gives a strong push for starting and climbing; fifth lets the engine turn slowly at highway speed, which saves fuel and noise.

More gears mean smaller steps between them, so the engine stays nearer its sweet spot. That is why 6-speed and 7-speed gearboxes help mileage compared with 4-speeds, and why the Part 2 point about wide torque plateaus matters: a wide plateau needs fewer shifts.

==========

🔩 2. THE MANUAL: CLUTCH AND GEARS

A manual gearbox joins the engine to the wheels through a clutch, a pair of friction discs the driver presses apart or together. Pressing the pedal disconnects the engine so a gear can be chosen; releasing it reconnects. Manuals are cheap, light, efficient and durable, and they give the driver full control. Their weakness is the city: heavy traffic means constant clutch work. That is why automatic gearboxes now sell in large numbers in Indian metros.

==========

🎯 3. THE FOUR KINDS OF AUTOMATIC

All automatics take the clutch and gear selection away from the driver. They do it in four different ways, and the way decides how a car feels and what it costs to own.

🔹 AMT (automated manual): How it works A manual gearbox with a computer-controlled robot working the clutch and shifts; Strength Cheapest automatic; manual-like mileage; Weakness Slow, jerky shifts, especially when pulling away; Indian examples Maruti Swift AMT, Tata Punch AMT.

🔹 Torque-converter automatic: How it works A fluid coupling in place of the clutch, plus planetary gear sets; Strength Smooth, tough, good for heavy loads and off-road; Weakness Heavier, costlier, a little less efficient; Indian examples Creta diesel 6-speed automatic; Thar.

🔹 CVT (continuously variable): How it works A belt running between two cone-shaped pulleys with no fixed gears; Strength Very smooth; keeps revs in the best band; Weakness Rubbery feel when accelerating hard; less suited to high torque; Indian examples Hyundai IVT (Creta petrol); Honda City.

🔹 DCT (dual-clutch): How it works Two clutches, one for odd gears and one for even; the next gear is pre-selected; Strength Fast shifts, sporty, efficient; Weakness Can be hesitant at crawling speed; costly to repair; Indian examples Creta 1.5 turbo (7-speed DCT); Skoda 1.5 TSI (7-speed DSG).

The e-CVT in hybrids is a different idea: it uses a planetary gear set to blend power from the petrol engine and one or two electric motors, with no belt and no clutch. Toyota's Innova Hycross hybrid and the Hyryder use this layout, and it is why they feel smooth and need no shifts. Part 7 explains hybrids in full.

iMT (Hyundai and Kia's clutchless manual) is a halfway option: it has a manual gearbox with a sensor that handles the clutch, so you shift yourself but need no pedal.* Which type suits you depends on traffic, budget and how much you drive; Part 11 returns to that choice.

==========

⛽ 4. DRIVETRAIN LAYOUTS: WHICH WHEELS GET THE POWER

🔹 Front-wheel drive (FWD): the engine and driven wheels sit together. It is cheap, compact and light, with good traction on wet roads. Almost every Swift, Nexon, Creta and City is FWD.

🔹 Rear-wheel drive (RWD): a shaft carries power to the rear. It gives balanced weight and better handling at the limit, but it takes up floor space. The BMW 330Li is RWD; the Mahindra Thar offers RWD on some versions.

🔹 All-wheel and four-wheel drive (AWD/4x4): power goes to all four wheels. AWD systems (Mahindra XUV700 AWD*) work automatically on roads; a true 4x4 (Thar 4x4*) adds a low-range gearbox that multiplies torque again for steep, rough ground. Both add weight, cost and a fuel penalty.

A differential sits between the driven wheels so the outer wheel can turn faster than the inner one in a corner. An open differential sends power to whichever wheel slips first; locking differentials force both wheels to turn together, which is what off-roaders use on loose ground.

==========

🧪 5. WHAT IT MEANS FOR A BUYER

🔹 City use, heavy traffic: an automatic, preferably CVT, torque converter or DCT, is worth the premium; an AMT is the budget option.

🔹 Highway use: a DCT or torque converter gives quick overtakes; a manual is cheaper and often a little more efficient.

🔹 Hills and rough roads: torque-converter automatic or manual with strong low-end torque; for serious off-roading choose a 4x4 with low range.

🔹 Mileage: manual ≥ AMT ≈ DCT ≥ CVT ≥ torque converter in most cases, but differences are small next to driving style (Part 2).*

==========

📝 SUMMARY

🔹 The transmission lets an engine with a narrow rev band move a car across all speeds; torque at the axle = engine torque × gear ratio × final drive.

🔹 Manuals are cheap and efficient; automatics trade some of that for traffic comfort.

🔹 AMT is a robot-driven manual: cheap but jerky. Torque converter is smooth and tough. CVT keeps revs steady. DCT is quick and sporty. e-CVT blends engine and motors in hybrids.

🔹 FWD is common and cheap; RWD helps handling; AWD/4x4 helps traction and off-road ability, at a cost in weight and fuel.

🔹 Choose by traffic, budget and terrain, not by the number of gears.

==========

➡️ NEXT: Part 4 of 12.

==========

*Unverified or general knowledge: gear ratios in Section 1 are illustrative, not from a brochure; XUV700 AWD and Thar 4x4 availability, the iMT description and the mileage ordering in Section 5 are not checked against official documents. Transmission offerings confirmed in November 2026 listings: Swift 5-speed AMT; Creta petrol 6MT or IVT, turbo 7-speed DCT only, diesel 6MT or 6-speed automatic; Thar 6-speed torque-converter automatic; Honda City CVT; Hyryder e-CVT; Skoda 1.5 TSI 7-speed DSG only. Punch AMT and Innova Hycross e-CVT were not re-verified. Sources: Autocar India, Honda Cars India, Wikipedia. Theory: Heywood; Gillespie, Fundamentals of Vehicle Dynamics. Thar RWD (launched with a 1.5-litre diesel in 2025) was cross-checked in November 2026.

The PDF above carries the diagrams for this part.

==========

🔗 See also: the rest of the Automobile Engineering series (parts 1 to 12).

notes.title: Automobile Engineering 4/12 — Chassis, Suspension, Steering and Brakes
notes.summary: The chassis is the skeleton that carries the engine, passengers and crash loads. Suspension keeps the tyres on the road over bumps, steering points the car, and brakes turn speed into heat. All four work through one small thing: the patch of rubber where each tyre meets the road.
notes.body:
🔧 CHASSIS, SUSPENSION, STEERING AND BRAKES

==========

⚡ TL;DR

The chassis is the skeleton that carries the engine, passengers and crash loads. Suspension keeps the tyres on the road over bumps, steering points the car, and brakes turn speed into heat. All four work through one small thing: the patch of rubber where each tyre meets the road. Stopping distance grows with the square of speed, which is why 120 km/h is far more dangerous than 80 km/h. For Indian roads the practical questions are ground clearance, ride comfort over potholes, and whether the car has ABS and ESC.

==========

🔧 1. THE CHASSIS AND BODY

Most modern cars use a monocoque (unibody): the floor, pillars and roof are one welded steel shell that is both body and frame. It is light, strong in a crash and cheap to mass-produce. Tough utility vehicles such as the Mahindra Thar and Scorpio-N use a separate ladder frame, two heavy steel rails with the body bolted on top.* It carries heavy loads and survives abuse, but is heavier and rides less smoothly. Electric cars add a new idea: the battery pack forms a flat structural floor (a 'skateboard'), which Part 6 covers.

==========

🔩 2. SUSPENSION: SPRINGS AND DAMPERS

A spring alone would bounce up and down after every bump, so each wheel also has a damper (shock absorber) that converts the bouncing into heat. The art is the trade-off: soft springs ride comfortably but let the body lean in corners; stiff springs corner flat but thump over potholes. Indian buyers usually want comfort and high ground clearance, so most cars are set softer and taller than European equivalents.*

🔹 McPherson strut (front): a strut combining spring and damper on a single bolt-on unit. It is compact and cheap, and used on the front of almost every mass-market car.*

🔹 Torsion beam (rear): two trailing arms joined by a twisting cross-beam. Simple and cheap; common on hatchbacks and compact SUVs.*

🔹 Multi-link (rear): several arms control each wheel separately, giving better ride and handling at higher cost. Typical in premium cars.

🔹 Solid axle with leaf or coil springs: a rigid beam across the rear, tough for loads and off-road. Typical in ladder-frame SUVs and pickups.*

Ground clearance is the gap between the lowest part of the underside and the road. India's speed breakers and broken roads make it a headline spec for SUV buyers. Higher clearance helps on bad roads but raises the centre of gravity, which increases body roll.

==========

🎯 3. STEERING

Almost all cars use a rack and pinion: a small gear (pinion) on the steering column moves a toothed bar (rack) sideways, turning the front wheels. A power-assist system lightens the effort. Older cars used hydraulic pumps driven by the engine; modern ones use electric power steering (EPS), a motor on the steering column. EPS saves fuel (no pump drag) and can vary the weight with speed, so the wheel is light in parking and firmer on the highway. The spec sheet's turning radius tells you how tight a U-turn the car can make, which matters more in a crowded city than 0–100 km/h time.

==========

⛽ 4. BRAKES

Brakes work by friction: pads clamp a disc (or shoes press a drum) and convert the car's kinetic energy into heat. Kinetic energy is ½ × mass × speed², so energy, and therefore braking distance, grows with the square of speed. Add the distance covered while the driver reacts (about 1.5 seconds is a common assumption) and the numbers rise fast.

🔹 Disc vs drum: discs shed heat better and resist fade; drums are cheaper and still used on the rear wheels of many small cars.*

🔹 ABS (anti-lock braking): pulses the brakes many times a second so the wheels never lock, letting you steer while braking hard. It has been compulsory on all new cars in India since 1 April 2019.

🔹 EBD and brake assist: distribute braking force between front and rear, and add full force when the system senses a panic stop.

🔹 ESC (electronic stability control): senses a skid and brakes individual wheels to straighten the car. Many safety experts rate it as important as airbags; Part 5 covers it.

🔹 Regenerative braking (EVs, hybrids): the motor works as a generator when you lift off, returning some energy to the battery. It cuts brake wear and boosts efficiency in the city.

==========

🧪 5. TYRES: THE PART THAT TOUCHES THE ROAD

Each tyre's contact patch is only about the size of a palm, and that patch carries every force: acceleration, braking and cornering.* A size such as 215/60 R17 reads: 215 mm tread width; sidewall height equal to 60% of that width (about 129 mm); R for radial construction; 17-inch wheel. A taller sidewall (higher aspect ratio) cushions bumps; large wheels with thin sidewalls look sporty but ride harder and are costlier to replace. Tyre pressure matters for safety, comfort and mileage (Part 2), and is the cheapest thing a driver can check.

==========

🔄 6. WHAT IT MEANS FOR A BUYER

🔹 Look at ground clearance and the rear suspension type if you drive on poor roads.

🔹 Test the ride over a speed breaker at 20–30 km/h; that tells more than a spec sheet.

🔹 Insist on ABS and ESC, particularly on faster cars and for highway use.

🔹 Check turning radius and steering lightness if most of your driving is in the city.

==========

📝 SUMMARY

🔹 A monocoque is a light unibody; a ladder frame is heavy and tough for utility vehicles.

🔹 Springs carry weight; dampers control bouncing; stiffer means sportier, softer means more comfortable.

🔹 Rack-and-pinion steering with electric assist is standard; turning radius matters in cities.

🔹 Brakes turn kinetic energy (½ mv²) into heat; stopping distance rises with the square of speed.

🔹 ABS stops wheels locking; ESC stops skids; regenerative braking saves energy in EVs and hybrids.

🔹 A tyre size code tells width, sidewall height and wheel diameter.

==========

➡️ NEXT: Part 5 of 12.

==========

*Unverified or general knowledge: which cars use ladder frames, which suspension types are common, the 'palm-sized' contact patch, drum-brake use on rear wheels and the claim that Indian cars are set softer than European ones are not checked against official documents. Stopping distances in Fig 2 are calculated from simple physics with stated assumptions (friction 0.7 dry, 0.4 wet, 1.5 s reaction); real cars and tyres vary. Theory: Gillespie, Fundamentals of Vehicle Dynamics. The 1 April 2019 ABS mandate for new cars was cross-checked in November 2026 (Autocar India, CarDekho).

The PDF above carries the diagrams for this part.

==========

🔗 See also: the rest of the Automobile Engineering series (parts 1 to 12).

notes.title: Automobile Engineering 5/12 — Safety Engineering
notes.summary: A car's safety has three jobs: help the driver avoid a crash, help everyone survive one, and help rescuers afterwards. Avoidance comes from brakes, tyres, ABS and stability control. Survival comes from a rigid passenger cell, crumple zones that absorb energy, seatbelts and airbags.
notes.body:
🔧 SAFETY ENGINEERING

==========

⚡ TL;DR

A car's safety has three jobs: help the driver avoid a crash, help everyone survive one, and help rescuers afterwards. Avoidance comes from brakes, tyres, ABS and stability control. Survival comes from a rigid passenger cell, crumple zones that absorb energy, seatbelts and airbags. In India, crash ratings from Bharat NCAP (government, since 2023) and Global NCAP (independent) now let buyers compare cars on tested performance instead of marketing. A star rating is meaningful only for the exact version tested and the protocol year it was tested under.

==========

🔧 1. THE PHYSICS: WHY SPEED IS THE ENEMY

In a crash, the car's kinetic energy (½ × mass × speed²) has to go somewhere. It goes into bending metal, which is the safety engineer's job to arrange. Doubling the speed quadruples the energy. Bharat NCAP's frontal offset test runs at 64 km/h; a crash at 120 km/h carries about 3.5 times that energy.* No structure can absorb that safely, which is why speed limits matter more than any feature.

==========

🔩 2. THREE LAYERS OF SAFETY

==========

🎯 3. HOW A CAR SURVIVES A CRASH

🔹 Rigid passenger cell: the cabin is built from very strong steel (often high-strength or hot-stamped grades) so it does not collapse onto occupants.

🔹 Crumple zones: the front and rear are designed to fold progressively, absorbing energy over a longer time. Stopping over a longer time means lower force on the body.

🔹 Seatbelts with pretensioners and load limiters: the belt tightens in the first milliseconds and then lets out a little so the chest is not injured. The belt is the single most important restraint; airbags assume you are wearing it.

🔹 Airbags: a front airbag cushions the head and chest; side and curtain airbags protect in side impacts and rollovers. Six airbags are not mandatory in India: a January 2022 draft notification lapsed, and in September 2023 the transport minister said six airbags would not be made compulsory and that Bharat NCAP should push makers to fit them. Several popular models, including the Swift and Dzire, now fit six as standard.

🔹 Child restraints (ISOFIX): standard anchor points let a child seat clip rigidly into the car. Child occupant protection is scored separately in NCAP tests.

==========

⛽ 4. HOW A CAR AVOIDS A CRASH

🔹 ABS prevents wheel lock under hard braking; ESC stops skids by braking single wheels. Global NCAP has pushed ESC as a key feature, and it is now rewarded in the protocol (see below).

🔹 Autonomous emergency braking (AEB) uses a radar or camera to brake automatically when a collision is near. It is part of the driver-assistance systems in Part 8.

🔹 Tyres and brakes in good condition matter more than any electronic feature; Part 4 covers stopping distances.

==========

🧪 5. CRASH TESTS: HOW TO READ THE STARS

Global NCAP, a UK-based charity, started crash-testing popular Indian cars in 2014 under its Safer Cars for India campaign. Its first round tested five cars, including the Swift, with no frontal airbags fitted; all scored zero stars for adult protection. Results pushed Toyota and Volkswagen to make frontal airbags standard across their Indian lineups.

Bharat NCAP is India's own programme. Its programme took effect on 1 October 2023 (announced 22 August 2023*), and crash tests began in December 2023. The current protocol (AIS-197) uses a 64 km/h frontal offset test, a 50 km/h side-barrier test and a pole side test, and carries ESC and pedestrian-protection requirements. The first 5-star results went to the Tata Harrier and Safari (adult 30.08/32, child 44.54/49). A tougher Bharat NCAP 2.0 (five crash tests, a 100-point scale, with curtain airbags and ESC required for any star rating) is in draft for October 2027. The programme is voluntary: makers choose which cars to submit.

🔹 Maruti Dzire (4th gen): Protocol / year Global NCAP, Nov 2024; Result Adult 31.24/34 (5 stars); child 39.20/49 (4 stars); first Maruti to score 5 stars.

🔹 Maruti Dzire: Protocol / year Bharat NCAP; Result 5 stars (29.46/41.57).

🔹 Maruti Swift (3rd gen): Protocol / year Global NCAP 2.0, 2022; Result Adult 19.19/34 (1 star), child 16.68/49 (1 star); the older Swift scored 2 stars each in 2018 under the previous protocol.

🔹 Tata Punch (petrol): Protocol / year Global NCAP, 2021 (older 17-point scale); Result Adult 16.45/17 (5 stars); child 40.89/49 (4 stars). Not comparable with 34-point scores.

🔹 Tata Punch.ev: Protocol / year Bharat NCAP, 2024; Result Adult 31.46/32 (5 stars); child 45.00/49 (5 stars); the 2026 facelift scored 31.09/32 and 45/49.

🔹 Tata Nexon: Protocol / year Global NCAP and Bharat NCAP; Result 5 stars in both (Bharat NCAP 29.41/43.83).

🔹 Tata Harrier, Safari: Protocol / year Bharat NCAP, Dec 2023; Result First Bharat NCAP results: adult 30.08/32, child 44.54/49 (5 stars each).

🔹 VW Taigun, Skoda Kushaq: Protocol / year Global NCAP, Oct 2022; Result Adult 29.64/34, child 42.00/49 (5 stars each).

🔹 Hyundai Creta: Protocol / year Global NCAP, 2022 (older protocol); Result 3 stars.

Not every popular car has a Bharat NCAP rating yet: as of November 2026 I found no Bharat NCAP result for the Swift, Creta, Hyryder or City. The Hyundai Venue, Kia Seltos and Toyota Innova Hycross have all been reported at 5 stars in Bharat NCAP.

Why scores aren't directly comparable. Global NCAP changed its protocol in July 2022 (adding side-impact protection and rear seatbelt reminders, and making ESC and side head airbags requirements for higher ratings) and again in August 2025 (rewarding safety equipment only if fitted as standard). A 5-star result in 2021 and one in 2024 reflect different tests. Always check which protocol, which variant (airbag count differs by trim) and which year.

==========

🔄 6. WHAT IT MEANS FOR A BUYER

🔹 Choose the variant that matches the tested one: the rating usually applies to a specific trim and airbag count.

🔹 Check which protocol and year the rating came from; newer protocols are stricter.

🔹 Prefer cars with six airbags, ESC and ISOFIX as standard, not as paid extras.

🔹 Wear the belt in the rear seat too; most rear passengers in India still do not.

==========

📝 SUMMARY

🔹 Safety has three layers: avoid the crash, survive it, help afterwards.

🔹 Crash energy rises with speed squared, so a structure that is safe at 64 km/h cannot protect at 120 km/h.

🔹 A rigid cell, crumple zones, belts with pretensioners and airbags protect occupants together.

🔹 ABS, ESC and AEB help avoid the crash.

🔹 Bharat NCAP (since 2023) and Global NCAP rate cars; ratings depend on the variant, the protocol and the year.

🔹 Prefer six airbags, ESC and ISOFIX as standard.

==========

➡️ NEXT: Part 6 of 12.

==========

*Unverified or general knowledge: the 3.5× comparison is arithmetic ((120/64)²); the 22 August 2023 Bharat NCAP announcement date, eCall availability and the seatbelt-usage remark were not re-checked, and the Creta's 3-star Global NCAP result is from 2022 under an older protocol. Cross-checked in November 2026: six-airbag status (MoRTH draft of 14 January 2022; minister's statement of 13 September 2023), Bharat NCAP dates, protocol and results, Dzire, Punch, Punch.ev, Nexon, Harrier, Safari, Kushaq results, the Swift's 2022 Global NCAP result (1 star adult 19.19/34 and child 16.68/49; Autocar India) and 2018 result (2 stars), the Creta and i20 3-star result (Autocar Professional), and 5-star Bharat NCAP reports for the Venue, Seltos and Hycross (Rushlane, 91wheels, Gaadify). Protocol history: Global NCAP (via Wikipedia).

The PDF above carries the diagrams for this part.

==========

🔗 See also: the rest of the Automobile Engineering series (parts 1 to 12).

notes.title: Automobile Engineering 6/12 — Electric Vehicles
notes.summary: An electric car swaps the engine, fuel tank and gearbox for a battery, an inverter and a motor. The battery's size in kWh is its fuel tank; the motor's torque is available from the first turn of the wheels.
notes.body:
🔧 ELECTRIC VEHICLES

==========

⚡ TL;DR

An electric car swaps the engine, fuel tank and gearbox for a battery, an inverter and a motor. The battery's size in kWh is its fuel tank; the motor's torque is available from the first turn of the wheels. Running costs per km are far lower than petrol or diesel, but the car costs more to buy, and what matters in practice is whether you can charge at home. Claimed range is a lab figure: the Nexon EV's 489 km claim compares with a user-reported 297 km. GST on EVs is 5%, against 18% or 40% for most petrol and diesel cars.

==========

🔧 1. HOW AN ELECTRIC CAR WORKS

🔹 Battery pack: thousands of cells storing energy as direct current. Capacity is measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh): a 45 kWh pack can deliver 45 kW for one hour.

🔹 Inverter: converts the battery's DC into AC for the motor and controls its speed and torque.

🔹 Motor: an electric motor makes its peak torque from standstill, with no need to rev up. The Nexon EV (45 kWh) is listed at 145 hp and 215 Nm; the Mahindra BE 6 (2024 launch version, 79 kWh pack) at 210 kW (282 hp) and 380 Nm. This is why EVs feel quick off the line.

🔹 Single-speed gear: electric motors work over a huge rev range, so one fixed gear is enough. There are no shifts.

🔹 Regeneration: lifting off the accelerator turns the motor into a generator, recovering part of the energy that a petrol car loses as brake heat.

==========

🔩 2. THE BATTERY: THE COSTLY HEART

The battery is the most expensive part of an EV, commonly estimated at 30–40% of the car's cost.* Two chemistries dominate: LFP (lithium iron phosphate), cheaper and longer-lived, and NMC (nickel-manganese-cobalt), more energy-dense and costlier.* A battery slowly loses capacity over years and charge cycles, which affects resale value; makers typically offer an eight-year battery warranty.* A thermal-management system heats or cools the pack, because batteries age faster when hot.

Importantly, EV platforms put the flat battery in the floor like a skateboard. That lowers the centre of gravity and frees cabin space. The Mahindra BE 6 and XEV 9e sit on Mahindra's INGLO platform; the Tata Punch.ev is the first car on Tata's acti.ev architecture.

==========

🎯 3. CHARGING

🔹 Ordinary 15 A home socket: Typical power about 3 kW; What it takes (Nexon EV 45 kWh) about 17.6 hours for 10–100%.

🔹 Home AC wall box: Typical power 7.2 kW; What it takes (Nexon EV 45 kWh) about 6.6 hours for 10–100%.

🔹 Public DC fast charger: Typical power 60 kW; What it takes (Nexon EV 45 kWh) about 40 minutes for 10–80%.

🔹 Fast charging on newer platforms: Typical power 140–180 kW; What it takes (Nexon EV 45 kWh) BE 6 Sporteq: under 20 minutes for 20–80% (59 kWh at 140 kW, 70 kWh at 160 kW, 79 kWh at 180 kW).

A rule of thumb: charging time ≈ energy needed ÷ charger power, plus extra at the top because the car slows charging above about 80%. Fast chargers are best for highway trips; overnight home charging does the daily work. If you cannot charge at home or work, an EV is much less convenient.

==========

⛽ 4. RANGE: CLAIMED VERSUS REAL

Claimed range comes from a standard lab test. Real range depends on speed (drag grows with the square, as in Part 2), air conditioning, temperature, load and driving style. The Nexon EV 45 kWh is listed at a claimed 489 km, while one listing gives a user-reported 297 km, about 39% lower. The BE 6 Sporteq (relaunched 15 August 2026) claims 548, 651 and 683 km for its 59, 70 and 79 kWh packs. As a quick check, divide the pack size by the range to get consumption: the Nexon's real-world figure works out to about 15 kWh per 100 km, against about 9 kWh per 100 km on the claim.

==========

🧪 5. THE MONEY QUESTION

On these assumptions, home-charged EV running costs are roughly one-sixth of petrol. Public fast charging is still well under half. But an EV costs more upfront, so the saving only pays back with enough kilometres. A simple break-even: extra purchase price ÷ saving per km. If an EV costs ₹4 lakh more and saves ₹6 per km, you need about 67,000 km to recover it (about 5–6 years at 12,000 km a year).

🔹 Tax: EVs pay 5% GST; since 22 September 2025 most petrol and diesel cars pay 18% (small cars) or 40% (larger cars). This narrows the price gap. There is no central purchase subsidy for private electric cars under PM E-DRIVE (its electric two-wheeler support was extended to 31 March 2028), so the 5% GST is the main tax benefit.

🔹 Unknowns: battery life, resale value and charging availability are still uncertain in India.

🔹 Best fit: a household with home charging, mostly city and short intercity use, ideally as a second car.

==========

📝 SUMMARY

🔹 An EV = battery (kWh) + inverter + motor + a single-speed gear; torque is instant.

🔹 The battery is the costly part (roughly 30–40% of the car's cost) and its chemistry and warranty matter.

🔹 Charging time ≈ energy ÷ charger power; home AC does the daily work, DC fast chargers handle trips.

🔹 Claimed range is a lab figure; the Nexon EV example shows real range about 40% below the claim.

🔹 Running cost per km is far below petrol, but the purchase premium means the saving needs enough km to pay back.

🔹 GST is 5% on EVs versus 18% or 40% on most other new cars.

==========

➡️ NEXT: Part 7 of 12.

==========

*Unverified or general knowledge: battery cost share (30–40%), LFP vs NMC description and the 8-year warranty norm were not checked against official sources. Cross-checked in November 2026: GST rates (56th GST Council), Nexon EV (145 hp, 215 Nm, 489 km claimed, 10–100% in 6 h 36 min on 7.2 kW; Autocar India, CarDekho), BE 6 Sporteq (59/70/79 kWh, 548/651/683 km, price ₹20.20–27.70 lakh ex-showroom; Autocar India), PM E-DRIVE (Ministry of Heavy Industries notification, 10 August 2026). The earlier BE 6 power and torque figures (210 kW, 380 Nm) are from its 2024 launch and were not re-verified for the Sporteq. Fuel prices in Fig 2 are assumptions, not quotes. Charging losses (about 10%) are ignored. Break-even example uses made-up figures to show the method.

The PDF above carries the diagrams for this part.

==========

🔗 See also: the rest of the Automobile Engineering series (parts 1 to 12).

notes.title: Automobile Engineering 7/12 — Hybrids, CNG and Ethanol
notes.summary: Between a pure petrol car and a pure EV sit three alternatives. Hybrids add an electric motor and a small battery to a petrol engine, giving big efficiency gains in city traffic without any charging. CNG burns compressed natural gas: low fuel cost, with some loss of power and boot space.
notes.body:
🔧 HYBRIDS, CNG AND ETHANOL

==========

⚡ TL;DR

Between a pure petrol car and a pure EV sit three alternatives. Hybrids add an electric motor and a small battery to a petrol engine, giving big efficiency gains in city traffic without any charging. CNG burns compressed natural gas: low fuel cost, with some loss of power and boot space. Ethanol blended into petrol (E20 today) is mostly a national energy policy that affects your car slightly. On claimed figures the Honda City hybrid and the Toyota Hyryder hybrid return about 27 to 28 km/l, about 57% to 61% more than the 17.4 km/l petrol Creta, although these are different cars.

==========

🔧 1. THE HYBRID FAMILY

🔹 Mild hybrid: What it adds Small 48-volt motor assisting the engine; Can it drive on electric alone? No; Examples Mercedes C-Class (48V, up to 20 hp and 200 Nm boost).

🔹 Strong hybrid: What it adds Bigger motor and battery, can move the car alone; Can it drive on electric alone? Yes, at low speed; Examples Toyota Hyryder, Innova Hycross, Honda City e:HEV.

🔹 Plug-in hybrid (PHEV): What it adds Large battery you can charge from a socket; Can it drive on electric alone? Yes, for tens of km; Examples MG Hector PHEV.

Strong hybrids matter most to mass-market buyers because they need no plug. Their trick is to let the electric motor do the work the engine does worst: pulling away and crawling in traffic. The petrol engine then runs mostly at steady, efficient loads, and the motor recaptures braking energy that would otherwise be lost.

Both hybrids on sale in the 1.5-litre class use the Atkinson cycle, a variant in which the intake valve stays open longer so the engine uses less of the air it takes in each cycle, trading peak power for efficiency; the electric motor makes up the missing punch.* The numbers show how the two makers split the work (in PS, the metric horsepower used in brochures; 1 PS is about 0.986 bhp):

🔹 Engine: Toyota Hyryder hybrid 1.5 L, 3-cylinder; Honda City e:HEV 1.5 L, 4-cylinder (Atkinson cycle).

🔹 Engine power / torque: Toyota Hyryder hybrid 92.45 PS / 122 Nm; Honda City e:HEV 98 PS / 127 Nm.

🔹 Electric motor power / torque: Toyota Hyryder hybrid 80 PS / 114 Nm; Honda City e:HEV 109 PS / 253 Nm.

🔹 Combined power: Toyota Hyryder hybrid 115.56 PS (about 114 bhp); Honda City e:HEV 126 PS (about 124 bhp).

🔹 ARAI claimed efficiency: Toyota Hyryder hybrid 27.97 km/l; Honda City e:HEV 27.26 km/l.

The City's motor is stronger than its engine and does most of the driving in many conditions; Toyota's system is slightly more efficient on paper. The Innova Hycross hybrid uses a 2.0-litre engine plus motor for about 184 bhp of system output, so the same idea scales up to a family MPV (Part 1).

==========

🔩 2. CNG: CHEAP FUEL, SMALL PENALTIES

CNG is natural gas stored under high pressure in a steel cylinder. The engine runs on it with a modified fuel system and usually can switch back to petrol. The Maruti Swift S-CNG shows both the benefit and the cost:

🔹 Efficiency: 32.85 km/kg claimed (ARAI).

🔹 Power: about 69.75 PS (68.8 bhp) and 101.8 Nm, against 80.46 bhp and 111.7 Nm for the petrol engine, which is roughly 14% less power and 9% less torque.

🔹 Boot space: the gas cylinder usually takes up luggage room; some makers fit twin smaller cylinders to keep more boot (for example Tata's iCNG range, with two 30-litre tanks instead of one 60-litre tank).

🔹 Availability: CNG stations exist mainly in some cities and along certain corridors, so check your area before buying.

On these assumptions the CNG Swift costs under half as much per km as the petrol Creta. These are different cars, so compare like for like within one model before deciding; still, the gap is why CNG dominates taxi fleets and high-mileage family cars. The break-even logic of Part 6 applies again: divide the CNG price premium by the saving per km to see how many kilometres it takes to pay back.

==========

🎯 3. ETHANOL: E20 AND FLEX FUEL

Ethanol is alcohol made from sugarcane or grain. Petrol in India is now sold blended with 20% ethanol (E20), which is the standard pump fuel nationwide. Ethanol holds less energy per litre than petrol (roughly two-thirds), so E20 has about 7% less energy per litre than pure petrol, by this arithmetic: 0.8 × 100 + 0.2 × 66 ≈ 93.* India's petroleum ministry (August 2025) put the mileage loss at about 1–2% for E10-designed cars calibrated for E20 and 3–6% for others, and the transport minister told Parliament in July 2026 that the drop is 2–6%. Newer engines are calibrated for E20 (the Swift is listed as E20-compatible). Older cars may need compatible rubber hoses and seals over time.

Flex-fuel engines can run on any blend up to nearly pure ethanol. They are a policy bet to cut crude-oil imports and support farmers. Critics raise concerns about food-versus-fuel land use, water use and lower mileage; supporters point to import savings and lower tailpipe carbon.* Part 10 looks at how these policies shape the market.

==========

⛽ 4. WHICH ONE FOR WHOM

🔹 Mostly city driving, wants an automatic and low fuel bills with no charging: strong hybrid.

🔹 High annual kilometres on a tight budget, with a CNG station nearby: CNG.

🔹 Can charge at home and drives short distances: EV (Part 6).

🔹 Long highway runs, heavy loads: diesel or a plain efficient petrol still make sense (Part 2).

==========

📝 SUMMARY

🔹 Mild hybrids assist the engine; strong hybrids can drive on electric alone; plug-ins add a chargeable battery.

🔹 A strong hybrid shines in city traffic because the motor handles low-speed work and recovers braking energy.

🔹 The City e:HEV and Hyryder hybrid claim about 27–28 km/l, compared with 17.4 km/l for a petrol Creta.

🔹 CNG cuts fuel cost per km sharply (the Swift S-CNG costs under half the petrol Creta per km on claimed figures, though they are different cars) but costs about 14% of power and some boot space on the Swift.

🔹 E20 petrol carries about 7% less energy per litre; official estimates of mileage loss are 1–6%.

🔹 Match the fuel to your kilometres, traffic and access to CNG or charging, not to the headline mileage.

==========

➡️ NEXT: Part 8 of 12.

==========

*Unverified or general knowledge: Atkinson-cycle description, E27/E30 plans, ethanol energy content (about two-thirds of petrol, textbook value) and the critics-and-supporters summary of flex-fuel policy were not checked against official documents. Cross-checked in November 2026: Hyryder hybrid (92.45 PS engine, 80 PS motor, 115.56 PS combined, 27.97 km/l; Autocar India), City e:HEV (98 PS engine, 109 PS motor, 126 PS combined, 27.26 km/l; Honda Cars India), Swift S-CNG (32.85 km/kg, 69.75 PS, 101.8 Nm; Team-BHP, Spinny), E20 mileage statements (Petroleum Ministry August 2025; Parliament reply July 2026, via Tribune, DriveSpark). Fuel prices in Fig 2 are assumptions, not quotes. Innova Hycross hybrid system output of about 184 bhp (183.7 hp, 139 kW; Autocar India), the Tata Punch iCNG twin 30-litre tanks (Rushlane) and the MG Hector plug-in hybrid (Autocar India) were also cross-checked.

The PDF above carries the diagrams for this part.

==========

🔗 See also: the rest of the Automobile Engineering series (parts 1 to 12).

notes.title: Automobile Engineering 8/12 — Software, Connectivity and Driver Assistance
notes.summary: A modern car is a computer network on wheels. Dozens of small computers (ECUs) run the engine, brakes, airbags and screens, and talk to each other over an internal network.
notes.body:
🔧 SOFTWARE, CONNECTIVITY AND DRIVER ASSISTANCE

==========

⚡ TL;DR

A modern car is a computer network on wheels. Dozens of small computers (ECUs) run the engine, brakes, airbags and screens, and talk to each other over an internal network. Newer cars add internet connectivity for apps, remote functions and over-the-air (OTA) updates, and cameras and radars for ADAS (advanced driver assistance systems). In India the ADAS you can buy today is Level 2 on the international scale: the car can help with steering and speed, but you remain responsible. ADAS has reached mainstream prices (the Mahindra XUV 3XO offered Level 2 ADAS from ₹11.99 lakh, in its AX5 L variant, at its April 2024 launch), but it was designed for orderly roads, and Indian roads are not always orderly.

==========

🔧 1. THE CAR AS A NETWORK OF COMPUTERS

Each function has its own small computer, an electronic control unit (ECU): engine management, transmission, ABS and ESC, airbags, air conditioning, instrument cluster, infotainment. A premium car can have well over a hundred.* They share data over an in-vehicle network, usually the CAN bus, so that for example the wheel-speed signal used by ABS is also available to the stability controller and the speedometer. The diagnostic port under the dashboard (OBD) lets a mechanic read fault codes from these ECUs, and BS6 norms made on-board diagnostics stricter (Part 2).

The industry buzzword is the software-defined vehicle: features that were once fixed in hardware are controlled by software that can be updated, and in some cases unlocked later through a paid subscription. That changes the business model: a car can earn revenue after the sale, and it also means two cars with identical hardware can differ in what they let you use.

==========

🔩 2. CONNECTIVITY: FROM SCREENS TO OVER-THE-AIR UPDATES

🔹 Infotainment: touchscreen, Android Auto and Apple CarPlay, voice assistants and navigation. Screen size and speed of response are now top reasons people choose one variant over another.

🔹 Connected-car apps: a built-in SIM card links the car to a phone app for remote lock and unlock, location, climate pre-cooling and trip data. Most major brands offer one (Hyundai Bluelink, Kia Connect, MG iSMART, Tata iRA, Mahindra Adrenox, Maruti Suzuki Connect).*

🔹 OTA updates: like a phone, a car can download new software and fix bugs without a visit to the workshop. Some updates are minor (maps, screen layouts); others change how the car drives or charges.

The trade-offs: a connected car collects data about where you go and how you drive. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 applies to personal data collected this way; its Rules were notified on 14 November 2025, with the core compliance duties phased in over 18 months. For vehicles specifically, the road ministry issued draft rules in June 2026 that would make cybersecurity (AIS-189) and software-update management (AIS-190) mandatory, with Level 3 and higher vehicles first in line from October 2026 for new models. Those rules were still in draft at the time of writing. Anything online can in principle be attacked, so makers must secure the network. And long-term support matters: a car sold today must still receive updates in eight years.

==========

🎯 3. ADAS: HOW FAR AUTOMATION GOES

Engineers describe how much of the driving a car does with a six-level scale from SAE International, from Level 0 (nothing) to Level 5 (everything, everywhere).

At Level 2, the car can steer and control speed together, for example adaptive cruise control with lane centring. But the driver must keep watching and be ready to take over at once. Levels 3 to 5 would let the car take responsibility in some or all conditions; they are not yet part of ordinary Indian car sales.*

🔹 Autonomous emergency braking (AEB): brakes if a collision is imminent. It is the most valuable feature, as Part 5 notes.

🔹 Adaptive cruise control (ACC): keeps a set distance from the car in front, slowing and speeding up with traffic.

🔹 Lane departure warning and lane keep assist: alert you or nudge the steering if you drift.

🔹 Blind-spot monitoring and rear cross-traffic alert: warn about cars you cannot see.

🔹 Driver monitoring: a cabin camera detects drowsiness or distraction.

==========

⛽ 4. ADAS MEETS INDIAN ROADS

ADAS was largely developed on roads with clear lane markings, predictable traffic and few unexpected obstacles. In India, markings are often faded or missing, two-wheelers filter through gaps, pedestrians and animals appear suddenly, and construction zones change the road layout. Lane-keeping depends on seeing markings, and emergency braking can trigger falsely or miss an unusual obstacle. Makers tune systems for local conditions, but owners often report that features behave inconsistently, so expect assistance, not autopilot.*

==========

🧪 5. A BUYER'S CHECKLIST

🔹 Check which ADAS functions are included and in which variant; the same name can cover very different feature sets.

🔹 Test them in real traffic on a test drive, not only on an empty road.

🔹 Ask how long software updates are supported and whether any features need a subscription.

🔹 Read the data and privacy terms of the connected-car app.

🔹 Treat ADAS as a safety net, not a replacement for attention.

==========

📝 SUMMARY

🔹 A car is a network of ECUs sharing data over a CAN bus; software increasingly defines what the car can do.

🔹 Connectivity brings apps, remote features and OTA updates, and raises questions about data, security and long-term support.

🔹 ADAS on sale in India is Level 2: the car assists, the driver stays responsible.

🔹 AEB is the most valuable ADAS feature; others add comfort.

🔹 Indian road conditions challenge systems designed for orderly roads; test them in real traffic.

==========

➡️ NEXT: Part 9 of 12.

==========

*Unverified or general knowledge: the number of ECUs in premium cars, the list of connected-car brands, the absence of Level 3+ cars in ordinary Indian sale (the draft rules cover such vehicles, but I found no confirmation of any on sale) and the statements on how ADAS behaves on Indian roads are general knowledge or reported owner experience, not tested here. Cross-checked in November 2026: the XUV 3XO launched on 29 April 2024 at an introductory ₹7.49 lakh for the base MX1 variant, which has no ADAS; the cheapest ADAS variant at launch was the AX5 L at ₹11.99 lakh (Autocar India, Mahindra press release); current range ₹7.79–15.04 lakh. SAE levels: SAE International standard J3016. DPDP Rules 2025 timeline (India Briefing) and the June 2026 draft cybersecurity and software-update rules (Autocar India) were also cross-checked.

notes.title: Automobile Engineering 9/12 — Platforms, Manufacturing and Supply Chain, and How to Read a Spec Sheet
notes.summary: A car company's biggest costs are fixed: developing the car and building the plant. So makers share a platform (the floor, suspension mounts and electrical architecture) across many models, so that one development bill is spread over lakhs of cars.
notes.body:
🔧 PLATFORMS, MANUFACTURING AND SUPPLY CHAIN, AND HOW TO READ A SPEC SHEET

==========

⚡ TL;DR

A car company's biggest costs are fixed: developing the car and building the plant. So makers share a platform (the floor, suspension mounts and electrical architecture) across many models, so that one development bill is spread over lakhs of cars. Inside a plant, steel becomes a body, the body is painted, the powertrain is fitted and the car is inspected. Behind the plant sits a supply chain of thousands of parts suppliers, which is where disruptions (chips, rare-earth magnets, battery cells) hit. The chapter ends with a practical skill: how to read a spec sheet and turn its numbers into meaning.

==========

🔧 1. PLATFORMS: ONE DESIGN, MANY CARS

A platform is the shared underbody and its engineering: wheelbase options, mounting points for engine and suspension, crash structure and wiring. Cars on one platform can look and feel quite different (hatchback, sedan, SUV) while sharing many unseen parts. The economics are the point: if developing a platform costs ₹2,000 crore (an illustrative number) and it underpins 5 lakh cars, development adds ₹40,000 to each car; on 1 lakh cars it adds ₹2 lakh. Break-even volume = fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost per car), so volume is what makes a car profitable.

🔹 Heartect: Maker Maruti Suzuki; Cars built on it (examples) Swift, Dzire.

🔹 ALFA-ARC: Maker Tata Motors; Cars built on it (examples) Punch, Altroz (petrol).

🔹 acti.ev: Maker Tata Motors; Cars built on it (examples) Punch.ev (first car on it).

🔹 INGLO: Maker Mahindra; Cars built on it (examples) BE 6, XEV 9e (electric, rear-motor layout).

🔹 MQB-A0-IN: Maker Volkswagen Group (Skoda, VW); Cars built on it (examples) Kushaq, Slavia, Taigun, Virtus.

🔹 TNGA GA-C*: Maker Toyota; Cars built on it (examples) Innova Hycross.

Notice the electric platforms: Tata and Mahindra built dedicated EV platforms (acti.ev, INGLO) rather than modifying petrol cars. A purpose-built floor lets the battery sit flat under the cabin, which improves space and handling (Part 6).

==========

🔩 2. INSIDE A CAR PLANT

🔹 Press shop: giant presses stamp steel coils into doors, roofs and floors.

🔹 Body shop: robots weld hundreds of panels into the body-in-white. Weld quality decides crash strength.

🔹 Paint shop: the body is cleaned, rust-proofed and coated; this is the most energy- and water-intensive stage.

🔹 Powertrain: engines and gearboxes are made or assembled (or, for EVs, battery packs and motors), usually in a separate line or plant.

🔹 Final assembly: the body and powertrain are 'married'; seats, wiring, glass and wheels are fitted on a moving line.

🔹 Quality and PDI: tests, inspection and a pre-delivery inspection before the car goes to a dealer.

Major Indian plants include Maruti Suzuki's at Manesar and Gurugram, Tata's at Sanand, Mahindra's at Chakan and Hyundai's near Chennai.* Plant capacity, shifts and how fast a model can be sold set a car's waiting period.

==========

🎯 3. THE SUPPLY CHAIN

A car has around 30,000 parts.* The maker designs, assembles and brands the car, but buys most parts from suppliers. Tier 1 suppliers (seats, electronics, transmissions) deliver complete systems to the plant; Tier 2 and Tier 3 supply components and raw materials to them. A shortage anywhere stops the line.

🔹 Localisation: the share of parts made in India. Higher localisation cuts import duty, currency risk and cost, and is a stated goal of programmes such as the government's production-linked incentive (PLI) scheme for the auto sector (approved in September 2021 with an outlay of about ₹26,000 crore).

🔹 Semiconductors: the chip shortage of 2021–22 forced several makers to cut production and extended waiting periods.*

🔹 EV-specific risks: battery cells and rare-earth magnets (used in many EV motors) are largely imported, so EV costs and supply are exposed to overseas policy and prices.*

🔹 Just-in-time: many suppliers deliver hours before parts are needed, which keeps stock low but makes disruptions costly.

==========

⛽ 4. HOW TO READ A SPEC SHEET

A spec sheet is a list of numbers; the skill is to ask what each one tells you. Use the Swift's figures from earlier parts as an example.

🔹 Engine cc, cylinders, aspiration: What it tells you Size and style of the engine (Part 1); Swift example and what to watch 1,197 cc, 3 cylinders, natural. Compare power per litre, not cc..

🔹 Power (bhp @ rpm): What it tells you Top-end performance (Part 2); Swift example and what to watch 80.46 bhp @ 5,700 rpm: you must rev to use it..

🔹 Torque (Nm @ rpm): What it tells you Pulling strength and its spread; Swift example and what to watch 111.7 Nm @ 4,300 rpm: a narrow, higher-rpm peak..

🔹 Kerb weight: What it tells you Power-to-weight, efficiency; Swift example and what to watch About 925 kg (listing)*, so about 87 bhp per tonne..

🔹 Transmission: What it tells you How it drives (Part 3); Swift example and what to watch 5-speed manual or 5-speed AMT..

🔹 ARAI mileage: What it tells you Comparison tool, not a promise (Part 2); Swift example and what to watch Expect real figures well below the claim..

🔹 Fuel tank: What it tells you Range = tank × real km/l; Swift example and what to watch 37 litres (listing)..

🔹 Boot space: What it tells you Luggage practicality; Swift example and what to watch 265 litres (listing)..

🔹 Ground clearance, turning radius: What it tells you Rough-road ability, city manoeuvres (Part 4); Swift example and what to watch Check both on the brochure..

🔹 Airbags, ESC, NCAP score: What it tells you Safety (Part 5); Swift example and what to watch Variant matters; check the tested version..

Two derived numbers are worth computing for any car. Specific output (power ÷ litres) compares engines of different sizes: the Swift manages 67 bhp per litre, the Nexon 1.2 turbo 99 and the Creta turbo 107. Power-to-weight (power ÷ tonnes) compares how lively cars feel: the Swift's 87 bhp per tonne is a good benchmark for a small, light car.* Together with torque spread, these two numbers explain most of what you will feel on a test drive.

==========

📝 SUMMARY

🔹 A platform is the shared underbody; reusing it spreads fixed development costs across many cars.

🔹 Break-even volume = fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost); volume decides profit.

🔹 A plant runs press shop, body shop, paint shop, powertrain, final assembly and quality checks.

🔹 Supply chains run in tiers; chips, rare-earth magnets and battery cells are the big risks.

🔹 Read a spec sheet by asking what each number implies; compute specific output and power-to-weight.

🔹 Always compare the exact variant: airbags, gearbox and weight differ by trim.

==========

➡️ NEXT: Part 10 of 12.

==========

*Unverified or general knowledge: the TNGA GA-C platform name for the Hycross, ALFA-ARC and acti.ev details, the plant locations, the number of parts in a car, the 2021–22 semiconductor shortage and EV-component import exposure, and the Swift's kerb weight (from a listing) were not checked against official documents. The ₹2,000 crore platform cost and volumes are made-up numbers to show the arithmetic. Cross-checked in November 2026: INGLO (BE 6, rear motor), MQB-A0-IN (Kushaq, Slavia, Taigun, Virtus) and Heartect (Dzire). Spec-sheet figures: Wikipedia and Autocar India listings. The auto PLI scheme (approved September 2021, about ₹26,000 crore; Business Standard) was cross-checked in November 2026.

The PDF above carries the diagrams for this part.

==========

🔗 See also: the rest of the Automobile Engineering series (parts 1 to 12).

notes.summary: India sold about 47 lakh passenger vehicles in FY2026 (SIAM wholesale 46.43 lakh, +7.9%; FADA retail 47.05 lakh, +13.0%). Maruti has about 39% but is losing share; utility vehicles are 67% of wholesale and EVs reached 4.25% of retail.
notes.body:
🔧 THE INDIAN CAR MARKET TODAY

==========

⚡ TL;DR

India sold about 47 lakh passenger vehicles in FY2026 (April 2025 to March 2026). Official SIAM wholesale was 46,43,439 units (+7.9%); FADA retail registrations were 47,05,056 (+13.0%). Maruti Suzuki still sells nearly two in five cars (about 39% share), but its share is slipping as Mahindra, Tata, Toyota and Skoda grow and Hyundai shrinks. The market is concentrated: three makers hold two-thirds of sales. Utility vehicles (SUVs plus MPVs) were 67% of wholesale. Electric cars reached 4.25% of FY2026 retail and were 7–9% of monthly sales by September–October 2026. As of November 2026, the numbers below are verified against SIAM, FADA and trade compilations; sources differ slightly.

==========

🔧 1. HOW BIG IS THE MARKET, AND WHICH NUMBER TO USE

Two data sets are used in India, and they answer different questions:

🔹 Wholesale (dispatches): cars the maker sent to dealers, reported monthly by SIAM and company statements. SIAM's official FY2026 figure is 46,43,439 units, up 7.9%. A trade compilation by Rushlane gives 46,83,208 (+8.4% on 43.2 lakh in FY2025); the maker shares in Section 2 use that compilation, because SIAM does not publish maker-wise numbers in the same form.

🔹 Retail (registrations): cars actually registered to buyers, from the government's VAHAN database via FADA. FY2026 came to 47,05,056, up 13.00% on 41.64 lakh. FADA's retail leaders: Maruti 18,68,386 (39.71%), Mahindra 6,31,638, Tata 6,13,513, Hyundai 5,78,337.

The two differ because dealer stock rises and falls. If makers dispatch more than dealers sell, stock builds up; wholesale grows faster than retail. A manager should read both: retail shows real demand, wholesale shows what the factories were doing.

==========

🔩 2. WHO SELLS WHAT: FY2026 MARKET SHARE

🔹 Maruti Suzuki: FY26 units 18,23,130; FY26 share 38.93%; Change in units +3.5%.

🔹 Mahindra: FY26 units 6,60,276; FY26 share 14.10%; Change in units +19.7%.

🔹 Tata Motors: FY26 units 6,31,387; FY26 share 13.48%; Change in units +14.1%.

🔹 Hyundai: FY26 units 5,84,906; FY26 share 12.49%; Change in units −2.3%.

🔹 Toyota: FY26 units 3,67,152; FY26 share 7.84%; Change in units +18.6%.

🔹 Kia: FY26 units 2,89,035; FY26 share 6.17%; Change in units +13.3%.

🔹 Skoda: FY26 units 75,555; FY26 share about 1.6%; Change in units +68.4%.

Other FY2026 movements: MG grew 17.3%, Honda fell 6.0% and Volkswagen fell 11.0%. VinFast, a new entrant, had 2,390 retail registrations (FADA) covering part of its first year in India. Maruti's wholesale share fell from about 40.8% to 38.9%.

==========

🎯 3. A CONCENTRATED MARKET

🔹 The top three makers (Maruti, Mahindra, Tata) hold 66.5% of the market; the top five add Hyundai and Toyota to reach 86.8%.

🔹 A standard concentration measure, the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (sum of squared shares), is about 2,150 from the six largest makers alone, a level that competition regulators in the US treat as highly concentrated (above 1,800).*

🔹 In the retail data, Mahindra ranked second for the full year, about 18,000 cars ahead of Tata; in the January–June 2026 data, Tata (14.6%) was ahead of Mahindra (13.8%). Rankings flip between periods, so always state the period.

For a manager, the message is that scale advantages (platforms, dealer networks, supplier leverage) are large, and Mahindra and Tata, whose lineups are mostly SUVs, grew faster than the overall market (19.7% and 14.1% against 8.4%).

==========

⛽ 4. WHAT ACTUALLY SELLS: BEST-SELLING MODELS

This is a selection, not a ranked top eight (Dzire, Punch, Nexon, Ertiga, WagonR and Creta are confirmed; Scorpio and Thar* are unverified, and other models may sit in between). Among these, five are SUVs (Punch, Nexon, Creta, Scorpio, Thar), one is a sedan (Dzire), one is an MPV (Ertiga) and one is a hatchback (WagonR). The Tata Punch topped annual sales in 2024 with 2,02,030 units, ending Maruti's long hold on the top spot. The picture moved again in April–September 2026 (H1 FY27): the Dzire (1,25,988) led the Punch (1,23,287) by only 2,701 units, followed by the Ertiga (1,12,557) and Nexon (1,11,919); the Creta sold 89,727 (−9.7%).

==========

🧪 5. FORCES SHAPING THE MARKET

🔹 SUV shift: buyers keep moving up from hatchbacks to compact and mid-size SUVs. Utility vehicles (SUVs plus MPVs) were 67% of FY2026 wholesale, up from 65% in FY2025, and about 68% in the first quarter of FY2027.

🔹 Tax (GST 2.0): from 22 September 2025, small petrol cars (up to 1,200 cc and 4 m) and small diesels (up to 1,500 cc) moved to 18% GST from 28%; larger cars moved to 40% with the compensation cess abolished; EVs stay at 5%; hybrids follow the same thresholds as petrol cars. This lowered the effective tax on small cars most. None of the sources I retrieved quantify its effect on sales.

🔹 Fuel choices: EVs were 1,99,923 retail units in FY2026 (4.25%, up from 2.61%), CNG was 21.98%. In 2026 EV share was 8.5–8.7% in September and 7.3% in October (36,640 units), with hybrids at 9.94% in October; January–October EV registrations totalled 2,87,453. Parts 6 and 7 cover these.

🔹 Safety: Bharat NCAP and Global NCAP ratings (Part 5) are now a marketing weapon, and six airbags are becoming common.

🔹 New entrants: VinFast and Chinese-linked brands such as MG show that capital and product can disrupt a concentrated market.

==========

🔄 6. HOW A MANAGER SHOULD READ THESE NUMBERS

🔹 Always note period (FY vs calendar half) and data type (wholesale vs retail).

🔹 Share is zero-sum; look at units and growth to see who is actually growing.

🔹 Look at models, not just brands: a few models carry a brand (Dzire, Punch, Nexon, Ertiga).

🔹 Policy changes (GST, safety rules, fuel norms) move demand faster than product launches.

==========

📝 SUMMARY

🔹 India sold about 47 lakh passenger vehicles in FY2026 (SIAM wholesale 46.43 lakh, +7.9%; FADA retail 47.05 lakh, +13.0%).

🔹 Maruti has about 39% but is losing share; Mahindra, Tata, Toyota and Skoda are growing, Hyundai is shrinking.

🔹 The market is concentrated: the top three hold 66.5%.

🔹 Compact SUVs dominate the best-seller list; utility vehicles are 67% of wholesale.

🔹 GST cuts, safety ratings, hybrids/CNG and EVs are the main forces to watch.

🔹 Always state the period and the data source when quoting market share.

==========

➡️ NEXT: Part 11 of 12.

==========

*Unverified or general knowledge: the HHI threshold is the US antitrust guideline value and is applied here as a rough indicator; the Scorpio (89,375) and Thar (67,252) H1 2026 figures could not be independently verified. Cross-checked in November 2026: SIAM FY2026 wholesale (46,43,439, +7.9%), FADA FY2026 retail (47,05,056, +13.00%; Maruti 18,68,386, 39.71%), maker table (Rushlane wholesale compilation, 46,83,208), Dzire, Punch, Nexon, Ertiga, WagonR and Creta H1 2026 figures, April–September 2026 model ranking, Punch 2024 sales (2,02,030), utility-vehicle share, EV share and GST rates (PIB, India Briefing). Maker and period data differ across sources; units and shares may be revised. For reference, the Mahindra Thar (3-door) sold 25,424 units in April–September 2026 (Autocar India) and the Scorpio 17,313 in September 2026 alone (AutoPunditz); neither covers the January–June 2026 window used in Fig 2.

The PDF above carries the diagrams for this part.

==========

🔗 See also: the rest of the Automobile Engineering series (parts 1 to 12).

notes.title: Automobile Engineering 11/12 — How to Buy a Car
notes.summary: Buying a car well is a sequence of decisions: a real budget, a body type, a fuel matched to your kilometres, safety non-negotiables, a shortlist of three, the right variant, then finance and negotiation. Over five years, depreciation is usually the biggest single cost.
notes.body:
🔧 HOW TO BUY A CAR

==========

⚡ TL;DR

Buying a car well is a sequence of decisions, not one: budget (on-road price and five-year cost, not the ex-showroom headline), need (body type and seats), fuel and tech (matched to your kilometres and charging access), safety (non-negotiables), a shortlist of three with real test drives, the right variant, then finance, insurance and negotiation. The numbers in this chapter use stated assumptions, so replace them with your own quotes. A key insight: over five years, depreciation (the fall in the car's value) is usually the largest single cost, bigger than fuel.

==========

🔧 1. START WITH THE REAL BUDGET

The ex-showroom price is not what you pay. Taxes and charges add roughly 15% or more.* The chart builds an on-road price for a ₹12 lakh ex-showroom car using assumed rates; yours will differ by state and variant.

🔹 Road tax and registration: paid to the state, varies a lot (some states waive it for EVs).*

🔹 Insurance: third-party insurance is compulsory by law; comprehensive cover adds protection for your own car.

🔹 TCS: tax collected at source of 1% applies on cars costing more than ₹10 lakh (Section 394 of the Income-tax Act, 2025; earlier Section 206C(1F)).

🔹 Extras: accessories, extended warranty, FASTag, handling charges. Ask for an itemised quote and drop anything you do not want.

Then set a ceiling for monthly cost. A common personal-finance rule of thumb is that your car EMI should be no more than about 15% of take-home pay, and total car costs (EMI, fuel, insurance, service) no more than 10% to 15%.* Treat these as starting points, not laws.

==========

🔩 2. CHOOSE BODY TYPE AND SIZE BY NEED

🔹 Hatchback: cheapest, easiest to park and run; best for city use and small families.

🔹 Sedan: smoother ride and a separate boot; falling out of fashion but strong in value (the Dzire is the top seller in Part 10).

🔹 Compact SUV: higher seating, ground clearance (Part 4), good for mixed Indian roads; the best-selling category.

🔹 MPV: three rows, for large families or fleet use (Ertiga, Innova Hycross).

🔹 Larger SUV or 4x4: highway comfort, space, off-road ability (Part 3); higher cost and running cost.

==========

🎯 3. CHOOSE FUEL AND TECHNOLOGY BY YOUR KILOMETRES

The right powertrain depends on how far you drive and what you can access. Use this table as a start, then do the break-even sum below.

🔹 Drive under about 8,000 km a year: Consider Petrol; Why Lowest purchase price; savings of other fuels rarely pay back.

🔹 Drive 12,000 km or more, mostly in the city: Consider Strong hybrid, CNG; Why Lower fuel bill per km (Part 7).

🔹 Can charge at home and drive mostly locally: Consider EV; Why Cheapest per km (Part 6).

🔹 Drive long highway distances, carry loads: Consider Diesel or efficient petrol; Why Torque and efficiency at steady speed (Part 2).

Break-even = extra price ÷ saving per km. Suppose the CNG version costs ₹90,000 more (an assumed premium) and saves ₹2 per km: you need 45,000 km to recover it, about 3.75 years at 12,000 km a year. If you will sell the car sooner, the premium may not pay back.

==========

⛽ 4. SET YOUR SAFETY NON-NEGOTIABLES

🔹 Six airbags, ESC and ISOFIX child-seat anchors as standard on the variant you buy (Part 5).

🔹 Check the NCAP rating for that variant, the protocol and the year.

🔹 Treat ADAS as a bonus, not a substitute (Part 8).

==========

🧪 5. SHORTLIST THREE, THEN TEST DRIVE PROPERLY

🔹 Ride over a speed breaker: How 20–30 km/h on a rough road; What it tells you Suspension comfort and clearance (Part 4).

🔹 Pulling away and overtaking: How From low speed, then at 60–80 km/h; What it tells you Torque spread and gearbox response (Parts 2–3).

🔹 Traffic crawl: How In stop-go conditions if possible; What it tells you Clutch effort or automatic smoothness.

🔹 Cabin and boot: How Sit in the back; pack your usual luggage; What it tells you Space and comfort for everyone.

🔹 Noise and vibration: How At idle and at 80 km/h; What it tells you Refinement; three-cylinder vs four (Part 1).

🔹 Visibility, controls, screen: How Park it; What it tells you Daily usability.

==========

🔄 6. PICK THE VARIANT

Variants of one model can differ by lakhs of rupees. Base variants often lack safety and convenience items; top variants add features that cost more than they are worth to many buyers. A common approach is to choose the mid-level variant that has the safety items you need, the gearbox you want and the screen and features you will actually use.* Check that the airbag count and ESC match what you read about the model.

==========

🌱 7. FINANCE, INSURANCE AND NEGOTIATION

A car loan's monthly instalment is: EMI = P × r × (1+r)n ÷ ((1+r)n − 1), where P is the loan, r the monthly rate and n the number of months. For ₹8 lakh at 9% a year (an assumed rate), the EMI is about ₹25,440 over 3 years, ₹16,607 over 5 years and ₹12,871 over 7 years. The longer the loan, the lower the EMI but the more interest you pay:

🔹 Down payment: a larger down payment cuts interest; avoid stretching tenure just to get a lower EMI.

🔹 Compare lenders: bank, dealer and NBFC rates vary; ask for the full cost including processing fees.

🔹 Insurance: compare comprehensive quotes from several insurers, not only the dealer's; consider a zero-depreciation add-on for a new car.*

🔹 Negotiate the whole deal: ask for the discount, free accessories or exchange bonus in writing; check waiting periods and the delivery date.

🔹 Inspect at delivery (PDI): check paint, panels, VIN, odometer reading, spare wheel and documents before you pay the balance.

==========

🛠️ 8. THE REAL COST OF OWNING A CAR

Total cost of ownership (TCO) = on-road price + fuel + service + insurance renewals + interest − resale value. A five-year illustration, with every number assumed (60,000 km at ₹6 per km for fuel, 50% resale of the ex-showroom price):

🔹 On-road price: ₹ lakh 13.94; Note From Fig 1.

🔹 Fuel: ₹ lakh 3.60; Note 60,000 km × ₹6.

🔹 Service and tyres: ₹ lakh 0.60; Note Assumed.

🔹 Insurance renewals (years 2–5): ₹ lakh 1.60; Note Assumed ₹0.40 lakh a year.

🔹 Loan interest: ₹ lakh 1.96; Note ₹8 lakh at 9%, 5 years.

🔹 Less: resale value: ₹ lakh −6.00; Note Assumed 50% of ex-showroom.

🔹 Net cost of ownership: ₹ lakh 15.70; Note About ₹3.1 lakh a year, about ₹26 per km.

In this example depreciation (on-road price minus resale value, ₹7.94 lakh) is about half of the net cost, while fuel is about one-sixth of gross outflows. That is why resale value matters as much as mileage when you compare two cars.* Cars with strong resale (often those from large, established brands) can cost less to own even if their price is higher.

==========

📝 SUMMARY

🔹 Budget on the on-road price and the five-year cost, not the ex-showroom headline.

🔹 Choose body type by need, and fuel by annual kilometres using break-even = extra price ÷ saving per km.

🔹 Make six airbags, ESC and ISOFIX non-negotiable on the variant you buy.

🔹 Test drive three cars on real roads and check ride, pull, traffic comfort, space and noise.

🔹 EMI falls as tenure rises, but interest paid rises sharply; keep the loan short.

🔹 Depreciation is often the largest ownership cost; resale value belongs in the comparison.

==========

➡️ NEXT: Part 12 of 12, the complete series in one PDF.

==========

*Unverified or general knowledge: the 15% on-road uplift, road-tax variation and EV waivers by state, the 15% and 10–15% personal-finance rules of thumb, the mid-variant heuristic, insurance add-on advice and the resale remark are general knowledge, not checked against official documents or your own quotes. The 1% TCS rule was cross-checked in November 2026 (TaxGuru, TDSMAN). Every rupee figure in this chapter (road tax 10%, insurance 3.5%, ₹0.20 lakh extras, 9% loan rate, ₹6 per km fuel, ₹90,000 CNG premium, 50% resale, service cost) is an assumption to show the method. The EMI formula is standard. Check current taxes and rates before deciding.

The PDF above carries the diagrams for this part.

==========

🔗 See also: the rest of the Automobile Engineering series (parts 1 to 12).
