notes.title: Rocketry with ISRO 0/7 — How Rockets Work
notes.summary: The basics of how a rocket flies, using NASA Glenn's Beginner's Guide to Rockets for the theory and ISRO's LVM3 for every worked number. Covers Newton's laws, the four forces, the four systems of a launch vehicle, solid versus liquid engines and staging. Four hand-solvable examples show that LVM3 must produce over 6.28 MN just to leave the pad, that 86% of its 640 t lift-off mass is propellant, and that only 1.25% reaches low Earth orbit as payload. The attached 13-page A4 PDF has the diagrams, practice problems, glossary and answer key for printing.
notes.body:
🚀 ROCKETRY WITH ISRO, CHAPTER 0: HOW ROCKETS WORK

==========

⚡ TL;DR

A rocket moves by throwing mass backwards. The hot gas it throws is pushed back, and the rocket is pushed forward with an equal force. That is why it works in empty space, where a jet engine or propeller cannot.

Four forces act on it (weight, thrust, drag, lift), it is built from four systems (structural, payload, guidance, propulsion), and it uses one of two engine types (solid or liquid). Almost every number in the chapter is worked out on ISRO's LVM3.

The headline result: about 86% of LVM3's lift-off mass is propellant, and only about 1.25% reaches low Earth orbit as payload.

The theory is from NASA Glenn's Beginner's Guide to Rockets. The ISRO figures are the nominal values published by ISRO, checked on 9 November 2026. The diagrams, worked examples, practice problems, glossary and answer key are in the attached 13-page A4 PDF, made for printing.

==========

🔁 1. WHY A ROCKET MOVES

Newton's three laws: a body keeps its motion unless a force acts on it (inertia); force equals mass times acceleration (F = m × a); and every action has an equal and opposite reaction.

The third law is the engine. The rocket burns propellant, the hot gas is flung out of the back, and the gas pushes the rocket the other way. NASA calls that gas the working fluid. A jet engine uses the surrounding air as its working fluid. A rocket carries its fuel and its oxygen source (the oxidiser) and uses its own exhaust, so it works in a vacuum. That is the biggest difference between a rocket and an aircraft.

The second law gives the motion. If thrust is bigger than weight, the rocket accelerates upward. One caution: F = m × a holds only for constant mass, and a rocket burns away most of its mass. The full treatment is in Chapter 2.

The first law explains the coast. LVM3 puts its satellite into a 180 × 36,000 km transfer orbit about 974 seconds after lift-off. After that no engine pushes the satellite. Inertia and gravity carry it the rest of the way.

==========

⚖️ 2. THE FOUR FORCES

Weight (m × g) pulls towards the Earth's centre through the centre of gravity (CG).

Thrust is the engine's push, normally along the rocket's axis. Swivelling the nozzle (gimballing) points it slightly off the CG line, which steers the rocket.

Drag is air resistance along the flight path. It acts through the centre of pressure (CP).

Lift on a rocket is not an aircraft's lift. It is the aerodynamic side force from fins and body, which helps point and steer it.

NASA lists four differences from an aircraft. An aircraft uses lift to beat weight; a rocket uses thrust. An aircraft makes its air forces with wings and tail; a rocket with fins, nose and body. An aircraft has far more lift than drag; a rocket usually has far more drag than lift. And a rocket's forces change dramatically in flight, because it burns most of its mass, speeds up and climbs into thinner air.

THE ONE NUMBER TO KNOW: thrust-to-weight (T/W). Below 1 the rocket cannot leave the ground. Above 1, and ignoring drag:

a = (T/W − 1) × g

With T/W = 1.5, a = 0.5 × 9.81 ≈ 4.9 m/s².

==========

🧱 3. THE FOUR SYSTEMS

Structural: the frame, fairings and fins. Strong yet light, and partly discarded along the way.

Payload: whatever the mission carries. It is the reason the rocket exists.

Guidance: sensors, computers and communications that keep the rocket stable and steer it.

Propulsion: engines, tanks, pumps, propellant and nozzle. In a full-size rocket this is most of what you see.

ISRO describes LVM3 as three stages plus the equipment bay and the encapsulated assembly (satellite, adaptor and fairing). It is 43.5 m tall, lifts off at 640 tonnes and carries 8 t to low Earth orbit or 4 t to geosynchronous transfer orbit.

==========

🔥 4. TWO KINDS OF ENGINE

Liquid engine: fuel and oxidiser in separate tanks, pumped into a combustion chamber. Heavier and more complex, but you can control or stop it.

Solid engine: fuel and oxidiser mixed and cast into one block (the grain). Simple, easy to handle, but once lit it burns until used up.

Either way the hot gas leaves through a nozzle, which turns heat into fast-moving exhaust.

LVM3 uses each where it fits. Two S200 solid boosters give the huge, simple push at lift-off. A liquid core stage, the L110 with two Vikas engines, takes over the long middle of the climb. The upper stage, the C25, is cryogenic: liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen kept extremely cold, burned in the CE-20 engine. PSLV alternates solid, liquid, solid, liquid across four stages.

==========

🪜 5. SHEDDING WEIGHT: STAGING

Reaching low Earth orbit takes roughly 9 to 10 km/s once gravity and drag losses are counted. An empty tank is dead weight you are still accelerating. Staging drops the empty parts so the remaining engines push less mass.

LVM3's nominal flight:

1️⃣ 113 s: the L110 core ignites at 41.5 km, while the boosters still burn.
2️⃣ 137 s: the two spent S200 boosters separate (they burned about 134 s).
3️⃣ 217 s: the fairing is jettisoned at 115 km, where the air is thin enough.
4️⃣ 313 s: the L110 burns out and separates; the C25 ignites.
5️⃣ 974 s: the satellite is injected into its 180 × 36,000 km transfer orbit.

==========

🧮 6. FOUR WORKED EXAMPLES ON LVM3

Data (ISRO): lift-off mass 640 t; S200 about 205 t of propellant each; L110 115 t; C25 28 t with a dry mass of 4,310 kg and a nominal thrust of 200 kN; burn times about 134 s, 200 s and 646 s. Use g = 9.81 m/s².

A. WHAT MUST THE BOOSTERS BEAT AT LIFT-OFF?
W = 640,000 × 9.81 = 6,278,400 N ≈ 6.28 MN. LVM3 lifts off on the two S200s alone, so together they must produce more than 6.28 MN, or over 3.14 MN each, just to hold the vehicle on the pad.

B. HOW MUCH IS PROPELLANT?
2 × 205 + 115 + 28 = 553 t. Share = 553 / 640 = 86.4%. Everything else (structure, engines, payload) is 87 t, or 13.6%. Payload to LEO is 8 / 640 = 1.25%, and to GTO 4 / 640 = 0.625%. Of every 100 kg on the pad, about 86 kg is propellant to be burnt and about 1.25 kg reaches low orbit as payload.

C. HOW FAST DOES IT BURN?
Average mass flow = propellant mass / burn time. One S200: 205,000 / 134 ≈ 1,530 kg/s. Both: about 3,060 kg/s. L110: 115,000 / 200 = 575 kg/s. C25: 28,000 / 646 ≈ 43 kg/s. At lift-off the two boosters burn about 3 tonnes of propellant every second, and each one burns about 35 times faster than the C25. Thrust equals mass flow times exhaust speed, which Chapter 1 uses.

D. CAN AN UPPER STAGE LIFT ITS OWN WEIGHT?
C25 mass = 28,000 + 4,310 = 32,310 kg. Weight = 32,310 × 9.81 ≈ 317 kN. T/W = 200 / 317 ≈ 0.63. Below 1, which is normal: it ignites high up and already moving fast, so it never has to hold itself up from rest.

==========

📌 7. SUMMARY

1️⃣ A rocket throws its own exhaust backwards, so it needs no air.
2️⃣ Four forces act on it: weight, thrust, drag and lift. Lift is only a steering side force.
3️⃣ T/W above 1 is needed to leave the pad: a = (T/W − 1) × g.
4️⃣ Four systems: structural, payload, guidance, propulsion. Propulsion is most of the vehicle.
5️⃣ Solid engines are simple and cannot be switched off; liquid engines are complex and controllable.
6️⃣ About 86% of LVM3's lift-off mass is propellant and about 1.25% reaches low orbit as payload. Staging drops dead weight to improve that.

➡️ NEXT: Chapter 1, Thrust and specific impulse. We turn "throw mass backwards" into a formula and find out why a cryogenic stage with a slow burn beats a booster that burns 35 times faster.

==========

* Asterisk = a figure from a public source rather than ISRO. The PSLV-XL lift-off mass of about 320 t used in the practice problems is a public-source figure, and public sources disagree on PSLV stage data. LVM3 figures are ISRO's nominal published values and vary slightly by mission. Burn rates are averages from nominal burn times; a real solid motor's flow rises and tails off. The T/W = 1.5 case is a what-if, not an ISRO figure.

Theory: NASA Glenn Research Center, Beginner's Guide to Rockets. ISRO data: ISRO's LVM3 launch vehicle page.

==========

🔗 The PDF has all the diagrams, six practice problems, a glossary and the answer key. Coming next: Rocketry with ISRO 1/7 — Thrust and Specific Impulse.

notes.title: Rocketry with ISRO 1/7 — Thrust and Specific Impulse
notes.summary: How a rocket's push is calculated and why some stages are more efficient than others. Covers the thrust equation, specific impulse, the nozzle and why liquid hydrogen gives the best exhaust speed, with every number worked on ISRO's LVM3. Rebuilding thrust from burn rate and Isp matches published values to within a few percent, and for the same total push the cryogenic C25 burns 38% less propellant than an S200 booster. The attached 10-page A4 PDF has diagrams, practice problems, glossary and answer key for printing.
notes.body:
🚀 ROCKETRY WITH ISRO, CHAPTER 1: THRUST AND SPECIFIC IMPULSE

==========

⚡ TL;DR

Thrust is mass flow times exhaust speed: F ≈ ṁ × vₑ. Specific impulse (Isp) is the fuel-economy number: thrust per unit weight of propellant burnt each second, in seconds. Higher is better.

LVM3's three stages show the trade-off. The solid S200 boosters burn 1,530 kg/s each at about 2.7 km/s exhaust speed. The cryogenic C25 burns just 43 kg/s at about 4.3 km/s. For the same total push, the C25 burns 38% less propellant.

Theory is from NASA Glenn's Beginner's Guide to Rockets. Propellant masses, burn times and C25 thrust are ISRO's published nominal values. Stage Isp values come from public references and differ by a few percent between sources. The diagrams, worked examples, practice problems, glossary and answer key are in the attached 10-page A4 PDF.

==========

🧮 1. THE THRUST EQUATION

Each second the engine throws out a mass of gas (mass flow rate ṁ, kg/s) at an exhaust velocity vₑ (m/s). NASA's equation has two terms:

F = ṁ × vₑ + (pₑ − p₀) × Aₑ

The first is momentum thrust. The second is pressure thrust: pₑ is exit pressure, p₀ is outside air pressure, Aₑ is exit area. It is zero when the two pressures match. For quick sums, F ≈ ṁ × vₑ.

==========

⚖️ 2. FLOW OR SPEED?

Thrust is a product, so it can be built from a big flow of moderate-speed gas or a small flow of very fast gas. A stage that wastes propellant must carry more of it, which makes it heavier and needs still more propellant (Chapter 2). So exhaust velocity is the number designers chase.

Chapter 0 showed each S200 burns about 35 times faster than the C25. That is not a quality gap. The booster needs huge thrust for a few minutes to lift 640 tonnes off the pad. The C25 works above the atmosphere on a lighter vehicle for almost eleven minutes.

==========

⛽ 3. SPECIFIC IMPULSE

Isp = F / (ṁ × g₀), so vₑ = Isp × g₀ and F = ṁ × g₀ × Isp, with g₀ = 9.80665 m/s².

Read it like miles per gallon: a higher Isp means less propellant for the same job.

Vacuum Isp (public references):
S200 solid HTPB: 274.5 s
L110 UH25 + N₂O₄: 293 s
C25 LOX + LH₂: 443 s

==========

🔥 4. THE NOZZLE

The chamber makes hot, high-pressure gas. The nozzle turns it into fast gas. Gas is squeezed through a narrow throat, where it reaches the speed of sound, then expands in the widening bell, getting faster as pressure and temperature fall.

A bell matches the outside pressure at one altitude only. Upper-stage nozzles are long and wide because outside pressure is near zero. The S200 is quoted at about 227 s at sea level and 274.5 s in vacuum, a 17% drop on the ground.

==========

🌬️ 5. WHY HYDROGEN WINS

At a given temperature, lighter exhaust molecules move faster. LOX/LH₂ gives a light water-vapour exhaust, so the C25 reaches 443 s against about 275 to 295 s for heavier propellants (Chapter 6 derives it).

The cost is bulk. Liquid hydrogen has a density of about 71 kg/m³, a fourteenth that of water, and must stay near −253 °C. So hydrogen is used on the upper stage, where each kilogram of stage mass costs the most payload.

==========

🔬 6. WORKED EXAMPLES ON LVM3

A. EXHAUST SPEED (vₑ = Isp × g₀)
S200: 2,692 m/s. L110: 2,873 m/s. C25: 4,344 m/s. Even the C25's exhaust is below orbital speed (about 7.8 km/s). A rocket can outrun its own exhaust (Chapter 2).

B. REBUILD THE THRUST
C25: ṁ = 28,000/646 = 43.3 kg/s, F = 43.3 × 4,344 ≈ 188 kN (ISRO nominal 200 kN, 6% off). L110: ṁ = 575 kg/s, F ≈ 1.65 MN (public range 1.59 to 1.69 MN). S200: ṁ = 1,530 kg/s, F ≈ 4.12 MN average each (public peak 5.15 MN; solid thrust is highest early in the burn).

C. PROPELLANT PER MN·s OF IMPULSE
S200: 371 kg. L110: 348 kg. C25: 230 kg. The C25 uses 38% less. Total impulse: S200 about 552 MN·s each, L110 about 330, C25 about 122.

D. THE BOOSTERS AT LIFT-OFF
Weight is 6.28 MN (Chapter 0). At sea-level Isp (227 s), average thrust is about 3.41 MN per S200, 6.81 MN for the pair, T/W about 1.08. Using the public peak thrust of 5.15 MN each gives 10.3 MN and T/W about 1.64. The truth lies between.

==========

📌 7. SUMMARY

1️⃣ F ≈ ṁ × vₑ, plus a pressure term.
2️⃣ Isp = F/(ṁ g₀) in seconds. Higher means less propellant for the same push.
3️⃣ The nozzle trades heat and pressure for speed. Sea-level and vacuum Isp differ.
4️⃣ Light exhaust is fast exhaust, so LOX/LH₂ reaches 443 s.
5️⃣ Boosters burn fast because their job is raw thrust; the C25 is the efficient stage.

➡️ NEXT: Chapter 2, weight and staging: how much of a rocket must be propellant to reach orbit.

==========

* Asterisk = a figure from a public reference rather than ISRO. Stage Isp and S200 peak thrust come from the LVM3 Wikipedia entry, which itself lists inconsistent values (S200 burn 128 to 134 s, L110 thrust 1.53 to 1.69 MN). ISRO's page gives no Isp or S200/L110 thrust. Average flows come from nominal burn times, so sums match published thrust to within a few percent only.

Theory: NASA Glenn Research Center, Beginner's Guide to Rockets.

==========

🔗 See also: Rocketry with ISRO 0/7 — How Rockets Work. Coming next: Rocketry with ISRO 2/7 — Weight and Staging.

The attached 10-page A4 PDF has diagrams, practice problems, glossary and answer key for printing.
notes.body:
🚀 ROCKETRY WITH ISRO, CHAPTER 2: WEIGHT AND STAGING

==========

⚡ TL;DR

The ideal rocket equation links exhaust speed to final speed: Δv = vₑ × ln(m₀/m_f). Speed grows with exhaust speed, but only with the logarithm of the mass ratio. So every extra bit of speed costs more propellant than the last.

A rocket can go faster than its own exhaust, at the price of a huge mass ratio. A mass ratio of 20 gives Δv = 3 vₑ and needs 95% of the vehicle to be propellant.

Staging beats a single big stage because dropping empty tanks lets the remaining engines push less mass. In a toy 100 t rocket it lifts Δv by 32% with the same propellant.

Theory is from NASA Glenn's Beginner's Guide to Rockets. ISRO data (640 t lift-off, 205 t per booster, 115 t, 28 t, C25 dry 4,310 kg, 4 t GTO payload) is nominal. The S200 (31 t) and L110 (9 t) dry masses are public figures, so the stage-by-stage LVM3 estimate is rough. The 10-page A4 PDF has diagrams, practice problems, glossary and answer key.

==========

⚖️ 1. WEIGHT IS THE ENEMY

A rocket must carry everything it burns, so each kilogram of payload needs many kilograms of propellant, and each extra kilogram of tank needs more again. NASA groups non-propellant mass as the empty weight (structure, engines, guidance, payload). The question: given an exhaust speed, how much of the vehicle must be propellant to reach a target speed?

==========

📐 2. THE IDEAL ROCKET EQUATION

Δv = vₑ × ln(m₀ / m_f)

vₑ is exhaust speed (Isp × g₀), m₀ is mass at the start of the burn and m_f at the end. R = m₀/m_f is the mass ratio. Turned around: R = e^(Δv/vₑ), and the propellant share is 1 − 1/R.

Δv = 1 vₑ needs 63% propellant, 2 vₑ needs 86%, 3 vₑ needs 95%. The equation ignores gravity and drag, which Chapter 3 adds.

LVM3's exhaust leaves the C25 at 4.3 km/s, yet the satellite is delivered at over 10 km/s. Speed is limited by mass ratio, not by exhaust speed.

==========

🪜 3. STAGING

An empty tank is dead weight that a single stage keeps pushing. Dropping it makes m_f smaller for the next burn. The Δv of each stage adds. The cost is complexity: more engines, more separations, more things that can fail.

==========

🔬 4. WORKED EXAMPLES

A. THE C25 ALONE (4 t payload, fairing ignored)
m₀ = 4,310 + 28,000 + 4,000 = 36,310 kg. m_f = 8,310 kg. R = 4.37. Δv = 4,344 × ln 4.37 ≈ 6,406 m/s.

B. PROPELLANT FOR Δv = 4,000 m/s
With the C25's vₑ (4,344 m/s): R = 2.51, propellant 60%. With the S200's vₑ (2,692 m/s): R = 4.42, propellant 77%.

C. SINGLE STAGE VERSUS TWO STAGES (toy 100 t rocket, 2 t payload, tanks 10% of each stage, vₑ = 3,000 m/s)
Single stage: R = 100/11.8 = 8.47, Δv ≈ 6,410 m/s.
Two stages (70 t + 28 t): stage 1 R = 2.70 gives ≈ 2,980 m/s; stage 2 R = 6.25 gives ≈ 5,500 m/s. Total ≈ 8,480 m/s, which is 32% more.

D. LVM3 STAGE BY STAGE (rough, vacuum Isp, three stages in series)
S200 pair: 640 t down to 230 t gives ≈ 2,755 m/s. L110: 168 t down to 53 t gives ≈ 3,315 m/s. C25: 44 t down to 16 t gives ≈ 4,395 m/s. Total ≈ 10.5 km/s, a little above the 9 to 10 km/s needed for orbit including losses. That is expected: vacuum Isp overstates ground-level push, and the model ignores the fairing and the core burning during the booster phase. Treat it as a sanity check, not an ISRO figure.

==========

📌 5. SUMMARY

1️⃣ Δv = vₑ ln(m₀/m_f): speed grows with exhaust speed and only logarithmically with mass ratio.
2️⃣ R = e^(Δv/vₑ); propellant share = 1 − 1/R.
3️⃣ A rocket can outrun its own exhaust, paying with propellant.
4️⃣ Staging adds the Δv of each stage and sheds dead weight.
5️⃣ LVM3 estimate: about 4.4 km/s from the C25 and 10.5 km/s in total.

➡️ NEXT: Chapter 3, motion and ascent: gravity and drag losses and how a vehicle climbs to orbit.

==========

* Asterisk = a public-reference figure or the author's estimate. S200 and L110 dry masses and stage Isp come from the LVM3 Wikipedia entry, whose values differ slightly between sections. The stage-by-stage Δv in Example D is the author's rough series model, not an ISRO figure. ISRO's page gives lift-off mass, propellant masses, burn times, C25 dry mass and payload.

Theory: NASA Glenn Research Center, Beginner's Guide to Rockets.

==========

🔗 See also: Rocketry with ISRO 1/7 — Thrust and Specific Impulse. Coming next: Rocketry with ISRO 3/7 — Motion and Ascent.

notes.title: Rocketry with ISRO 3/7 — Motion and Ascent
notes.summary: Why orbit is mostly sideways speed and how a launch vehicle gets there. Covers orbital speed and period, the three phases of an ascent, gravity and drag losses, max-Q and the Earth's rotation bonus, with worked examples on LVM3's 180 × 36,000 km transfer orbit (10.27 km/s at perigee, 1.59 km/s at apogee). The attached 10-page A4 PDF has diagrams, practice problems, glossary and answer key for printing.
notes.body:
🚀 ROCKETRY WITH ISRO, CHAPTER 3: MOTION AND ASCENT

==========

⚡ TL;DR

Orbit is not "beyond gravity". At 180 km, gravity is still about 95% of its surface value. A satellite stays up because it moves sideways at about 7.8 km/s, so the ground curves away as fast as it falls. About 95% of the energy of that orbit is speed, not height.

So an ascent starts vertical, tips over in a gravity turn, and ends in a long, nearly flat burn that builds speed. Gravity loss and drag loss take some of the engines' Δv on the way, and an eastward launch gets up to 0.45 km/s free from the Earth's rotation.

The theory is from NASA Glenn's Beginner's Guide to Rockets. The LVM3 event times and the 180 × 36,000 km transfer orbit are ISRO's nominal values. Constants and the Δv-budget ranges are standard textbook values; the drag example uses assumed numbers, not ISRO data. The 10-page A4 PDF has diagrams, practice problems, glossary and answer key.

==========

🌍 1. WHAT "BEING IN ORBIT" MEANS

A satellite is always falling towards the Earth but moves sideways so fast that the ground curves away beneath it. For a circular orbit:

v = √(μ/r), period T = 2π√(r³/μ), with r = R_E + altitude, R_E = 6,371 km, μ = 398,600 km³/s².

At Sriharikota (about 13.7° N) the ground already moves east at about 452 m/s, roughly 6% of orbital speed. That is why most Indian launches head east or south-east over the sea; polar missions go south and give up the bonus.

==========

📈 2. THE SHAPE OF AN ASCENT

Vertical rise: a few seconds straight up to clear the pad.
Pitch-over and gravity turn: gravity bends the path towards horizontal while thrust stays along the flight direction, so there is little sideways load.
Horizontal acceleration: above the atmosphere the upper stage burns nearly flat until it reaches orbital speed.

LVM3's nominal timeline: 0 s lift-off on two S200 boosters; 137 s boosters separate; 217 s fairing off at 115 km; 313 s L110 burns out and the C25 ignites; 974 s injection into 180 × 36,000 km.

==========

⚡ 3. ORBIT IS MOSTLY SPEED

At 180 km a kilogram has kinetic energy ½v² = 30.4 MJ but potential energy of only 1.7 MJ. Speed share = 95%.

==========

📉 4. LOSSES

Gravity loss: every second of burning spends about 9.8 m/s of Δv fighting gravity. A vertical burn loses g × t; turning early cuts the loss.

Drag loss: drag = ½ρv² × Cd × A. The ½ρv² part is dynamic pressure q. It rises with speed, falls as air thins, and peaks at max-Q.

Typical Δv to low orbit (public textbook ranges): orbital speed 7.8 km/s, plus 1.0 to 1.5 for gravity, 0.2 to 0.3 for drag and steering, minus about 0.4 for Earth's rotation, giving about 8.6 to 9.2 km/s before margin. That is why Chapter 0 said roughly 9 to 10.

==========

🔬 5. WORKED EXAMPLES

A. ORBITAL SPEED AND PERIOD
r = 6,551 km: v ≈ 7.80 km/s, period ≈ 88 minutes. At 400 km: 7.67 km/s.

B. ENERGY
Kinetic ≈ 30.4 MJ/kg, potential ≈ 1.72 MJ/kg, so 95% is speed.

C. GRAVITY LOSS
Vertical worst case for the 134 s S200 burn: 9.81 × 134 ≈ 1,315 m/s. g is 9.68 m/s² at 41.5 km and 9.46 m/s² at 115 km.

D. THE TRANSFER ORBIT
For 180 × 36,000 km: perigee speed ≈ 10.27 km/s, apogee speed ≈ 1.59 km/s, period ≈ 10.6 h. Circularising at apogee needs 3.07 − 1.59 ≈ 1.48 km/s more, which the satellite's own engine adds. ISRO's job ends at the transfer orbit.

E. MAX-Q WHAT-IF (assumed values: 11 km altitude, 400 m/s, Cd 0.3, A = 12.6 m², 400 t)
q ≈ 29 kPa, drag ≈ 110 kN, about 2.8% of weight. Small as a fraction, but 29 kPa across the nose is what the structure must survive.

==========

📌 6. SUMMARY

1️⃣ Orbit means falling around the Earth: about 7.8 km/s at 180 km, period 88 min.
2️⃣ 95% of the energy of that orbit is speed, so the ascent turns horizontal.
3️⃣ Gravity loss and drag loss take some Δv; Earth's rotation gives some back for eastward launches.
4️⃣ Typical Δv to low orbit is about 8.6 to 9.2 km/s plus margin.
5️⃣ LVM3 delivers 10.27 km/s at perigee of the transfer orbit; the satellite adds the rest.

➡️ NEXT: Chapter 4, aerodynamics: where drag comes from and why shape matters.

==========

* Asterisk = typical or assumed value. ISRO's page gives event times, the fairing separation altitude and the transfer orbit, but not altitude and speed at each moment. The Δv-budget ranges are textbook values, and Example E uses assumed numbers (altitude, speed, Cd, area, mass), not ISRO data.

Theory: NASA Glenn Research Center, Beginner's Guide to Rockets.

==========

🔗 See also: Rocketry with ISRO 2/7 — Weight and Staging. Coming next: Rocketry with ISRO 4/7 — Aerodynamics.

notes.title: Rocketry with ISRO 4/7 — Aerodynamics
notes.summary: Where drag comes from and why shape and size matter. Covers the drag equation, Mach number, the transonic drag peak, nose shapes and the scaling law that makes big rockets lose proportionally less to drag, with worked examples on LVM3's 5 m fairing. Using the real frontal area raises Chapter 3's drag estimate by 56%, and doubling speed quadruples drag. The attached 9-page A4 PDF has diagrams, practice problems, glossary and answer key for printing.
notes.body:
🚀 ROCKETRY WITH ISRO, CHAPTER 4: AERODYNAMICS

==========

⚡ TL;DR

Drag is D = Cd × ½ρv² × A. It grows with the square of speed, with frontal area and with a shape number (Cd), and it falls as the air thins. Double the speed and drag quadruples.

Mach number (speed divided by the speed of sound, about 340 m/s at sea level and 295 m/s at 11 km) changes the rules. Drag rises steeply through the transonic range around Mach 1, peaks, then eases off above it. Pointed or ogive noses and slender bodies cut drag.

LVM3's widest section, the 5 m fairing, sets its frontal area (19.6 m², not the 12.6 m² of the 4 m body). And big rockets lose proportionally less to drag: drag/weight falls as 1/L with size.

The theory is from NASA Glenn's Beginner's Guide to Rockets. ISRO publishes the dimensions (43.5 m tall, 4 m body, 5 m fairing) and the fairing release at 115 km and 217 s, but not drag coefficients or Mach numbers, so those are typical or assumed values. The 9-page A4 PDF has the diagrams, practice problems, glossary and answer key.

==========

🌬️ 1. THE DRAG EQUATION

D = Cd × ½ρv² × A

ρ is air density, v speed, A frontal area and Cd a shape number found by wind-tunnel or flow-simulation tests. Halve the density and drag halves.

==========

🔊 2. MACH NUMBER

Speed of sound a = √(γRT), with γ = 1.4 and R = 287 J/(kg·K). Mach number M = v/a. Well below Mach 1 the air flows smoothly round the rocket. Near and above Mach 1 pressure piles up in thin shock waves and drag behaves differently.

==========

📈 3. WHY DRAG CHANGES NEAR MACH 1

Cd stays roughly flat in subsonic flight, climbs steeply through the transonic range, peaks near Mach 1, then falls somewhat in supersonic flight. A shock wave is a very thin region where pressure, density and temperature jump suddenly. Shocks cost energy, which shows up as drag. A pointed, smoothly curved nose weakens them.

==========

🔺 4. SHAPE

Blunt noses have the highest drag; cones are simple and low-drag; an ogive (a smooth curve, typical of fairings) gives low drag and more room inside for the payload. Boosters, shoulders and fins add drag too. Fineness ratio (length over diameter) for LVM3 is about 10.9 on the 4 m body, or 8.7 on the 5 m fairing.

==========

📏 5. WHY BIG ROCKETS LOSE LESS

Scale a rocket by L: area grows as L², mass as L³, so drag/weight falls as 1/L. Small launchers face a bigger drag penalty.

==========

🔬 6. WORKED EXAMPLES

A. SPEED OF SOUND
340 m/s at sea level, 295 m/s at 11 km. The 400 m/s what-if from Chapter 3 is Mach 1.36.

B. DRAG WITH THE REAL FRONTAL AREA (assumed: 11 km, 400 m/s, 400 t)
q ≈ 29,100 Pa. Using the 5 m fairing (19.6 m²): Cd 0.3 gives 171 kN (4.4% of the 3.9 MN weight); Cd 0.5 gives 286 kN (7.3%). That is 56% above Chapter 3's 110 kN, which used the 4 m body.

C. DRAG AND SPEED
At the same density and Cd 0.3: 100 m/s gives 10.7 kN, 200 m/s gives 42.9 kN, 400 m/s gives 171 kN. Doubling speed quadruples drag.

D. SCALE EFFECT
A geometrically similar model one tenth the size has area 1/100 and mass 1/1000, so its drag/weight is 10 times larger.

E. HEATING
Stagnation temperature T0 = T(1 + 0.2M²). At 216.65 K and Mach 1.36 that is about 296 K (23 °C), so the nose barely warms at max-Q. Heating climbs steeply with speed, so it matters later. By 115 km the air is millions of times thinner than at sea level and the fairing is dropped.

==========

📌 7. SUMMARY

1️⃣ D = Cd × ½ρv² × A: grows with v² and area, falls with air density.
2️⃣ Mach number = v/a; a is 340 m/s at sea level and 295 m/s at 11 km.
3️⃣ Drag peaks around Mach 1 because of shock waves.
4️⃣ Pointed or ogive noses and slender bodies cut drag; the widest section sets frontal area.
5️⃣ Big rockets lose proportionally less to drag (drag/weight falls as 1/L).

➡️ NEXT: Chapter 5, stability and control: why the centre of pressure must sit behind the centre of gravity and how a rocket is steered.

==========

* Asterisk = typical or assumed value. ISRO does not publish LVM3's drag coefficients or Mach numbers. The 400 t, 400 m/s, 11 km case is an assumption carried over from Chapter 3, and the Cd-versus-Mach curve is a textbook shape. NASA's guide develops shock-wave and Euler-equation mathematics that this series deliberately skips.

Theory: NASA Glenn Research Center, Beginner's Guide to Rockets.

==========

🔗 See also: Rocketry with ISRO 3/7 — Motion and Ascent. Coming next: Rocketry with ISRO 5/7 — Stability and Control.

notes.title: Rocketry with ISRO 5/7 — Stability and Control
notes.summary: Why the centre of pressure belongs behind the centre of gravity and how a rocket is steered. Covers static stability, stability margin in calibres, thrust vector control by gimballing or flex nozzles, and the sensor, computer and actuator loop. Worked what-if examples (ISRO does not publish these values) show a 4° gimbal on the L110 gives about 15 times the turning moment of the same tilt on the C25. The attached 8-page A4 PDF has diagrams, practice problems, glossary and answer key for printing.
notes.body:
🚀 ROCKETRY WITH ISRO, CHAPTER 5: STABILITY AND CONTROL

==========

⚡ TL;DR

Two points decide whether a rocket flies straight. The centre of gravity (CG) is the balance point; weight acts through it. The centre of pressure (CP) is where the total air force acts. If the CP sits behind the CG, a sideways gust turns the nose back into the airflow. If the CP is ahead, the same gust turns the nose further away and the rocket tumbles.

Fins at the tail pull the CP aft. Many large vehicles instead fly with active control: sensors measure the tilt, a flight computer compares it with the plan, and a swivelling engine (or flex nozzle) corrects it many times a second. Side force = F sin θ, and turning moment = F sin θ × arm length.

The theory is from NASA Glenn's Beginner's Guide to Rockets. ISRO does not publish LVM3's CG, gimbal angles or moments of inertia, so every number in the worked examples is a labelled what-if. The 8-page A4 PDF has the diagrams, practice problems, glossary and answer key.

==========

⚖️ 1. CG AND CP

A side force at the CP turns the rocket about the CG. CP behind CG restores the nose to the flight path, like the feathers on an arrow. CP ahead of CG makes things worse.

Stability margin = (distance of CP behind CG) / body diameter, in calibres. Model rockets aim for about 1 to 2. Large launch vehicles often fly with a CP close to or ahead of the CG for part of the flight and rely on control instead.

==========

🎯 2. STEERING BY SWIVELLING THRUST

Tilt the nozzle by a small angle θ and part of the thrust becomes a side force at the tail, a distance L from the CG:

side force = F × sin θ
moment = F × sin θ × L

This is thrust vector control. Publicly, ISRO steers the S200 boosters with a flex nozzle and the liquid engines by gimballing. Roll is handled by tilting engines differentially or with small separate thrusters.

==========

🔁 3. THE CONTROL LOOP

Gyroscopes and accelerometers measure how the vehicle is turning. The flight computer compares that with the planned path and commands the actuators. The rocket responds and the sensors measure again, many times a second. ISRO's equipment bay (EB) at the top of the vehicle houses the guidance equipment.

==========

🔬 4. WORKED EXAMPLES (all what-ifs)

A. STABILITY MARGIN
4 m body, CG 28 m from the nose, CP 31 m: margin = 3/4 = 0.75 calibres. Stable but marginal by the model-rocket rule, so real launchers lean on active control.

B. C25 GIMBAL (4°, arm 8 m)
Side force = 200 × sin 4° ≈ 13.95 kN. Moment ≈ 111.6 kN·m.

C. L110 GIMBAL (4°, arm 15 m)
Side force = 1,652 × sin 4° ≈ 115.2 kN. Moment ≈ 1.73 MN·m, about 15 times the C25's.

D. HOW FAST THE C25 TURNS
44 t as a 20 m rod: I ≈ 1.47 × 10⁶ kg·m². Angular acceleration ≈ 0.076 rad/s² ≈ 4.4°/s². Turning 10° from rest takes about 2.1 s. A large vehicle nudges, it does not swerve.

==========

📌 5. SUMMARY

1️⃣ CP behind CG is stable; CP ahead tumbles.
2️⃣ Stability margin in calibres = (CP behind CG) / diameter.
3️⃣ Active control (guidance plus a swivelling thrust) replaces stability on many large vehicles.
4️⃣ Side force = F sin θ; moment = F sin θ × L.
5️⃣ Sensors, computer and actuators form a loop repeated many times per second.

➡️ NEXT: Chapter 6, gas physics: why hot gas expands and what temperature and molecular weight do to exhaust speed.

==========

* Asterisk = assumed value. The CG, CP, gimbal angles, arm lengths and inertia in the examples are assumptions to show the method. ISRO's page gives the C25 thrust (200 kN) and vehicle length (43.5 m); the L110 thrust is Chapter 1's estimate. The flex-nozzle and gimbal description is from public ISRO descriptions.

Theory: NASA Glenn Research Center, Beginner's Guide to Rockets.

==========

🔗 See also: Rocketry with ISRO 4/7 — Aerodynamics. Coming next: Rocketry with ISRO 6/7 — Gas Physics.

notes.title: Rocketry with ISRO 6/7 — Gas Physics
notes.summary: What temperature and molecular weight do to exhaust speed. Covers the ideal-gas law, why lighter molecules move faster, and the exhaust-velocity formula derived from energy conservation in an isentropic nozzle. Illustrative sums reproduce the 1.6 : 1 exhaust-speed gap between ISRO's cryogenic C25 and S200 booster: the LOX/LH2 flame is not hotter, its exhaust is lighter. The attached 8-page A4 PDF has diagrams, practice problems, glossary and answer key for printing.
notes.body:
🚀 ROCKETRY WITH ISRO, CHAPTER 6: GAS PHYSICS

==========

⚡ TL;DR

Temperature measures how fast molecules move. At the same temperature every molecule has the same average energy, so lighter molecules move faster (speed goes as 1/√M, M being molar mass). That is the root reason hydrogen-fuelled engines reach higher exhaust speed.

Energy conservation in an isentropic (no heat loss, no friction) nozzle gives the exhaust-velocity formula: vₑ = √[2γ/(γ−1) × (Ru/M) × Tc × (1 − (pe/pc)^((γ−1)/γ))]. Exhaust speed rises with chamber temperature (as √Tc), falls with molar mass (as 1/√M), and rises with a bigger pressure drop.

A LOX/LH₂ flame is not hotter than a solid's. The C25's exhaust is simply lighter, which is why it reaches 443 s against the S200's 274.5 s. Illustrative sums reproduce the 1.6 : 1 exhaust-speed gap to within a few percent.

The theory is from NASA Glenn's Beginner's Guide to Rockets. ISRO does not publish chamber temperatures, exhaust composition or nozzle pressure ratios, so the values in the sums are illustrative textbook-typical numbers, checked against the Isp values from Chapter 1. The 8-page A4 PDF has diagrams, practice problems, glossary and answer key.

==========

🌡️ 1. THE GAS LAW

p = ρ × Rs × T, with Rs = Ru/M and Ru = 8.314 J/(mol·K). For air, Rs = 287 J/(kg·K). Temperature is a measure of how fast molecules move: average kinetic energy per molecule is proportional to T. So at the same temperature, a lighter molecule moves faster. Steam (M = 18) is about 1.56 times faster than CO₂ (M = 44). Hydrogen (M = 2) is almost 4 times faster than nitrogen (M = 28).

==========

🔥 2. WHERE EXHAUST SPEED COMES FROM

Energy conservation: ½vₑ² = cp × (Tc − Te), with cp = γ/(γ−1) × Rs and Te/Tc = (pe/pc)^((γ−1)/γ). Chamber gas is hot and almost still; through the nozzle it cools and speeds up, and the heat it gives up becomes motion.

The second law says real flows lose some energy to friction and heat, so the isentropic formula is the ceiling.

==========

🔬 3. WORKED EXAMPLES

A. AIR DENSITY
Sea level: 101,325 / (287 × 288.15) ≈ 1.225 kg/m³. At 11 km: 22,632 / (287 × 216.65) ≈ 0.364 kg/m³. These are the densities used in Chapters 3 and 4.

B. LIGHT VERSUS HEAVY
Steam against CO₂: 1.56 times faster. Hydrogen against nitrogen: 3.7 times faster.

C. vₑ FOR LOX/LH₂ AND A SOLID (illustrative values)
LOX/LH₂ (Tc 3,500 K, M 13.5 g/mol, γ 1.20, pe/pc 0.002): vₑ ≈ 4,085 m/s. Aluminised solid (Tc 3,400 K, M 28 g/mol, γ 1.18, pe/pc 0.01): vₑ ≈ 2,585 m/s. The ratio is 1.58, close to the 443 / 274.5 = 1.61 from Chapter 1. The computed values land within about 5% of the exhaust speeds implied by the published Isp (4,344 and 2,692 m/s).

D. HOW MUCH HEAT BECOMES MOTION
LOX/LH₂: exit temperature about 1,242 K, and about 65% of the heat energy becomes kinetic energy. Solid: exit temperature about 1,684 K and about 50%.

==========

📌 4. SUMMARY

1️⃣ p = ρRsT, with Rs = Ru/M. Lighter molecules move faster at the same temperature.
2️⃣ vₑ = √[2γ/(γ−1) × (Ru/M) × Tc × (1 − (pe/pc)^((γ−1)/γ))].
3️⃣ vₑ rises with √Tc, falls with 1/√M, and rises with a bigger pressure drop.
4️⃣ LOX/LH₂ is not hotter than a solid; its exhaust is lighter. That is why the C25 reaches 443 s.
5️⃣ Illustrative sums reproduce the gap between C25 and S200 to within a few percent.

➡️ NEXT: Chapter 7, the capstone: SSLV, PSLV and LVM3 compared using everything from Chapters 0 to 6.

==========

* Asterisk = illustrative value. Chamber temperatures, molar masses, γ and pressure ratios are textbook-typical values for each propellant type, not ISRO data. Exhaust speeds implied by Isp come from public references (Chapter 1), which differ by a few percent between sources.

Theory: NASA Glenn Research Center, Beginner's Guide to Rockets.

==========

🔗 See also: Rocketry with ISRO 5/7 — Stability and Control. Coming next: Rocketry with ISRO 7/7 — Capstone: SSLV, PSLV and LVM3.

notes.title: Rocketry with ISRO 7/7 — Capstone: SSLV, PSLV and LVM3
notes.summary: A capstone that applies every idea in the series to ISRO's three launchers. SSLV, PSLV-XL and LVM3 are each 82% to 86% propellant; payload to low orbit is 0.42%, 1.19% and 1.25% of lift-off mass, and LVM3 delivers about 1.5 times PSLV's payload per tonne to GTO thanks to its cryogenic upper stage. LVM3 data are ISRO's; SSLV and PSLV data are from public references that disagree with themselves, so results are good to a few percent. The attached 9-page A4 PDF has diagrams, practice problems, glossary and answer key for printing.
notes.body:
🚀 ROCKETRY WITH ISRO, CHAPTER 7: CAPSTONE — SSLV, PSLV AND LVM3

==========

⚡ TL;DR

Three launchers, one toolkit. SSLV (120 t), PSLV-XL (320 t) and LVM3 (640 t) are each 82% to 86% propellant. Only LVM3 carries any cryogenic propellant, and it is just 5% of the total.

Payload as a share of lift-off mass: 0.42% for SSLV to low Earth orbit, 1.19% for PSLV, 1.25% for LVM3. To geosynchronous transfer orbit, LVM3 delivers about 1.5 times as much payload per tonne as PSLV (0.625% against 0.41%). That gain comes from the cryogenic upper stage.

Peak lift-off thrust-to-weight falls with size, from about 2.1 (SSLV) to at most 2.9 (PSLV) to 1.6 (LVM3). Propellant-weighted average Isp is about 287 s for LVM3 and 272 s for PSLV, so efficiency is won at the top of the stack, not by the average.

LVM3 figures are ISRO's nominal values. SSLV and PSLV figures come from public references that disagree with themselves in places, so comparisons are good to a few percent. The 9-page A4 PDF has the diagrams, practice problems, glossary and answer key.

==========

🪜 1. THREE VEHICLES, THREE JOBS

SSLV: 34 m, 2 m diameter, 120 t. Three solid stages plus a liquid velocity-trimming module. About 500 kg to low Earth orbit (500 km).
PSLV-XL: 44 m, 2.8 m, 320 t. Solid, liquid, solid, liquid, plus 6 solid strap-ons. 3,800 kg to LEO (200 km), 1,750 kg to a 620 km sun-synchronous orbit, 1,300 kg to GTO.
LVM3: 43.5 m, 4 m body (5 m fairing), 640 t. Two solid boosters, liquid core, cryogenic upper stage. 8,000 kg to LEO, 4,000 kg to GTO.

Each step is two to three times heavier than the last.

==========

⛽ 2. WHERE THE PROPELLANT SITS

SSLV: 99.2 t solid, 0.05 t liquid.
PSLV-XL: 219 t solid, 44.5 t storable liquid.
LVM3: 410 t solid, 115 t storable liquid, 28 t cryogenic.

Chapter 1's rule: solids give about 260 to 275 s, storable liquids about 290 to 295 s, LOX/LH₂ about 443 s.

==========

🔬 3. WORKED EXAMPLES

A. PROPELLANT LEDGER
SSLV 99,250 kg = 82.7%. PSLV 263,500 kg = 82.3%. LVM3 553,000 kg = 86.4%.

B. PAYLOAD FRACTION
SSLV LEO 0.42%. PSLV LEO 1.19%, SSO 0.55%, GTO 0.41%. LVM3 LEO 1.25%, GTO 0.625%. For the same trip to GTO, LVM3 delivers about 1.5 times as much per tonne as PSLV.

C. LIFT-OFF THRUST-TO-WEIGHT (peak thrust, an upper bound)
SSLV 2,496 / 1,177 ≈ 2.12. PSLV 9,068 / 3,139 ≈ 2.89 if all six strap-ons burn together (about 2.44 with four). LVM3 10,300 / 6,278 ≈ 1.64. The small rocket leaves briskly; heavy LVM3 lifts off more gently, at the price of more gravity loss.

D. AVERAGE ISP, WEIGHTED BY PROPELLANT
LVM3 ≈ 287 s, PSLV ≈ 272 s. LVM3's 443 s cryogenic stage carries only 5% of the propellant, so it lifts the average by just 15 s. Efficiency is won at the top of the stack, where each kilogram is worth the most.

E. CHOOSE THE VEHICLE
A 600 kg satellite to 500 km: SSLV is about 100 kg short, so PSLV. A 3,000 kg communication satellite to GTO: only LVM3 (4,000 kg against PSLV's 1,300 kg). A 150 kg demonstrator on demand: SSLV. Match payload to the smallest vehicle that fits.

==========

📌 4. SUMMARY

1️⃣ SSLV, PSLV-XL and LVM3 weigh 120 t, 320 t and 640 t.
2️⃣ All three are 82% to 86% propellant; only LVM3 carries cryogenic propellant, and just 5% of its total.
3️⃣ Payload fraction to LEO: 0.42%, 1.19%, 1.25%. To GTO, LVM3 beats PSLV by about 1.5 times.
4️⃣ Peak lift-off T/W falls with size.
5️⃣ Average Isp is about 287 s for LVM3 and 272 s for PSLV; top-stage efficiency matters most.

✅ SERIES COMPLETE. You can now read any launch-vehicle spec sheet and say what each number means.

==========

* Asterisk = public-reference figure. SSLV and PSLV data come from Wikipedia entries retrieved 10 November 2026, which disagree with themselves: SSLV LEO payload is 500 kg in the text and 375 to 525 kg in the infobox, and no Isp is given. PSLV stage thrust, propellant and burn times differ between the infobox and text (for example PS2 propellant 42 t against 41.5 t), and the SSO payload is 1,750 or 1,800 kg. Stage Isp for PSLV and the S200 come from the same references. LVM3 data are ISRO's nominal values from Chapter 0. LEO orbits differ by vehicle (200 km at 30° for PSLV, 500 km for SSLV), so compare within a column and treat the numbers as rough.

Theory: NASA Glenn Research Center, Beginner's Guide to Rockets.

==========

🔗 See also: Rocketry with ISRO 6/7 — Gas Physics, and the full series starting at Rocketry with ISRO 0/7 — How Rockets Work.

notes.title: Psychology for Managers 0/12 — How Psychology Knows Things
notes.summary: The toolkit behind every psychology finding, applied to sales and management. Covers the four goals of psychology, the early schools, seven modern perspectives (all pointed at one salesperson's resignation), descriptive methods, correlation versus causation and the randomised experiment. Ends with the replication crisis: in 2015 only 36% of 100 re-run studies held up, so the series checks every finding. The attached 17-page A4 PDF has the diagrams, worked examples, practice problems, glossary and answer key.
notes.body:
🧠 PSYCHOLOGY FOR MANAGERS, PART 0: HOW PSYCHOLOGY KNOWS THINGS

==========

⚡ TL;DR

Psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes. Its four goals (describe, explain, predict, control) are the same four jobs a manager does when diagnosing a problem.

This part is about the toolkit, not the findings. Descriptive methods (observation, case studies, surveys) tell you what is happening, never why. Correlation lets you predict but never proves cause. Only an experiment with random assignment and a control group shows cause and effect.

The headline result: when 100 published psychology studies were re-run in 2015, only 36% repeated their result, at about half the original strength. So every later part of this series carries a "Held up?" check.

The chapter structure follows Ciccarelli & White, Psychology (4th ed.), Chapter 1. The text, examples and diagrams are original. The diagrams, worked examples, practice problems, glossary and answer key are in the attached 17-page A4 PDF, made for printing.

==========

🎯 1. WHAT PSYCHOLOGY IS

Behaviour is what can be observed: a purchase, a resignation, a reaction time. Mental processes are what cannot be seen directly: memory, attitudes, emotions, decisions. The word that matters is scientific. Folk wisdom says both "birds of a feather flock together" and "opposites attract", so it explains any outcome after the fact and predicts nothing.

The four goals, in field-sales terms:
• Describe: order frequency fell 20% at 30 dealers in Q2.
• Explain: a competitor offered longer credit and dealers are cash-constrained.
• Predict: dealers with high outstanding balances are most at risk.
• Control: targeted credit terms for the at-risk group.

"Control" just means changing behaviour deliberately: therapy, training, nudges, incentive design.

==========

🏛️ 2. FIVE EARLY SCHOOLS

Psychology became a science in 1879, when Wilhelm Wundt opened the first psychology lab in Leipzig.

• Structuralism (Wundt, Titchener): break experience into parts by introspection. It died because no one could verify introspection. A method nobody else can check is not a method.
• Functionalism (William James): ask what the mind is for. Its descendants include industrial/organisational psychology.
• Gestalt (Wertheimer): the whole differs from the sum of its parts. We perceive a brand, not a list of attributes.
• Psychoanalysis (Freud): an unconscious mind drives behaviour. Most specific claims failed testing, but the idea that people don't fully know why they act survives in consumer research.
• Behaviourism (Watson, Skinner): study only observable behaviour; reinforced behaviour is repeated. Every incentive scheme is applied behaviourism.

==========

🔭 3. SEVEN MODERN PERSPECTIVES

Lenses, not rivals. Point all seven at one case: a top salesperson suddenly resigns.
• Psychodynamic: an unconscious pattern of leaving when controlled?
• Behavioural: did the rewards stop, or did effort get punished with higher targets?
• Humanistic: did they feel there was no room to grow?
• Cognitive: how did they weigh the offer, and what did they believe about their future?
• Sociocultural: did peers leave? What does the team culture reward?
• Biopsychological: is chronic stress or sleep loss from travel wearing them down?
• Evolutionary: did a loss of status inside the group trigger an exit?

A good diagnosis uses two or three. The manager's mistake is having only one.

==========

👥 4. WHO DOES WHAT

A psychologist holds an academic degree in psychology. A psychiatrist is a medical doctor and can prescribe medication. In India, practising clinical psychologists register with the Rehabilitation Council of India. For business, the relevant fields are I/O, social and consumer psychology.

==========

🔬 5. THE SCIENTIFIC METHOD

Question → hypothesis → test → conclusions → report so others can repeat it.

A hypothesis needs an operational definition: the exact way a vague idea will be measured. "Dealer satisfaction" is vague. "Score on a five-question 1–5 survey, collected by someone other than the dealer's own ASM" is operational.

==========

👀 6. DESCRIBING BEHAVIOUR

• Naturalistic observation: real setting, no control, and people change when watched (observer effect). A mystery shopper does it properly.
• Laboratory observation: more control, less realism.
• Case study: rich, but you can't generalise from one case. That includes business-school cases.
• Survey: scalable, but fails on unrepresentative samples and courtesy bias. Ask a dealer about service in front of the ASM and you have measured politeness.

==========

📈 7. CORRELATION

r runs from −1 to +1. The sign gives direction and the size gives strength.

Worked example: five dealers with ASM visits of 2, 4, 5, 7, 8 per month and orders of ₹3, 4, 6, 6, 9 lakh give r ≈ +0.93 (data invented for teaching).

That does not mean visits cause orders. Orders may cause visits, because ASMs go where the money is. Or a third variable, store size, may drive both. Correlation supports prediction, never cause.

==========

🧪 8. THE EXPERIMENT

Independent variable: what you change. Dependent variable: what you measure. The experimental group gets the treatment; the control group doesn't, or gets a placebo. Random assignment spreads every hidden difference evenly across the groups. Double-blinding prevents placebo and experimenter effects.

Worked example: randomly split 40 dealers. The 20 on a new scheme grow 12% and the 20 controls grow 7%. The scheme's real effect is 5 points, not 12. If ASMs had picked the scheme dealers, the gap could be pure selection bias.

==========

⚖️ 9. ETHICS

Informed consent, minimal harm, confidentiality and debriefing. The rules exist because the field broke them, as in Milgram's 1960s obedience studies. A pilot scheme affects real pay and careers, so the same principles apply.

==========

🔁 10. WHAT'S HELD UP: THE REPLICATION CRISIS

In 2015 the Open Science Collaboration re-ran 100 studies from three leading journals. In the originals, 97% were significant. In the repeats, 36% were, and effects were roughly half the size. The textbook edition this series follows was written just before this landed.

Findings that failed:
• Ego depletion: a 23-lab replication with more than 2,000 participants found almost no effect.
• Power posing: no hormone effect in larger tests, and an original author disowned it in 2016.
• Wansink's food research: Cornell found misconduct in 2018 and many papers were retracted.
• Stanford Prison Experiment: archival work showed the guards were coached. It is now a cautionary tale.

Causes: small samples, p-hacking, publication bias. Fixes: preregistration, larger samples, registered reports.

Six questions before you believe a finding:
1️⃣ Experiment or only a correlation?
2️⃣ How big was the sample?
3️⃣ Independently replicated?
4️⃣ Preregistered?
5️⃣ How large is the effect, not just whether it is "significant"?
6️⃣ Who paid, and who benefits if it's true?

==========

📝 SUMMARY

1️⃣ Psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes, with four goals: describe, explain, predict, control.
2️⃣ Structuralism failed on unverifiable introspection. Functionalism, Gestalt, psychoanalysis and behaviourism left ideas that survive.
3️⃣ Use more than one of the seven perspectives.
4️⃣ Descriptive methods show what, never why.
5️⃣ Correlation predicts but never proves cause.
6️⃣ Only a randomised experiment with a control group shows cause and effect.
7️⃣ Roughly two in three findings failed to repeat in one large check, so price every claim with the six questions.

➡️ NEXT: Part 1, The brain and nervous system.

==========

Spine: Ciccarelli, S. K. & White, J. N., Psychology, 4th ed. (Pearson), Chapter 1. Text, examples and figures are original. Replication figures: Open Science Collaboration, Science (2015); Hagger et al., Perspectives on Psychological Science (2016). Worked-example data are invented for teaching.

==========

notes.body:
🧠 PSYCHOLOGY FOR MANAGERS, PART 1: THE BRAIN AND NERVOUS SYSTEM

==========

⚡ TL;DR

Every behaviour is something the nervous system did. Neurons fire all-or-none and pass signals chemically across synapses; myelin makes them about a hundred times faster. The sympathetic nervous system and stress hormones fire the same way for a public dressing-down as for physical danger.

The cortex has four lobes, with the prefrontal cortex handling planning and self-control, and it is the first to suffer from fatigue and stress. The brain rewires with practice, so skills are physically trainable.

The headline result: 'left-brained vs right-brained people' and 'we use 10% of our brain' are myths, and most neuromarketing claims rest on reverse inference. In the worked example, an amygdala 'lighting up' means only about a 23% chance the viewer felt fear.

The chapter structure follows Ciccarelli & White, Psychology (4th ed.), Chapter 2. The text, examples and diagrams are original.

==========

⚡ 1. THE NEURON: THE BASIC UNIT

The nervous system is built from neurons, cells specialised to carry messages. The human brain has roughly 86 billion of them. Each has three working parts:

• Dendrites — branches that receive signals from other neurons.
• Cell body (soma) — keeps the cell alive and adds up incoming signals.
• Axon — a long fibre that carries the signal away to the next cell. Many axons are wrapped in myelin, a fatty insulation that makes signals travel much faster.

A neuron either fires or doesn't — the all-or-none principle. It fires when the inputs it receives push it past a threshold; the electrical pulse that then runs down the axon is the action potential. A strong stimulus doesn't make a bigger pulse. It makes the neuron fire more often, and recruits more neurons.

Neurons don't touch. At the end of the axon is a tiny gap, the synapse. The electrical signal is converted into chemical messengers, neurotransmitters, which cross the gap and either excite the next neuron (make it more likely to fire) or inhibit it (less likely). Most psychiatric drugs work at the synapse, by changing how much of a neurotransmitter is released or how long it lingers.

• Glutamate: The main excitatory messenger; learning and memory — Involved in nearly every fast signal in the brain.
• GABA: The main inhibitory messenger; calms activity — Anti-anxiety drugs and alcohol boost its effect.
• Acetylcholine: Muscle movement; attention and memory — Lost early in Alzheimer's disease.
• Dopamine: Movement; reward learning, motivation — Better described as "wanting" and prediction than as "pleasure" (see section 8).
• Serotonin: Mood, sleep, appetite — Target of the most common antidepressants (SSRIs).
• Norepinephrine: Alertness, arousal — Part of the stress response.
• Endorphins: The body's own pain relievers — Released under stress, pain and hard exercise.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE 1 · WHY MYELIN MATTERS

A signal travels from your toe to your spinal cord, about 1.2 m. A well-myelinated axon carries it at about 100 m/s; an unmyelinated one at about 1 m/s.

Myelinated:    time = 1.2 m / 100 m/s = 0.012 s = 12 ms
Unmyelinated:  time = 1.2 m / 1 m/s   = 1.2 s

A hundredfold difference. Fast pain (the sharp "ouch") travels on myelinated fibres; the dull ache that follows comes on slower, unmyelinated ones. Multiple sclerosis is the immune system attacking myelin, which is why it slows and scrambles movement and sensation. Note the scale too: a typical human reaction time is around 200–250 ms, so most of the delay is the brain processing the signal, not the wire carrying it.

==========

🗺️ 2. THE MAP OF THE NERVOUS SYSTEM

The system has two halves. The central nervous system (CNS) is the brain and spinal cord — the decision-maker. The peripheral nervous system (PNS) is everything else — the wiring that connects the CNS to the body.

• The spinal cord carries messages up and down, and also handles simple reflexes on its own — you pull your hand off a hot pan before the brain registers pain.
• The somatic nervous system controls voluntary muscles and carries sensation in.
• The autonomic nervous system runs the organs without your say-so. Its sympathetic branch prepares for emergencies: heart rate and blood pressure up, digestion paused, pupils wide, sugar released for energy. Its parasympathetic branch reverses all that once the threat passes.

The sympathetic system cannot tell a leopard from a quarterly review. A public dressing-down in a sales meeting triggers the same racing heart and dry mouth as physical danger. That response was built for short, physical emergencies. Part 9 covers what happens when it stays switched on for months.

==========

💧 3. THE ENDOCRINE SYSTEM: SLOWER MESSENGERS

Alongside the nerves runs a second communication system: glands that release hormones into the blood. Hormones are slower than nerve signals — seconds to hours rather than milliseconds — but their effects last longer.

• The pituitary gland, controlled by the brain's hypothalamus, is called the master gland because it directs the others.
• The adrenal glands release adrenaline (fast, during the fight-or-flight response) and cortisol (slower; mobilises energy during prolonged stress, and in excess over long periods it harms health).
• Oxytocin is involved in childbirth, breastfeeding and bonding. Testosterone and oestrogen are the main sex hormones. Both oxytocin and testosterone feature in popular business claims that the evidence does not support well (section 8).

==========

🔬 4. HOW WE LOOK INSIDE

Much of what we know came from damage: studying what a person loses after a stroke or injury to one area. Modern tools look at living, healthy brains:

• EEG records electrical activity through the scalp. Excellent timing (milliseconds), poor location. Used for sleep research (Part 3).
• CT and MRI scans show structure — a detailed picture of the brain, but not what it's doing.
• fMRI shows activity indirectly, by tracking oxygen-rich blood flowing to busy regions. Good location, but the blood response lags the neural activity by several seconds.
• PET tracks a mildly radioactive tracer, showing which areas use the most energy.

Keep the fMRI limitation in mind: a brightly coloured scan shows where blood flow rose by a few per cent, averaged across people and many trials. It is not a picture of a thought.

==========

🧱 5. THE BRAIN FROM THE BOTTOM UP

A useful way to picture the brain is in layers, from the oldest structures that keep you alive to the newest that let you plan a quarter.

THE BRAINSTEM AND CEREBELLUM: LIFE SUPPORT AND COORDINATION

The medulla controls breathing and heart rate. The pons relays signals and helps regulate sleep. The reticular formation, a network running through the brainstem, controls alertness and filters which incoming information gets attention. The cerebellum at the back coordinates movement and balance and stores learned motor skills — typing, riding a bike, driving.

THE LIMBIC SYSTEM: EMOTION AND MEMORY

• Thalamus — the relay station; nearly all incoming senses (except smell) pass through it on the way to the cortex.
• Hypothalamus — small but powerful: hunger, thirst, body temperature, sex drive, and control of the pituitary. It links the brain to the hormone system.
• Hippocampus — essential for forming new long-term memories (Part 5).
• Amygdala — involved in fear and in flagging emotionally important events, which is why emotional events are remembered better.

THE CORTEX: THE OUTER LAYER

The cerebral cortex is the wrinkled outer layer, folded so that a large surface fits inside the skull. It is divided into four lobes on each side:

• Occipital lobe (back) — processes vision.
• Parietal lobe (top) — touch, temperature, body position; its front strip, the somatosensory cortex, maps the body's surface.
• Temporal lobe (sides) — hearing and understanding language (Wernicke's area, usually on the left).
• Frontal lobe (front) — planning, judgement, self-control, personality, and producing speech (Broca's area). Its rear strip, the motor cortex, controls voluntary movement.

Most of the cortex is association areas, which combine information rather than handle one sense. The frontal association areas, the prefrontal cortex, are the last to mature — into the mid-20s — and are the most sensitive to fatigue, alcohol and stress.

The classic case is Phineas Gage, a railway foreman who in 1848 survived an iron rod driven through his frontal lobe. Accounts described a sober, capable man becoming impulsive and unreliable. Historians now think the later stories were exaggerated and that Gage recovered more than the textbooks once said. But the core lesson has held: the frontal lobe is central to planning and self-control.

==========

🌗 6. TWO HEMISPHERES

The brain has a left and a right half, joined by a thick band of fibres, the corpus callosum. Each half mostly controls the opposite side of the body. In most people language is handled mainly on the left; the right is relatively stronger at some spatial and face-recognition tasks.

The evidence comes from split-brain patients (Roger Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga, from the 1960s), whose corpus callosum had been cut to control severe epilepsy. Shown a word only to the right hemisphere, they couldn't say it, but could pick out the object with the left hand. One striking finding: the speaking left hemisphere would confidently invent a reason for actions it hadn't caused. Gazzaniga called it the interpreter — and it is a useful warning about how readily people explain their own behaviour after the fact.

==========

🌱 7. PLASTICITY: THE BRAIN CHANGES WITH USE

The brain is not fixed after childhood. Neuroplasticity is its ability to rewire with experience: strengthening connections that are used and pruning ones that aren't. London taxi drivers, who must memorise thousands of streets, were found to have a larger rear hippocampus than comparison groups, and the size tracked years on the job. Skills built by deliberate practice are, physically, changes in the brain. That is the biological basis for the claim that capability is trainable, not fixed.

==========

🔁 8. HELD UP? FIVE NEURO-CLAIMS CHECKED

• "We only use 10% of our brain": False — Imaging shows activity across the whole brain over a day; damage almost anywhere causes some deficit.
• "People are left-brained (logical) or right-brained (creative)": False — Specific functions do lean to one side, but a 2013 University of Utah scan study of over 1,000 people found no evidence that individuals are left- or right-brain dominant overall.
• "Dopamine is the pleasure chemical": Oversimplified — Dopamine tracks wanting and prediction — it spikes for an unexpected reward and dips when an expected one fails to come. That is closer to "craving" than "enjoyment".
• "A sniff of oxytocin makes people trust you": Not supported — A famous 2005 study found nasal oxytocin raised trust in an investment game. Later replications and reviews found the effect unreliable.
• "Brain scans show what consumers really want": Mostly overstated — Scans can add some predictive power, but the usual claim relies on reverse inference (worked example 2).

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE 2 · THE REVERSE-INFERENCE TRAP

A neuromarketing agency shows that a client's ad "lights up the amygdala" and claims viewers felt fear-driven urgency. Suppose (illustrative numbers):

• When people genuinely feel fear, the amygdala activates 80% of the time.
• But it also activates for 30% of non-fear moments — anything novel, surprising or important.
• While watching ads, people feel genuine fear only 10% of the time.

P(fear | amygdala active)
  = P(active | fear) × P(fear) / P(active)
  = (0.8 × 0.1) / (0.8 × 0.1 + 0.3 × 0.9)
  = 0.08 / (0.08 + 0.27) = 0.08 / 0.35 ≈ 0.23

Given activation, the chance the viewer felt fear is only about 23%. Most brain regions do many jobs, so "region X lit up, therefore the person felt Y" is weak unless the region is highly specific to Y. Ask any neuro-vendor: how specific is that region?

==========

📝 SUMMARY

1️⃣ Neurons receive signals through dendrites and send them along the axon; myelin speeds them up. Firing is all-or-none; intensity is coded by how often neurons fire.
2️⃣ At the synapse, neurotransmitters carry the signal chemically. Glutamate excites, GABA calms; dopamine is about wanting and prediction more than pleasure; serotonin relates to mood.
3️⃣ The CNS (brain and spinal cord) decides; the PNS connects. Its sympathetic branch triggers fight-or-flight and the parasympathetic calms the body. Workplace threats trigger the same response as physical danger.
4️⃣ Hormones are slower but longer-lasting. Adrenaline and cortisol drive the stress response.
5️⃣ EEG has good timing, fMRI good location; neither is a picture of a thought.
6️⃣ Brainstem: life support. Cerebellum: coordination and motor skills. Limbic system: emotion and memory (amygdala, hippocampus). Cortex: four lobes, with the prefrontal cortex handling planning and self-control.
7️⃣ The hemispheres specialise in some functions, but "left-brained" and "right-brained" people don't exist.
8️⃣ Neuroplasticity: the brain rewires with practice, so skills are physically trainable.
9️⃣ Treat neuromarketing claims with care: reverse inference is weak unless the brain region is specific.

➡️ NEXT: Psychology for Managers 2/12 — Sensation and Perception

==========

Sources: chapter structure follows Ciccarelli & White, Psychology, 4th ed. (Pearson), Ch. 2; text and figures are original. Left/right brain: Nielsen et al., PLOS ONE, 2013. Taxi drivers: Maguire et al., PNAS, 2000. Oxytocin and trust: Kosfeld et al., Nature, 2005, and later reviews of replication failures. Reverse inference: Poldrack, Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 2006. Worked-example numbers are illustrative.

==========

notes.body:
🧠 PSYCHOLOGY FOR MANAGERS, PART 2: SENSATION AND PERCEPTION

==========

⚡ TL;DR

Sensation is the raw signal; perception is what the brain makes of it, and most marketing battles are won at perception.

Weber's law says a change is noticed only when it is a big enough proportion of the original. That is why packs shrink by a few grams instead of prices rising by a round rupee, and why a ₹500 discount feels generous on ₹5,000 and invisible on ₹50,000.

The headline result: expectations change experience itself. The same wine labelled at a higher price was rated more pleasant and lit up pleasure-linked brain areas. Subliminal advertising, by contrast, rests on a 1957 study its author admitted was meaningless.

The chapter structure follows Ciccarelli & White, Psychology (4th ed.), Chapter 3. The text, examples and diagrams are original.

==========

👁️ 1. SENSATION VERSUS PERCEPTION

Sensation is the raw input: light hitting the eye, pressure on the skin, molecules on the tongue. Each sense organ converts its kind of energy into nerve signals — a step called transduction. Perception is what the brain does with those signals: organising them, interpreting them, and giving them meaning. Sensation tells you there are red and white shapes on a shelf. Perception tells you it's a can of Coke, and that you want one.

The distinction matters because most marketing battles are won or lost at the perception stage. Two products can deliver identical sensations and be perceived very differently.

==========

📏 2. THRESHOLDS: WHAT WE NOTICE

The absolute threshold is the smallest amount of a stimulus a person can detect half the time — the faintest sound, the dimmest light. The more commercially useful number is the difference threshold, or just noticeable difference (JND): the smallest change a person can detect half the time.

In the 1830s Ernst Weber found that the JND is not a fixed amount but a fixed proportion of the original. This is Weber's law:

ΔI = k × I
ΔI = the just noticeable change
I  = the starting intensity
k  = Weber fraction (constant for a given sense)

If you're holding a 1 kg bag, you might need about 20 g more to notice the difference; holding 10 kg, you'd need about 200 g. The fraction differs by sense — we are much more sensitive to some changes than others — but the proportional logic holds over a wide middle range.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE 1 · SHRINKFLATION AND WEBER'S LAW

A biscuit brand sells a 100 g pack. Input costs rise. Suppose consumer tests show that people notice a change in pack weight about half the time once it reaches 10% (k = 0.10; illustrative).

JND = k × I = 0.10 × 100 g = 10 g

Cut to 95 g → change 5 g  < 10 g → mostly unnoticed
Cut to 88 g → change 12 g > 10 g → mostly noticed

Price: ₹10 → ₹11 is a 10% change, and a whole
rupee on a round number is very easy to notice.

This is why brands shrink packs in small steps instead of raising round-number prices. The same law works in reverse for improvements: a "new, improved" change must clear the JND, or customers won't perceive any difference and the investment is wasted. Weber's law tells you how big a visible change has to be.

Shrinkflation is legal in India if the label states the true net quantity, as the Legal Metrology rules require. It is also widely reported in the press — customers notice eventually, especially when someone points it out.

Sensory adaptation is the senses' tendency to stop responding to an unchanging stimulus. You stop smelling your own perfume within minutes, and stop hearing the ceiling fan. Related is habituation, where the brain learns to ignore a repeated, unimportant stimulus — the reason the same banner ad in the same spot stops being seen. Change is what grabs attention.

==========

🌈 3. VISION

Light enters through the cornea and pupil; the lens focuses it onto the retina at the back of the eye. The retina has two kinds of receptor:

• Rods — about 120 million, very sensitive to dim light, no colour, mostly in the edges of vision.
• Cones — about 6 million, need brighter light, see colour and fine detail, concentrated in the centre (the fovea).

Where the optic nerve leaves the eye there are no receptors at all — the blind spot. You never notice it because the brain fills in the gap, an early hint of how much perception is construction.

Colour is explained by two theories that are both right, at different stages. The trichromatic theory: three types of cone respond most to short (blue), medium (green) and long (red) wavelengths, and every colour is a mix of their signals. The opponent-process theory: further along, cells work in opposing pairs (red–green, blue–yellow, black–white). Stare at a red patch, then look at a white wall, and you see a green afterimage as the tired red signal lets green dominate.

Red–green colour blindness is common in men — roughly 1 in 12 in many populations. Practical point: a sales dashboard that shows good and bad territories only in red and green is unreadable to a meaningful share of your managers. Add labels, shapes or a blue–orange palette.

==========

👂 4. HEARING

Sound is vibration in the air. Its frequency is heard as pitch, its amplitude as loudness (measured in decibels, dB), and its mix of frequencies as timbre — why a flute and a violin playing the same note sound different. The decibel scale is logarithmic: every 10 dB is ten times the sound intensity. Long exposure above about 85 dB — heavy traffic, a loud factory floor — can permanently damage hearing, which is a real occupational issue in manufacturing plants.

==========

👃 5. TASTE, SMELL, TOUCH AND PAIN

Taste receptors detect five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami (savoury, the taste of glutamate). Most of what we call "flavour", though, is smell. Hold your nose and an apple and a raw onion are surprisingly hard to tell apart.

Smell has an unusual route: it is the one sense that doesn't pass through the thalamus first, and it connects closely to the limbic system's emotion and memory areas. That is the logic behind scent marketing — hotel lobbies, car showrooms, the bakery smell near a supermarket entrance. The effects in studies are real but usually modest, and they depend on the scent fitting the product.

The skin senses pressure, temperature and pain. The gate-control theory of pain says signals pass through a "gate" in the spinal cord that other inputs can partly close: rubbing a bumped elbow really does reduce the pain. The brain can also close the gate from above — attention and expectation change how much something hurts.

==========

🧩 6. PERCEPTION: HOW THE BRAIN ORGANISES

The Gestalt psychologists (Part 0) showed that we organise sensations into wholes using predictable rules:

• Figure–ground — we separate an object from its background. Packaging that doesn't stand out from the shelf behind it fails at this first step.
• Proximity — things close together are seen as a group. Products shelved together are read as a range.
• Similarity — things that look alike are grouped. A consistent pack colour across a range is "brand blocking".
• Closure — we complete incomplete shapes. Several well-known logos rely on it.
• Continuity — we follow smooth lines and patterns.

The brain also holds things constant as the input changes. Size constancy: a person walking away doesn't seem to shrink. Colour constancy: a white shirt looks white under yellow bulbs and blue daylight, though the light reaching your eye is very different. Constancy has limits, which matters in a paint store — under tube lights a warm shade can read cooler than on the customer's wall, which is why shade cards and sample pots exist.

Depth comes from both eyes together (each sees a slightly different view) and from single-eye cues artists use: nearer objects overlap farther ones, parallel lines converge in the distance, distant things look hazier and smaller. Illusions such as the Müller-Lyer lines (two equal lines that look different lengths because of the arrow-fins on their ends) show these normally helpful rules misfiring.

==========

🍷 7. EXPECTATION SHAPES EXPERIENCE

Bottom-up processing builds perception from the raw features upward. Top-down processing uses what you already know and expect to interpret them. Both run all the time, and top-down influence is far stronger than most people assume. A perceptual set is a readiness to perceive something in a particular way — and it changes not only what we judge, but what we actually experience.

The clearest commercial demonstration is a 2008 study by Hilke Plassmann and colleagues. Participants tasted wines in a brain scanner and were told the price. The same wine, labelled at $90 instead of $10, was rated more pleasant — and activity rose in a brain area linked to experienced pleasantness. The price did not just change the opinion; it changed the experience. Blind taste tests across many categories show the same pattern: labels and brands shift ratings even when the product is identical.

For a manager the implication cuts two ways. Presentation, price and brand are part of the product, not decoration around it. And internal product tests should be run blind, or your team's expectations will contaminate the result.

==========

🔁 8. HELD UP? SUBLIMINAL ADVERTISING AND OTHER CLAIMS

In 1957 market researcher James Vicary claimed that flashing "Eat Popcorn" and "Drink Coca-Cola" on a cinema screen too briefly to see had raised popcorn sales by 58% and Coke by 18%. It caused a panic and calls for bans. In 1962 Vicary admitted the study's data were too small to mean anything, and it is widely regarded as fabricated.

Real research since then has found that a stimulus below awareness can have small, short-lived effects. In a 2006 Dutch study, a subliminal brand name nudged choice of a drink — but only among people who were already thirsty, and only briefly. There is no good evidence that subliminal messages can make people want something they didn't already want.

• Hidden messages in ads control buying: No — The famous study was faked; real effects are tiny and need a matching need.
• Price and brand change how a product tastes: Yes — Repeated in blind and branded tests; supported by brain-imaging work.
• Small pack reductions go unnoticed: Largely — Weber's law is robust. Customers do eventually notice, often via media coverage.
• Specific colours reliably cause specific emotions (red = urgency, blue = trust): Weak — Colour effects exist but depend heavily on context and culture; universal "colour psychology" charts are mostly folklore.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE 2 · SAME RUPEE, DIFFERENT FEELING

A dealer gets ₹500 off on a ₹5,000 order and ₹500 off on a ₹50,000 order. Same rupees. Weber's law predicts very different perceived value, because perception tracks the proportion:

₹500 / ₹5,000  = 10%  → clearly felt
₹500 / ₹50,000 =  1%  → barely registers

To make a discount feel the same on the bigger order, you would need roughly 10% of it — ₹5,000. So large orders call for different levers: a free item, extended credit, or a gift that is valued in its own right, rather than a small cut to a large number.

==========

📝 SUMMARY

1️⃣ Sensation is detecting energy and converting it to nerve signals (transduction); perception is organising and interpreting those signals.
2️⃣ The JND follows Weber's law: the noticeable change is a constant proportion of the starting level (ΔI = k × I). It explains small-step shrinkflation and why improvements must be large enough to be seen.
3️⃣ Sensory adaptation and habituation make unchanging stimuli disappear; change grabs attention.
4️⃣ Rods see dim light, cones see colour and detail. Colour works through three cone types and then opposing pairs. Around 1 in 12 men are red–green colour blind.
5️⃣ Most flavour is smell; smell links directly to emotion and memory areas. Pain passes through a "gate" that other inputs and expectations can partly close.
6️⃣ Gestalt principles — figure–ground, proximity, similarity, closure, continuity — govern how shelves and packs are read.
7️⃣ Top-down expectations change actual experience: the same wine with a higher price tastes better. Run product tests blind.
8️⃣ Subliminal advertising doesn't work as claimed; the 1957 study was faked.

➡️ NEXT: Psychology for Managers 3/12 — Consciousness, Sleep and Attention

==========

Sources: chapter structure follows Ciccarelli & White, Psychology, 4th ed. (Pearson), Ch. 3; text and figures are original. Wine and price: Plassmann et al., PNAS, 2008. Subliminal priming: Karremans, Stroebe & Claus, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 2006. Vicary's 1962 admission was reported in Advertising Age. Weber fractions in the worked examples are illustrative.

==========
