notes.body:
🧠 PSYCHOLOGY FOR MANAGERS, PART 3: CONSCIOUSNESS, SLEEP AND ATTENTION

==========

⚡ TL;DR

Attention is a narrow spotlight: about half of people in one famous study missed a gorilla walking through a video, and multitasking is really costly task-switching. A phone call while driving competes for the same attention even hands-free.

Sleep cycles every 90 minutes or so, with deep sleep early and REM late. Six hours a night for two weeks impairs attention as much as one to two nights without any sleep, and the people affected barely notice. Long hours awake impair performance like alcohol.

The headline result: a 3-second microsleep at 60 km/h means 50 metres with nobody steering. Sleep and travel policy is a safety issue, not a perk.

The chapter structure follows Ciccarelli & White, Psychology (4th ed.), Chapter 4. The text, examples and diagrams are original.

==========

💡 1. WHAT CONSCIOUSNESS IS

Consciousness is your awareness of yourself and your surroundings at a given moment: what you're thinking, feeling and perceiving. Waking consciousness is the ordinary clear, organised state. Altered states are shifts in the quality or pattern of awareness — sleep, dreaming, daydreaming, hypnosis, meditation, and the effects of drugs. Much of the brain's work never reaches consciousness at all: you don't experience the calculations that keep you balanced or that turn a shape into a word. Consciousness is more like a spotlight than a room.

==========

🔦 2. ATTENTION: A NARROW SPOTLIGHT

Selective attention is the ability to focus on one input and filter out the rest. The classic example is the cocktail-party effect: in a noisy room you follow one conversation and tune out the others — yet you'll still notice if someone across the room says your name. The filter isn't a wall; it lets through things that matter to you.

The cost of a narrow spotlight is that we miss things we assume we'd see. In a famous 1999 study by Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris, people counted basketball passes in a video. About half failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit who walked through the middle of the game and thumped their chest. This is inattentional blindness: failing to see something in plain view because attention is elsewhere. Its cousin, change blindness, is failing to notice a change between one view and the next.

THE MULTITASKING MYTH

For anything that needs thought, the brain doesn't run tasks in parallel; it switches between them. Each switch has a cost in time and errors, and the costs are largest for complex or unfamiliar tasks. People who believe they multitask well tend to perform no better, and in some studies worse. Two tasks combine smoothly only if one is so practised that it's nearly automatic — walking while talking, not drafting an email during a negotiation.

The most serious case is the phone while driving. A hands-free kit frees the hands but not the attention; the conversation still competes for the same limited capacity. For a sales force that spends half its working life on the road, "no calls while driving" is a safety rule, not a courtesy.

==========

⏰ 3. THE BODY CLOCK

Circadian rhythms are biological cycles of roughly 24 hours — body temperature, alertness, hormone levels. The master clock is a small cluster of cells in the hypothalamus, the suprachiasmatic nucleus, which is reset daily by light reaching the eyes. As evening light fades, the clock signals the pineal gland to release melatonin, which makes you sleepy. Bright screens late at night delay that signal.

Two features matter at work. Most people have a natural dip in alertness in the early afternoon — the post-lunch slump is mostly the clock, not the lunch. And the clock adjusts slowly: jet lag and rotating night shifts leave people working while their body expects sleep, with more errors and accidents in those hours.

==========

🌙 4. THE STAGES OF SLEEP

Using the EEG (Part 1), researchers found that sleep is not one state but a repeating cycle:

• N1 — light sleep, a few minutes; easily woken; sometimes a sudden jerk.
• N2 — true sleep; bursts of activity called sleep spindles; about half the night is spent here.
• N3 — deep, slow-wave sleep; hardest to wake from; the body's physical repair and growth-hormone release are concentrated here.
• REM (rapid eye movement) sleep — the brain is highly active, the eyes dart, and most vivid dreams occur. The body's major muscles are temporarily paralysed, so you don't act out your dreams.

==========

😴 5. WHAT SLEEP LOSS COSTS

Why we sleep has several answers, all partly right: to conserve energy and stay safe at night (the adaptive view), to repair the body and clear the brain's waste products (the restorative view), and to consolidate the day's learning into long-term memory. Whatever the reason, the cost of skipping it is well measured.

In a 2003 laboratory study by Hans Van Dongen and colleagues, people restricted to six hours a night for two weeks declined steadily on attention tests until they were as impaired as people kept awake for one to two nights straight. The most important finding: the six-hour group rated themselves as only slightly sleepy. Chronic sleep loss impairs the judgement you would use to notice it.

Other studies have compared fatigue with alcohol. After about 17–19 hours awake — up at 6 am, still driving home at midnight — performance on some tests falls to the level seen at a blood-alcohol concentration of about 0.05%. India's legal driving limit is 0.03%.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE 1 · THE MICROSLEEP

A tired driver can fall into a microsleep: a lapse of a few seconds, often with eyes open, that the driver may not even notice. How far does the car travel during a 3-second microsleep?

60 km/h = 60,000 m / 3,600 s ≈ 16.7 m/s
3 s × 16.7 m/s ≈ 50 m

80 km/h ≈ 22.2 m/s → 3 s × 22.2 ≈ 67 m

Fifty to seventy metres — two and a half to three cricket pitches — with nobody steering. That is the case for a company rule capping driving after a long day, or for paying for a night's stay over pushing a rep to drive home.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE 2 · SLEEP DEBT OVER A WEEK

A manager needs about 8 hours but sleeps 6 on weeknights, then 9 on Saturday and Sunday.

Weekday shortfall: 5 nights × (8 − 6) h = 10 h
Weekend payback:   2 nights × (9 − 8) h =  2 h
Net debt carried into Monday            =  8 h

A weekend lie-in recovers some alertness, but studies of "catch-up" sleep show it does not fully reverse the effects of a week of restriction, and the pattern itself disturbs the body clock. Regular hours beat recovery binges.

==========

🩺 6. SLEEP DISORDERS

• Insomnia — persistent trouble falling or staying asleep. The most effective long-term treatment is a structured talking therapy, cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), not sleeping pills.
• Obstructive sleep apnoea — the airway repeatedly closes during sleep, so breathing stops briefly many times an hour. Signs include loud snoring, gasping and heavy daytime sleepiness. It is common, underdiagnosed and a known risk factor for road accidents among professional drivers. It is treatable.
• Narcolepsy — sudden, uncontrollable attacks of sleep during the day, sometimes going straight into REM.
• Sleepwalking and night terrors happen in deep N3 sleep and are usually not remembered; nightmares are bad dreams in REM and usually are.

==========

💭 7. DREAMS

Freud saw dreams as disguised wish-fulfilment, with a hidden meaning to decode. There is little scientific support for that. The activation-synthesis theory (Hobson and McCarley, 1977) proposed that during REM the brainstem sends random signals and the cortex stitches them into a story. Later views add that dreams draw heavily on the day's concerns and may help process emotions and memories. The honest summary: we know when dreams happen better than why.

==========

🌀 8. HYPNOSIS

Hypnosis is a state of focused attention in which a person becomes more responsive to suggestion. It is real in the sense that people's experience changes — it can reduce how much pain bothers someone, which is why it has a role alongside medical treatment. People differ widely in how hypnotisable they are. Two views compete: that hypnosis splits awareness into separate streams (dissociation), or that it is people playing the role of a hypnotised person in response to expectations (social-cognitive theory). What it cannot do is reliably recover hidden memories; it makes people more confident in what they recall, including things that never happened (Part 5).

==========

☕ 9. PSYCHOACTIVE DRUGS

Psychoactive drugs alter thinking, perception, mood or behaviour. Repeated use can bring tolerance (needing more for the same effect), withdrawal (unpleasant symptoms on stopping), and dependence, which can be physical, psychological or both. The main groups:

• Stimulants speed up the nervous system: caffeine, nicotine, and illegal drugs such as cocaine and amphetamines.
• Depressants slow it down: alcohol, and sedatives. Alcohol first reduces inhibition, which is why it feels like a stimulant at a party, and in larger amounts impairs judgement, coordination and memory.
• Opioids relieve pain and produce euphoria; they carry a high risk of dependence.
• Hallucinogens alter perception, for example LSD; cannabis has mixed effects.

The workplace version is mostly legal drugs. Caffeine masks sleepiness without repaying sleep debt, and late in the day it delays sleep further. Alcohol is built into many sales cultures through dealer meets and channel parties; it helps people fall asleep but fragments the second half of the night, cutting REM. Hosting the party is a business choice. Making drinking part of how people are judged is a culture problem.

==========

🔁 10. HELD UP?

• "I can multitask": No — The brain switches, with costs. Only highly automatic tasks combine well.
• "I'm fine on five or six hours": Rarely — True short sleepers exist but are rare. Most restricted sleepers are impaired and don't feel it.
• "Weekend lie-ins cancel weekday debt": Partly — Some recovery, not full.
• "You can learn new material while asleep": No — Sleep strengthens what you learned while awake; you can't absorb new complex information while asleep.
• "Hypnosis recovers buried memories": No — It raises confidence, not accuracy.
• A short nap restores alertness: Yes — Naps of about 10–20 minutes improve alertness without deep-sleep grogginess.

==========

📝 SUMMARY

1️⃣ Consciousness is moment-to-moment awareness; sleep, dreams, hypnosis and drugs are altered states. Most brain processing never becomes conscious.
2️⃣ Attention is a narrow spotlight. Inattentional blindness means we miss things in plain view. Multitasking is really task-switching, with costs; phone calls while driving are dangerous even hands-free.
3️⃣ The circadian clock (suprachiasmatic nucleus, melatonin, light) runs on about 24 hours and explains the afternoon dip, jet lag and shift-work errors.
4️⃣ Sleep cycles roughly every 90 minutes through N1, N2, N3 (deep) and REM (dreams, muscle paralysis). Deep sleep comes early; REM late.
5️⃣ Six hours a night for two weeks impairs attention as much as one to two nights without sleep, and people don't notice. Long hours awake impair like alcohol. A 3-second microsleep at 60 km/h is 50 m unsteered.
6️⃣ Sleep apnoea is common and a road-safety risk; insomnia is best treated with CBT-I.
7️⃣ Dream theories range from Freud (little support) to activation-synthesis.
8️⃣ Hypnosis raises suggestibility and can ease pain, but doesn't recover memories.
9️⃣ Drugs are stimulants, depressants, opioids or hallucinogens; tolerance, withdrawal and dependence follow repeated use. Caffeine masks sleep debt; alcohol disrupts sleep.

➡️ NEXT: Psychology for Managers 4/12 — Learning

==========

Sources: chapter structure follows Ciccarelli & White, Psychology, 4th ed. (Pearson), Ch. 4; text and figures are original. Inattentional blindness: Simons & Chabris, Perception, 1999. Sleep restriction: Van Dongen et al., Sleep, 2003. Fatigue and alcohol: Williamson & Feyer, Occupational and Environmental Medicine, 2000. Activation-synthesis: Hobson & McCarley, American Journal of Psychiatry, 1977. India's limit of 30 mg per 100 ml blood: Motor Vehicles Act, s. 185.

==========

notes.body:
🧠 PSYCHOLOGY FOR MANAGERS, PART 4: LEARNING

==========

⚡ TL;DR

Every dealer scheme is a learning experiment: a target behaviour, a consequence, and a schedule.

Classical conditioning is how brands borrow feelings from music, festivals and celebrities. Operant conditioning is how consequences shape behaviour: reinforcement increases it, punishment decreases it, and removing a hassle is an underused reward. Teams also learn by watching what leaders do and what gets publicly rewarded.

The headline result: a quarterly bonus is a fixed-interval schedule, and fixed-interval schedules produce a slow start and a rush before the deadline, exactly the quarter-end hockey stick. Shorter intervals, rewards on secondary sales and variable elements flatten it.

The chapter structure follows Ciccarelli & White, Psychology (4th ed.), Chapter 5. The text, examples and diagrams are original.

==========

🔔 1. CLASSICAL CONDITIONING: LEARNING BY ASSOCIATION

In the 1890s the Russian physiologist Ivan Pavlov was studying digestion in dogs when he noticed they began to salivate before food arrived — at the sight of the assistant who fed them. He then paired a neutral sound with food. After repeated pairings, the sound alone produced salivation. The terms:

• Unconditioned stimulus (UCS) — triggers a response naturally, with no learning (food).
• Unconditioned response (UCR) — the natural response (salivation to food).
• Conditioned stimulus (CS) — a once-neutral stimulus that, after pairing, triggers the response (the bell).
• Conditioned response (CR) — the learned response to the CS (salivation to the bell).

Four further features matter in practice. Extinction: if the CS keeps appearing without the UCS, the response fades. Spontaneous recovery: after a break, an extinguished response briefly returns. Generalisation: similar stimuli trigger the response too. Discrimination: with training, the learner responds only to the exact stimulus.

WHERE IT SHOWS UP IN BUSINESS

Advertising is largely classical conditioning: pair a brand (neutral) with music, celebrities, happiness or festivals (stimuli that already produce good feelings), often enough that the brand alone produces a warm response. Generalisation explains why look-alike packaging works for copycat brands, and why a scandal around one product can hurt the whole range. Conditioning also works against you. A dealer who is shouted at during every visit learns to feel tense when your rep's bike pulls up.

Two classic studies set the limits. In 1920 John Watson and Rosalie Rayner conditioned an infant, "Little Albert", to fear a white rat by pairing it with a loud noise; the fear generalised to other furry things. The study would be unethical today and was methodologically weak, but it showed emotions can be conditioned. And in the 1960s John Garcia found that rats learned to avoid a taste after a single pairing with nausea hours later — conditioned taste aversion. Not all associations are equally easy: we are biologically prepared to learn some, like linking food with illness, very fast. One bad experience with a product can do what a hundred good adverts can't undo.

==========

🎯 2. OPERANT CONDITIONING: LEARNING BY CONSEQUENCES

Classical conditioning is about involuntary responses. Operant conditioning is about voluntary behaviour and what follows it. Edward Thorndike's law of effect (1898): behaviour followed by a pleasing consequence is more likely to be repeated; behaviour followed by an unpleasant one, less likely. B. F. Skinner turned this into a precise science from the 1930s.

The vocabulary trips everyone up, so note it carefully. Reinforcement always increases a behaviour; punishment always decreases it. Positive means something is added; negative means something is taken away.

• Increase behaviour: Positive reinforcement — a bonus for hitting target — Negative reinforcement — no more daily call-reports once a rep's pipeline is healthy
• Decrease behaviour: Positive punishment — a public reprimand for a missed target — Negative punishment — losing the company car for a quarter

"Negative reinforcement" is not punishment. It strengthens behaviour by removing something unpleasant — and it is one of the most underused tools in management. Freedom from micromanagement is a powerful reward.

WHY PUNISHMENT USUALLY DISAPPOINTS

Punishment can stop a behaviour quickly, but it has known side effects. It tells people what not to do, not what to do. It works mainly when the punisher is present, so the behaviour goes underground. It produces fear and resentment toward the person punishing. And it models aggression. Punishment works best when immediate, consistent, and paired with reinforcement of the right alternative behaviour.

SHAPING

Complex behaviour rarely appears fully formed to be rewarded. Shaping reinforces successive approximations: reward the first step toward the goal, then require a bit more before the next reward. A new rep is praised for completing a dealer call, then for a call with a proper order review, then for a call that brings in a new product line.

==========

📅 3. SCHEDULES OF REINFORCEMENT

When the reward arrives matters as much as what it is. Continuous reinforcement (every time) teaches a new behaviour fastest but extinguishes fastest when rewards stop. Partial reinforcement is slower to learn but far more durable. There are four partial schedules:

• Fixed ratio (FR): Reward after every n responses — High rate, pause after each reward — Commission on every 10 units
• Variable ratio (VR): Reward after an unpredictable number — Highest, steadiest rate; hardest to extinguish — Lottery, scratch cards, cold calling
• Fixed interval (FI): First response after a set time is rewarded — Slow start, rush just before the deadline ("scallop") — Quarterly target bonus
• Variable interval (VI): First response after an unpredictable time — Slow but steady — Surprise audits, random checks

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE 1 · THE QUARTER-END HOCKEY STICK

A company pays its sales team on a quarterly target — a fixed-interval schedule. A typical territory's quarter (illustrative):

Month 1:  25% of quarterly volume
Month 2:  30%
Month 3:  45%   ← the "scallop"

Month 3 vs month 1: 45 / 25 = 1.8 times

This is exactly what fixed-interval schedules produce in the lab: little effort early, a burst near the deadline. In channel sales the burst is often "loading" — pushing stock onto distributors with extra discounts — which then depresses the next quarter's first month. Remedies follow from the schedule: monthly or weekly targets (shorter intervals), rewards tied to secondary sales (what dealers actually sell on), or some variable elements so effort pays off throughout the quarter.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE 2 · PRICING A VARIABLE-RATIO SCHEME

A painter loyalty programme gives one scratch card per 10-litre purchase. Prizes: 1 card in 20 wins ₹1,000; 1 card in 5 wins ₹50; the rest win nothing.

Expected value per card
  = (1/20 × ₹1,000) + (1/5 × ₹50)
  = ₹50 + ₹10 = ₹60

It costs the same on average as a flat ₹60 cashback per purchase. But a variable-ratio schedule tends to produce steadier engagement and is slower to extinguish once prizes stop, and the occasional ₹1,000 winner becomes word-of-mouth. Two caveats. Payouts must be real and visible, or trust collapses. And this is the same mechanism that makes gambling compelling, so it should never be designed to exploit people who can't afford it.

==========

👀 4. LEARNING BY WATCHING

We don't have to be rewarded ourselves to learn. In Albert Bandura's 1961 Bobo doll studies, children who watched an adult attack an inflatable doll later copied the attacks, often with the same words; children who watched a calm adult did not. Observational learning needs four things: attention to the model, memory of what they did, the ability to reproduce it, and motivation to do so — often from seeing the model rewarded (vicarious reinforcement).

The management implication is direct: teams copy what leaders do and what gets rewarded, far more than what the policy says. If the rep who quietly over-promises to dealers wins "Salesman of the Quarter", everyone has just learned the real rule. Role models, ride-alongs and shadowing are observational learning on purpose.

==========

💡 5. LEARNING BY THINKING

• Latent learning — Edward Tolman found rats that explored a maze without reward learned its layout anyway, and used it immediately once food appeared. Learning can happen without showing in behaviour until there's a reason to use it. A new rep riding along for a month may know more than his reports show.
• Insight — Wolfgang Köhler's chimpanzees, after failing to reach bananas, suddenly stacked boxes or joined sticks. Some problems are solved by a sudden restructuring, not by trial and error.
• Learned helplessness — Martin Seligman found that animals exposed to shocks they couldn't control later stopped trying to escape even when escape was possible. In 2016 Seligman and Steven Maier revised the explanation: passivity is the brain's default response to prolonged bad events, and what has to be learned is that you have control. The workplace version is a rep who keeps missing targets set impossibly high, and who stops trying. Restoring some control — targets he can influence, small wins — is the fix.

==========

🔁 6. HELD UP?

• Classical and operant conditioning, schedule effects: Robust — Among the most replicated findings in psychology, across species.
• Rewards kill intrinsic motivation ("overjustification"): Conditional — Expected, tangible rewards for an activity people already enjoy can reduce their interest once rewards stop. For dull tasks, or for unexpected and verbal rewards, the effect is small or absent. Still debated.
• "10,000 hours of practice makes an expert": Overstated — A 2014 meta-analysis found deliberate practice explained about a quarter of performance differences in games, a fifth in music, about a sixth in sports — and under 1% in professions. Practice matters; it isn't the whole story.
• Little Albert proves phobias are conditioned: Weak evidence — One child, poor controls. Conditioning does contribute to fears, from better later studies.
• Children imitate aggression they watch: Holds — Repeated in lab settings; how much it explains real-world violence is debated.

▸ INCENTIVE DESIGN CHECKLIST

1. Reward the behaviour you want, not a proxy that can be gamed (secondary sales, not loading).
2. Keep the gap between behaviour and reward short.
3. Choose the schedule deliberately; long fixed intervals create deadline rushes.
4. Use negative reinforcement: remove hassle as a reward.
5. Punish sparingly, immediately and with a clear alternative.
6. Watch what you publicly reward — everyone else is learning from it.

==========

📝 SUMMARY

1️⃣ Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour due to experience.
2️⃣ Classical conditioning pairs a neutral stimulus with one that naturally triggers a response, until the neutral one triggers it alone. It underlies brand advertising; extinction, generalisation and discrimination follow predictable rules. Some associations, like taste aversion, form in one trial.
3️⃣ Operant conditioning: consequences shape voluntary behaviour. Reinforcement increases behaviour, punishment decreases it; positive adds, negative removes. Punishment has side effects; shaping builds complex behaviour step by step.
4️⃣ Schedules: variable ratio gives the highest, most durable response; fixed interval produces deadline rushes — the quarter-end hockey stick.
5️⃣ Observational learning (Bandura) needs attention, memory, ability and motivation. Teams copy what leaders model and reward.
6️⃣ Cognitive learning: latent learning, insight, and learned helplessness, now understood as the default that a sense of control reverses.
7️⃣ Rewards can undermine interest in enjoyable tasks under some conditions; "10,000 hours" overstates the role of practice.

➡️ NEXT: Psychology for Managers 5/12 — Memory

==========

Sources: chapter structure follows Ciccarelli & White, Psychology, 4th ed. (Pearson), Ch. 5; text and figures are original. Bobo doll: Bandura, Ross & Ross, 1961. Learned helplessness revision: Maier & Seligman, Psychological Review, 2016. Overjustification: Deci, Koestner & Ryan, Psychological Bulletin, 1999. Practice: Macnamara, Hambrick & Oswald, Psychological Science, 2014. Worked-example figures are illustrative.

==========

🔗 The PDF has the diagrams, worked examples, practice problems, glossary and answer key. Coming next: Psychology for Managers 5/12 — Memory

notes.body:
🧠 PSYCHOLOGY FOR MANAGERS, PART 5: MEMORY

==========

⚡ TL;DR

Memory fails at three points: getting information in, keeping it, and getting it back out. Working memory holds only about four chunks for about 20 seconds, so chunking and meaning-based rehearsal decide what survives.

Forgetting is steep in the first day and then levels off. Quizzes beat re-reading, spaced reviews beat one long session, and practice in field-like conditions beats a hotel ballroom.

The headline result: memory is rebuilt every time, not replayed. One word in a question raised speed estimates of a crash and made people remember broken glass that wasn't there. In a dispute over what was promised, both sides can be honest and wrong, so write it down.

The chapter structure follows Ciccarelli & White, Psychology (4th ed.), Chapter 6. The text, examples and diagrams are original.

==========

🗂️ 1. THE THREE-STAGE MODEL

The most useful map is the information-processing model (Atkinson and Shiffrin, 1968). Information passes through three stores, each with its own capacity and duration:

SENSORY MEMORY

Every sense holds a brief, detailed copy of its input. In 1960 George Sperling flashed a grid of 12 letters for a twentieth of a second. People could report only about four — but if a tone told them which row to report after the grid vanished, they could report almost any row. The whole image was there for a fraction of a second, then faded. Visual (iconic) memory lasts well under a second; auditory (echoic) memory a few seconds, which is why you can "replay" what someone just said. Only what you attend to moves on.

SHORT-TERM AND WORKING MEMORY

Short-term memory (STM) holds what you are thinking about right now. Two limits define it. Duration: without rehearsal, most of it is gone within about 20 seconds. Capacity: George Miller's famous 1956 estimate was "seven, plus or minus two" items; more recent work puts the true limit nearer four meaningful chunks.

Chunking — grouping items into meaningful units — is how we beat the limit. Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch (1974) refined STM into working memory: an active workspace with a central controller (the central executive), a verbal store you hear in your head (the phonological loop), and a visual one (the visuospatial sketchpad). A dealer reading out a long order while you also check stock on screen is loading both, and the central executive is the bottleneck.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE 1 · CHUNKING

A rep must remember a dealer code: 4 0 7 2 1 9 8 3 5 6 1.

As single digits:   11 items → well over capacity
As chunks:          407 · 219 · 835 · 61  → 4 chunks
With meaning:       "Kochi-407", "2019", "835", "61"
                    → easier still

Same information, a third the load. This is why phone numbers, PINs and SKU codes are printed in groups, and why a pitch with "three reasons" is remembered and one with eleven isn't. In product training, organise features into a few named groups before presenting the details.

Two kinds of rehearsal keep information alive. Maintenance rehearsal — repeating it over and over — holds it in STM but transfers it poorly to long-term memory. Elaborative rehearsal — linking it to what you already know, asking what it means — encodes it much more durably. Craik and Lockhart's levels-of-processing idea (1972) makes the same point: the more deeply you think about the meaning of something, the better you remember it.

==========

🏛️ 2. LONG-TERM MEMORY

Long-term memory (LTM) has no practical capacity limit. It holds two broad kinds of knowledge:

• Procedural (implicit) memory — skills and habits: driving, typing, the routine of a dealer visit. Often hard to put into words, and resistant to forgetting.
• Declarative (explicit) memory — facts you can state. It splits into semantic memory (general knowledge: the price list, the capital of Kerala) and episodic memory (personal events: what happened at last month's dealer meet).

LTM is organised by meaning. One model pictures it as a semantic network of linked ideas: think "premium emulsion" and related nodes — price, brand, a particular customer — become easier to reach. This is why a strong brand association pays off at the shelf: the cue triggers the whole network.

==========

🔑 3. GETTING IT BACK OUT

Retrieval cues are stimuli that help you access a memory. The encoding specificity principle: memory is best when the conditions at retrieval match those at encoding. In a classic 1975 study, divers who learned word lists underwater recalled them better underwater, and those who learned on land recalled better on land. Train reps in conditions that resemble the field — role-plays with real dealer objections, not slides in a hotel ballroom.

Recognition (picking the right answer from options) is much easier than recall (producing it from nothing). That's why customers who can't name your brand will still pick it out on a shelf — and why brand-recall surveys understate what a brand has achieved.

The serial position effect: in a list, people remember the first items (primacy, because they got more rehearsal) and the last ones (recency, still in working memory) better than the middle. If you're one of six agencies pitching, avoid the middle slots. In a presentation, put your key point first and repeat it last.

THE TESTING EFFECT

Retrieving information strengthens it more than re-reading it. In a 2006 study by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke, students who studied a passage once and then took recall tests forgot far less a week later than students who re-read it several times — even though the re-readers felt more confident. Quizzes after training aren't just assessment; they are the training.

==========

🧩 4. MEMORY IS RECONSTRUCTED, NOT REPLAYED

Memory is not a recording. Each time you remember, you rebuild the event from fragments, filling gaps with what is likely, what you expect and what you've heard since.

Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer (1974) showed people a film of a car crash, then asked how fast the cars were going when they "smashed into" or "contacted" each other. The "smashed" group estimated about 41 mph on average; the "contacted" group about 32 mph. A week later, people in the "smashed" group were about twice as likely to say they had seen broken glass. There was none. One word changed the memory itself. This is the misinformation effect.

Later work went further: by repeatedly suggesting a childhood event, such as being lost in a shopping mall, researchers led a minority of participants (about a quarter in one early study) to "remember" an event that never happened. Even vivid flashbulb memories of dramatic events fade and drift like ordinary memories; what stays high is the person's confidence.

For a manager the lesson is practical. In a dispute over what was promised, both sides can be honest and wrong, and confidence proves nothing. Write it down: confirm terms on WhatsApp or email the same day. When investigating an incident, ask open questions ("What happened next?") rather than leading ones ("Did he shout at you?").

==========

📉 5. FORGETTING

In the 1880s Hermann Ebbinghaus memorised lists of nonsense syllables and measured how much he retained over time. The forgetting curve drops steeply at first, then levels off:

Why do we forget?

• Encoding failure — it never got in. In a classic 1979 study, most Americans couldn't pick the correct design of a penny from a set of near-copies, despite handling thousands. They never needed the detail, so it was never encoded.
• Decay — unused memory traces may fade over time, though this is hard to prove.
• Interference — other memories get in the way. Proactive interference: old learning disrupts new (last year's price list keeps surfacing). Retroactive interference: new learning disrupts old (after learning the new scheme, you can't recall the old one's details).
• Retrieval failure — the memory is there but the cue is wrong: the tip-of-the-tongue feeling.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE 2 · A TRAINING PLAN THAT SURVIVES THE WEEK

On Monday, reps learn 20 key facts about a new range. Using Ebbinghaus's shape as a rough guide, by the next Monday they might retain about a quarter — 5 facts — if nothing else happens.

Session  (Mon):  learn all 20, end with a recall quiz
Review 1 (Tue):  10-minute quiz on WhatsApp
Review 2 (Thu):  role-play using the facts
Review 3 (Mon+): quiz on the 5 most-missed facts

This uses three robust findings at once: the testing effect (quizzes, not re-reading), the spacing effect (reviews spread out beat one long session), and encoding specificity (role-play resembles the field). Total extra time: under an hour. Expected result: most of the 20, not five.

==========

🧬 6. THE BIOLOGY OF MEMORY

New long-term memories are stabilised over hours to years in a process called consolidation, which relies heavily on the hippocampus (Part 1) and on sleep (Part 3). The most studied patient in psychology, Henry Molaison ("H.M."), had parts of both hippocampi removed in 1953 to control epilepsy. Afterwards he could not form new declarative memories — anterograde amnesia — though his older memories and his ability to hold a conversation for a few minutes survived. Yet he improved at a mirror-drawing task over days without remembering ever having done it. Procedural and declarative memory depend on different systems. Retrograde amnesia, the loss of memories from before an injury, is the reverse. Alzheimer's disease typically attacks the hippocampus early, which is why recent memories go first.

==========

🔁 7. HELD UP?

• People learn best in their preferred "learning style" (visual, auditory, kinaesthetic): No — A 2008 review found almost no evidence that matching teaching to a person's preferred style improves learning. Match the method to the material instead.
• Memory works like a video recording: No — It's reconstructed each time; the misinformation effect is one of the best-replicated findings in the field.
• Testing and spacing improve retention: Robust — Replicated across hundreds of studies, ages and materials.
• Brain-training games make you smarter: Little evidence — A 2016 review found people get better at the trained games but gains rarely transfer to everyday thinking.
• Listening to Mozart raises IQ: No — The original small effect was brief, came from arousal and mood, and failed to replicate reliably.

==========

📝 SUMMARY

1️⃣ Memory involves encoding, storage and retrieval, and can fail at each step.
2️⃣ Sensory memory holds a full copy for under a second; only what you attend to moves on.
3️⃣ Working memory holds about four chunks for about 20 seconds without rehearsal. Chunking beats the limit; elaborative rehearsal encodes far better than repetition.
4️⃣ Long-term memory is effectively unlimited: procedural (skills) and declarative (semantic facts, episodic events), organised by meaning.
5️⃣ Retrieval is best when conditions match learning (encoding specificity). Recognition beats recall. First and last items are remembered best. Testing yourself beats re-reading.
6️⃣ Memory is reconstructed: one word in a question changed speed estimates and created memories of broken glass. Confidence isn't accuracy — write agreements down.
7️⃣ Forgetting is steep at first, then levels off. Causes: encoding failure, decay, interference, retrieval failure. Spaced quizzes after training preserve most of what was taught.
8️⃣ The hippocampus consolidates new declarative memories; H.M. lost that ability but could still learn skills.
9️⃣ "Learning styles", the Mozart effect and brain-training games don't hold up.

➡️ NEXT: Psychology for Managers 6/12 — Thinking, Decisions, Intelligence and Language

==========

Sources: chapter structure follows Ciccarelli & White, Psychology, 4th ed. (Pearson), Ch. 6; text and figures are original. Sperling, 1960. Miller, 1956; Cowan, Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 2001. Baddeley & Hitch, 1974. Godden & Baddeley, 1975. Loftus & Palmer, 1974. Roediger & Karpicke, Psychological Science, 2006. Learning styles: Pashler et al., Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 2008. Brain training: Simons et al., Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 2016. Ebbinghaus, 1885. Worked-example figures are illustrative.

==========

notes.body:
🧠 PSYCHOLOGY FOR MANAGERS, PART 6: THINKING, DECISIONS, INTELLIGENCE AND LANGUAGE

==========

⚡ TL;DR

Most judgements are made by fast, intuitive System 1, and it fails in predictable ways. An irrelevant number anchors estimates, the same choice framed as lives saved or lives lost flips preferences, and losses weigh about twice as much as gains.

Intelligence shows a strong general factor. IQ tests are reliable and moderately predict job performance; multiple intelligences have weak support and emotional intelligence is useful but not more important than IQ. Adult IQ is about half heritable, yet average scores rose about three points a decade last century.

The headline result: base rates dominate. If 1 in 10 hires becomes a star, an interview that flags 80% of stars and 20% of the rest gives a flagged candidate only about a 31% chance of being one.

The chapter structure follows Ciccarelli & White, Psychology (4th ed.), Chapter 7, with heuristics and biases expanded. The text, examples and diagrams are original.

==========

🧱 1. THE BUILDING BLOCKS OF THOUGHT

Cognition is the mental activity of thinking, understanding, remembering and communicating. Two of its building blocks:

• Mental images — picture-like representations. We manipulate them much as we would real objects: in classic experiments, the time people take to mentally rotate a shape rises with the angle of rotation.
• Concepts — mental categories that group objects, events or ideas. Formal concepts have strict rules (a triangle has three sides). Natural concepts form through experience and have fuzzy edges. We judge category members against a prototype, the most typical example. Ask someone to name a "premium car" and you'll hear a few prototypes; a brand that sits close to the prototype gets the category's associations for free.

==========

🧩 2. PROBLEM SOLVING

There are three broad ways to solve a problem. Trial and error works for simple problems with few options. An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure that guarantees a solution if followed — a checklist, a formula, a pricing calculator — but can be slow. A heuristic is a rule of thumb that is fast and usually works, but can fail: "price at the competitor's level", "work backwards from the goal", "break it into smaller problems".

Three barriers block good solutions:

• Functional fixedness — seeing objects only in their usual role. In Karl Duncker's candle problem, people given a candle, matches and a box of drawing pins struggle to fix the candle to a wall. The answer is to empty the box and pin it up as a shelf. Seeing the box only as a container is the block. Business version: seeing a distributor only as a logistics channel, not as a source of market intelligence.
• Mental set — sticking with a method that worked before, even when a simpler one exists.
• Confirmation bias — seeking and favouring evidence that supports what you already believe, and ignoring what doesn't. It is the most damaging bias in reviews and investigations: once a manager decides a rep is weak, every missed call confirms it and every good month is "luck".

==========

⚖️ 3. HEURISTICS AND BIASES

From the 1970s Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky showed that human judgement departs from logic in systematic, predictable ways. Kahneman later popularised a two-system description. System 1 is fast, automatic and intuitive; System 2 is slow, effortful and deliberate. Most judgements are made by System 1, and System 2 is lazy about checking them. The main shortcuts:

AVAILABILITY

We judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. Vivid, recent or emotional events feel more common than they are. After one dealer defaults loudly, a sales head may tighten credit for everyone, though the default rate hasn't changed.

REPRESENTATIVENESS AND BASE RATES

We judge whether something belongs to a category by how much it resembles our prototype, and ignore how common the category actually is (the base rate). A candidate who "looks like" your star salesperson — confident, talkative, a former athlete — feels like a likely star, even if only a small share of such candidates ever become stars.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE 1 · BASE-RATE NEGLECT IN HIRING

Of 100 sales hires, historically 10 become top performers. Your interviewers are fairly good: they rate 80% of future top performers as "star material", but also rate 20% of the others that way. A candidate is rated "star material". What's the chance they become a top performer?

Future stars rated "star":    80% of 10 =  8
Others rated "star":          20% of 90 = 18
Total rated "star":                       26

P(top performer | rated star) = 8 / 26 ≈ 31%

Most people guess around 80%. The true figure is about 31%, because ordinary performers vastly outnumber stars. This is the same arithmetic as the reverse-inference trap in Part 1. When the base rate is low, even a good test produces mostly false positives.

ANCHORING

An initial number pulls later estimates toward it, even when it is obviously irrelevant. In a 1974 study, Tversky and Kahneman spun a wheel rigged to stop at 10 or 65, then asked people what percentage of UN member countries were African. Those who saw 10 gave a median estimate of 25%; those who saw 65, 45%. A random number moved the answer by 20 points. In negotiation, the first price on the table anchors the range — which is why the side that opens with a credible, ambitious number usually ends better off, and why MRPs are printed well above the street price.

FRAMING

The same choice described differently leads to different decisions. In Tversky and Kahneman's 1981 "disease problem", people chose between programmes to fight an outbreak expected to kill 600. Described in terms of lives saved ("200 people will be saved"), 72% chose the certain option. Described in terms of lives lost ("400 people will die"), only 22% did. The outcomes were identical.

LOSS AVERSION

Losses hurt more than equal gains please — by roughly a factor of two in many studies. Most people refuse a coin flip to win ₹1,500 or lose ₹1,000, despite its positive expected value, and typically want a potential gain about twice the potential loss before they accept. This is why "don't lose your 5% loyalty bonus" can motivate more than "earn a 5% bonus", and why customers stick with what they have (the status quo bias).

SUNK COST AND OVERCONFIDENCE

The sunk-cost fallacy is continuing to invest in something because of what you've already spent — the failing product launch kept alive "because we've already put ₹2 crore into it". Only future costs and benefits should count. Overconfidence is the near-universal tendency to be more sure of our judgements than accuracy justifies. When people say they are "90% sure" of a range, the truth often falls inside it far less than 90% of the time. Forecasts need wider ranges than feel natural.

▸ DEBIASING A DECISION: FIVE HABITS

1. Ask for the base rate first: "How often does this usually happen?"
2. Reframe: state the choice as a gain and as a loss and see if your answer changes.
3. Make your own estimate before you see anyone else's number.
4. Ignore sunk costs: "If we were starting today, would we invest?"
5. Assign someone to argue the other side, and run a "pre-mortem": imagine it failed and list why.

==========

🎨 4. CREATIVITY

Convergent thinking narrows to a single correct answer. Divergent thinking generates many possible answers — the core of creativity. A practical finding: group brainstorming, in which people shout out ideas together, reliably produces fewer and no better ideas than the same number of people working alone and then pooling their lists. The causes are people waiting their turn and forgetting their idea (production blocking), fear of judgement, and coasting. The better method: individuals write ideas silently first, then the group combines and builds on them.

==========

📊 5. INTELLIGENCE

A working definition: intelligence is the ability to learn from experience, solve problems, and adapt to new situations. The main theories:

• Spearman's g (1904): people who do well on one kind of mental test tend to do well on others. He proposed a general ability, g, plus specific abilities. This pattern is one of the most replicated findings in psychology.
• Gardner's multiple intelligences (1983): eight or so separate intelligences — linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinaesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal, naturalist. Popular in schools, but the proposed intelligences correlate with one another and with g, and there is little evidence they are independent.
• Sternberg's triarchic theory: analytical (the kind IQ tests measure), creative, and practical intelligence ("street smarts"). Useful as a reminder that test smarts aren't the whole story.

MEASURING IT

Alfred Binet built the first practical test in Paris in 1905 to identify children who needed extra help at school. The modern standard is David Wechsler's tests. Scores are set so the population average is 100 and the standard deviation is 15, following the bell-shaped normal curve.

A good test must be reliable (gives consistent scores on retesting) and valid (measures what it claims to, and predicts what it should). IQ tests are highly reliable. They predict school results well and job performance moderately. A large 2022 re-analysis by Paul Sackett and colleagues revised earlier estimates downward, putting general mental ability among the useful predictors of job performance but behind well-designed structured interviews (Part 11).

NATURE, NURTURE AND THE FLYNN EFFECT

Twin and adoption studies put the heritability of adult IQ at roughly 50%, higher in adulthood than childhood. Heritability is a statement about variation within a population in a given environment — not a claim that intelligence is fixed in an individual. The Flynn effect proves the point: average scores on IQ tests rose by about three points per decade across much of the twentieth century, far too fast for genes, pointing to better nutrition, schooling and more abstract everyday thinking. In some countries the rise has recently stalled or reversed.

EMOTIONAL INTELLIGENCE

Emotional intelligence (EI) — perceiving, understanding and managing emotions in yourself and others — became famous through Daniel Goleman's 1995 book, which suggested it could matter more than IQ. Research supports EI as a real and somewhat useful construct, especially in jobs heavy on emotional labour such as sales and service. But much of what it predicts overlaps with personality and general ability, and the "matters more than IQ" claim is not supported.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE 2 · READING A CUT-OFF

A recruiter screens graduates with an aptitude test scaled like IQ (mean 100, SD 15) and sets the cut-off at 130. What share of the population passes?

130 = 100 + 2 × 15  → two SDs above the mean
Above +2 SD on a normal curve ≈ 2.5%
(precise value ≈ 2.3%)

About 1 in 40. If the applicant pool is a typical cross-section, a cut-off that high rejects nearly everyone — including many who would perform well, since test scores predict performance only moderately. Cut-offs should be set from evidence about the job, not from what sounds rigorous.

==========

🗣️ 6. LANGUAGE

Language is a system for combining symbols into meaningful messages. Its layers: phonemes (basic sounds), morphemes (smallest units of meaning — "unpaid" has two), grammar and syntax (rules for combining words), semantics (meaning), and pragmatics (how meaning depends on social context — "Can you send the order?" is a request, not a question about ability). Pragmatics is where most cross-regional and cross-language misunderstandings in a national sales force happen.

Does language shape thought? The strong version of the Sapir–Whorf hypothesis — that language determines what you can think — has been rejected. A weaker version has some support: Russian has separate basic words for light and dark blue, and Russian speakers distinguish those shades slightly faster. Language nudges attention and memory; it doesn't imprison thought. The business equivalent: the words a company uses for things ("dealer" or "partner", "cost" or "investment") shape what people notice.

==========

🔁 7. HELD UP?

• Anchoring and framing effects: Robust — Replicated in large multi-lab projects, though effect sizes vary.
• Losses loom about twice as large as gains: Mostly — Strong for meaningful stakes; some researchers argue it's weaker or absent for small amounts. The "2×" is an average, not a constant.
• Reading words about old age makes you walk slower: Failed — A famous 1996 "priming" study did not replicate in 2012; many similar behavioural-priming effects have also failed.
• There are many independent intelligences: Weak — The proposed intelligences correlate; little evidence for independence.
• Group brainstorming produces more ideas: No — Individuals working separately, then pooling, consistently do better.
• Emotional intelligence matters more than IQ: Overstated — EI adds some prediction in emotion-heavy jobs; not more than general ability.

==========

📝 SUMMARY

1️⃣ Thinking uses mental images and concepts; natural concepts are judged against a prototype.
2️⃣ Problems are solved by trial and error, algorithms or heuristics. Barriers: functional fixedness, mental set, and confirmation bias.
3️⃣ Judgement is mostly fast System 1. Predictable biases: availability, representativeness with base-rate neglect, anchoring, framing, loss aversion, sunk cost and overconfidence.
4️⃣ When base rates are low, even good screening produces mostly false positives — a "star" rating meant only about a 31% chance in the worked example.
5️⃣ Silent individual idea generation beats group brainstorming.
6️⃣ Intelligence shows a strong general factor (g). IQ is scaled to mean 100, SD 15; tests are reliable and moderately predict job performance. Multiple-intelligence theory has weak support.
7️⃣ Adult IQ is about 50% heritable, yet scores rose about three points per decade in the twentieth century: heritable doesn't mean fixed.
8️⃣ Emotional intelligence is useful in emotion-heavy jobs but not more important than general ability.
9️⃣ Language has layers from phonemes to pragmatics. It nudges thought but doesn't determine it.

➡️ NEXT: Psychology for Managers 7/12 — Development Across the Lifespan

==========

Sources: chapter structure follows Ciccarelli & White, Psychology, 4th ed. (Pearson), Ch. 7; text and figures are original. Tversky & Kahneman, Science, 1974 and 1981. Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow, 2011. Brainstorming: Diehl & Stroebe, 1987. Priming replication: Doyen et al., PLOS ONE, 2012. Selection validity: Sackett et al., Journal of Applied Psychology, 2022. Flynn effect: Flynn, 1987 and later reviews. Worked-example figures are illustrative.

==========

🔗 The PDF has the diagrams, worked examples, practice problems, glossary and answer key. Coming next: Psychology for Managers 7/12 — Development Across the Lifespan

notes.body:
🧠 PSYCHOLOGY FOR MANAGERS, PART 7: DEVELOPMENT ACROSS THE LIFESPAN

==========

⚡ TL;DR

Genes and environment interact, and a one-time survey across age groups mixes up age with the era people grew up in. That cohort trap sits under most 'older employees can't handle technology' and 'Gen Z wants purpose' claims.

Vygotsky's zone of proximal development is the best model of coaching: support someone just beyond what they can do alone, then withdraw it. Erikson's generativity stage makes many people in their forties and fifties natural mentors.

The headline result: ability doesn't decline as a block. Fluid intelligence (speed, new problems) falls from the thirties, while crystallised intelligence (knowledge, judgement) keeps rising into the sixties, so mixed-age teams cover both. The marshmallow test, the five stages of grief and big generational differences at work don't hold up well.

The chapter structure follows Ciccarelli & White, Psychology (4th ed.), Chapter 8. The text, examples and diagrams are original.

==========

❓ 1. THE BIG QUESTIONS AND HOW THEY ARE STUDIED

Two debates run through the field. Nature versus nurture: how much of development is driven by genes and how much by environment? The modern answer is that they interact. Genes set ranges and tendencies, and environment determines where in the range a person ends up; environments can even change which genes are switched on (epigenetics). And continuity versus stages: is development smooth and gradual, or a series of distinct steps? Most traits change gradually, though some stage theories remain useful as maps.

Three research designs, each with a trap:

• Cross-sectional — compare different age groups at one time. Quick, but age differences get mixed up with cohort effects: differences due to the era people grew up in, not their age.
• Longitudinal — follow the same people for years. Shows true change, but slow, expensive and prone to drop-outs.
• Cross-sequential — follow several age groups over time; combines both and separates age from cohort.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE 1 · AGE OR ERA?

A 2026 survey of a sales force finds that reps aged 25 use the CRM app 40 times a week, and reps aged 50 use it 10 times. HR concludes: "People get worse with technology as they age."

Cross-sectional finding:  25-year-olds 40 / week
                          50-year-olds 10 / week
Possible explanations:
  Age effect:     ability to adopt tech declines with age
  Cohort effect:  50-year-olds grew up without smartphones
  Role effect:    50-year-olds are senior; juniors log more

A cross-sectional survey can't tell these apart. To separate them, follow the same people over time, compare people of the same age in different roles, or train both groups and measure the change. The likely answer is mostly cohort and role — and the remedy for cohort is training, not hiring younger.

==========

👶 2. BEGINNINGS

Prenatal development runs from the fertilised egg (the zygote) through the embryo stage, when the major organs form, to the foetus. Substances that can harm the developing baby are called teratogens; alcohol is among the most common, and can cause lifelong learning and behavioural problems. Newborns arrive with reflexes such as grasping and rooting (turning toward a touch on the cheek), and with senses ready to learn: within days they prefer their mother's voice and faces over other patterns. The brain grows rapidly in the first years, forming far more connections than it keeps, then pruning those that go unused — plasticity in action (Part 1).

==========

🧠 3. HOW THINKING DEVELOPS

PIAGET'S FOUR STAGES

Jean Piaget, observing children from the 1920s, argued that thinking develops through four qualitatively different stages. Children are not just adults who know less; they think differently.

• Sensorimotor (0–2): Learning through the senses and action. Object permanence — knowing a hidden object still exists — develops.
• Preoperational (2–7): Language and symbols, but thinking is egocentric (hard to take another's view) and fails at conservation: a child thinks a tall thin glass holds more than a short wide one with the same water.
• Concrete operational (7–11): Logical thinking about concrete things; conservation mastered.
• Formal operational (12+): Abstract and hypothetical reasoning: "what if" and systematic testing of ideas.

Piaget's broad sequence has held up, but later research showed he underestimated infants (some understand object permanence earlier than he thought), that progress is more gradual and uneven than neat stages suggest, and that many adults reason formally only in areas they know well.

VYGOTSKY: LEARNING WITH OTHERS

Lev Vygotsky stressed that children learn through interaction with more skilled people. His zone of proximal development (ZPD) is the gap between what a learner can do alone and what they can do with help. Teaching works best inside that zone, through scaffolding: support that is gradually withdrawn as competence grows. This is the best single model of field coaching. A rep who can already run a routine dealer visit alone doesn't need you on that call. He needs you on the first collections conversation with a difficult dealer — then less on the second, and not at all by the fifth.

==========

🤝 4. ATTACHMENT, TEMPERAMENT AND PARENTING

In the 1950s Harry Harlow raised infant monkeys with two artificial "mothers": one made of wire that gave milk, one covered in soft cloth that gave none. The infants spent most of their time clinging to the cloth mother and ran to her when frightened. Comfort, not just food, drives the bond. Mary Ainsworth's Strange Situation test — briefly separating a toddler from the parent and observing the reunion — identified attachment patterns: secure (upset at separation, easily comforted on return), avoidant, ambivalent (clingy and hard to soothe), and later disorganised. Secure attachment is linked to better social adjustment later, though the links are moderate, not destiny.

Babies also differ from birth in temperament: some are "easy", some "difficult", some "slow to warm up". Temperament is partly inherited and partly stable over time — an early root of adult personality.

Diana Baumrind described parenting styles: authoritarian (strict rules, little warmth or explanation), permissive (warm, few demands), authoritative (clear expectations with warmth and explanation) and, added later, uninvolved. In Western studies authoritative parenting is linked with the best outcomes; the picture varies more across cultures. The parallel with management styles is obvious and reasonably well supported: high standards plus warmth and explanation usually beats either harshness or indulgence.

==========

🪜 5. ERIKSON'S EIGHT STAGES

Erik Erikson proposed that each life stage brings a central social conflict to resolve. His theory is hard to test precisely, but it remains a useful map of the concerns people bring to work at different ages.

• 0–1: Trust vs mistrust — Whether the world is reliable
• 1–3: Autonomy vs shame and doubt — Doing things for oneself
• 3–6: Initiative vs guilt — Taking the lead in play and plans
• 6–12: Industry vs inferiority — Feeling competent at tasks
• Teens: Identity vs role confusion — Who am I, what do I stand for
• 20s–30s: Intimacy vs isolation — Close relationships and commitment
• 40s–60s: Generativity vs stagnation — Contributing to the next generation
• 65+: Integrity vs despair — Making peace with the life lived

The stage most useful to managers is generativity. Many people in their forties and fifties want to mentor and leave something behind. A senior rep who has plateaued in sales may be your best trainer, if the role is offered as recognition rather than as a demotion.

==========

🧑 6. ADOLESCENCE AND MORAL REASONING

Adolescence begins with puberty and ends, culturally, with taking on adult roles — later today than a generation ago. The brain's reward systems become highly active in the teens while the prefrontal cortex, which handles planning and self-control, keeps maturing into the mid-twenties. That mismatch helps explain risk-taking, especially with peers watching. It also means that the 22-year-old trainee's brain is still finishing development.

Lawrence Kohlberg described moral reasoning in three levels: preconventional (avoid punishment, gain reward), conventional (follow rules and social expectations), and postconventional (reason from principles such as justice, even against rules). Critics, notably Carol Gilligan, argued it overvalued abstract justice compared with care for relationships, and later research found that how people reason about dilemmas predicts their actual behaviour only modestly. Most compliance problems in sales are better explained by incentives and norms (Parts 4 and 10) than by stages of moral reasoning.

==========

👴 7. ADULTHOOD AND AGEING

Adulthood is usually divided into early (20s–30s), middle (40s–60s) and late adulthood. Physical capacities peak in the twenties and decline gradually. The more important news for managers is about mental ability, which does not decline as a block. Raymond Cattell and John Horn distinguished two kinds:

• Fluid intelligence — speed, working memory and solving new problems. It peaks in early adulthood and declines gradually from the thirties.
• Crystallised intelligence — accumulated knowledge, vocabulary and expertise. It keeps rising or holds steady well into the sixties.

The management implication: older employees often learn a new software system more slowly, but bring judgement, relationships and pattern recognition that take decades to build. Teams that pair them with younger colleagues, each covering the other's weaker side, beat teams that are uniform in age.

The midlife crisis — a dramatic upheaval around 40 to 50 — is much less common than its fame suggests; most adults report midlife as stable, and large surveys find life satisfaction tends to dip in midlife but only modestly. In later life, people who stay active and socially connected tend to fare better (activity theory), and older adults increasingly focus on emotionally meaningful relationships over new contacts.

DEATH AND GRIEF

Elisabeth Kübler-Ross's 1969 description of five stages of dying — denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance — became famous and is often applied to grief and even to organisational change. Research does not support a fixed sequence. People move between these feelings in different orders or skip some, and studies of bereavement find that many people are resilient, returning to normal functioning within months. Using "the five stages" to manage a restructuring is folklore. Offer time, flexibility and support, without expecting a timetable.

==========

🔁 8. HELD UP?

• Delaying a marshmallow at age 4 predicts adult success: Much weaker — A 2018 replication with about 900 children found a smaller link, which mostly disappeared after controlling for family background and early ability.
• Grief follows five fixed stages: No — No fixed sequence; resilience is common.
• Generations (millennials, Gen Z) want fundamentally different things at work: Mostly not — Meta-analyses find small generational differences in work attitudes; most gaps reflect age and career stage, which every generation passes through.
• Fluid ability declines, crystallised knowledge grows: Robust — Consistent across longitudinal and cross-sectional studies.
• Midlife crisis is near-universal: No — A minority experience it; satisfaction dips modestly on average.

==========

📝 SUMMARY

1️⃣ Genes and environment interact. Cross-sectional studies confuse age with cohort; longitudinal and cross-sequential designs separate them.
2️⃣ Piaget: sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete and formal operational stages. The sequence holds, but he underestimated infants and stages are less tidy.
3️⃣ Vygotsky: teach within the zone of proximal development with scaffolding that is withdrawn as skill grows — the model for field coaching.
4️⃣ Attachment is built on comfort (Harlow); Ainsworth's patterns predict later adjustment moderately. Temperament is partly inborn. Authoritative parenting — standards plus warmth — has the best outcomes in most studies.
5️⃣ Erikson's eight stages map life's central concerns; generativity in midlife makes experienced staff good mentors.
6️⃣ The prefrontal cortex matures into the mid-twenties. Kohlberg's moral stages predict behaviour only modestly.
7️⃣ Fluid intelligence declines from the thirties; crystallised intelligence grows into the sixties. Mixed-age teams cover both.
8️⃣ The marshmallow test, five stages of grief, the universal midlife crisis and big generational differences at work don't hold up.

➡️ NEXT: Psychology for Managers 8/12 — Motivation and Emotion

==========

Sources: chapter structure follows Ciccarelli & White, Psychology, 4th ed. (Pearson), Ch. 8; text and figures are original. Marshmallow replication: Watts, Duncan & Quan, Psychological Science, 2018. notes.body:
🧠 PSYCHOLOGY FOR MANAGERS, PART 8: MOTIVATION AND EMOTION

==========

⚡ TL;DR

Maslow's needs are universal but not strictly ordered. The better-supported model is self-determination theory: people stay motivated when they have autonomy, competence and relatedness.

Expectancy theory multiplies three beliefs: can I hit it, will I be paid, do I want it. Raise a target until a rep thinks he has a 15% chance and motivation falls by about three-quarters, whatever the bonus. Specific, difficult goals raise performance, but narrow, extreme targets breed loading and cheating.

The headline result: nobody can reliably read lies from faces. Across hundreds of studies accuracy is about 54%, barely above guessing. The pen-in-mouth facial-feedback study also failed a 17-lab replication.

The chapter structure follows Ciccarelli & White, Psychology (4th ed.), Chapter 9. The text, examples and diagrams are original.

==========

🔋 1. THE CLASSIC THEORIES

• Instinct theory — behaviour is driven by inborn, fixed patterns. Early psychologists listed thousands of "instincts", which explained nothing. Abandoned for humans.
• Drive-reduction theory (Clark Hull) — a need (food, water) creates a tension, a drive, that pushes us to act until the need is met and the body returns to balance (homeostasis). Good for hunger and thirst; it can't explain why people seek out challenge, novelty or risk.
• Arousal theory — people seek an optimal level of stimulation: too little and we're bored, too much and we're overwhelmed. Some people, high in sensation seeking, need more than others.
• Incentive theory — behaviour is pulled by external rewards, not just pushed by internal drives. The basis of every incentive scheme (Part 4).

THE YERKES–DODSON LAW

In 1908 Robert Yerkes and John Dodson found that performance improves with arousal up to a point, then falls. The best level of arousal is lower for complex tasks and higher for simple ones.

The lesson for target-setting: pressure that energises a rep doing routine order-taking can wreck the judgement of a key-account manager negotiating a complex deal. The original study used mice and electric shocks, and the precise inverted U is only loosely supported in humans, but the broad pattern is widely observed.

==========

🔺 2. MASLOW'S HIERARCHY — AND WHAT REPLACED IT

Abraham Maslow (1943) proposed that needs are arranged in a hierarchy: physiological (food, sleep), safety, belonging, esteem, and at the top self-actualisation — fulfilling one's potential. Lower needs must be largely met before higher ones motivate. (The pyramid drawing came later, from management writers, not from Maslow.)

The categories are useful. The strict order isn't well supported. A 2011 study of over 60,000 people in 123 countries by Louis Tay and Ed Diener found that the needs were indeed universal, but people reported meeting social and respect needs even when basic needs were unmet, and these contributed to well-being independently. A field rep on a modest salary still cares intensely about recognition and belonging.

SELF-DETERMINATION THEORY

The best-supported modern theory, from Edward Deci and Richard Ryan, says that people are naturally motivated when three psychological needs are met:

• Autonomy — feeling that you choose your actions, not that they're forced on you.
• Competence — feeling effective and growing in skill.
• Relatedness — feeling connected to others.

Work that meets these needs sustains effort without constant external pressure; work that frustrates them leaves people dependent on carrots and sticks. A manager's practical levers: let reps plan their own beat within clear targets (autonomy), give specific feedback and skill coaching (competence), and build a team that knows each other (relatedness).

MCCLELLAND'S THREE NEEDS

David McClelland focused on three learned needs that vary between people: the need for achievement (to excel and master challenges), affiliation (to be liked and belong) and power (to influence others). High achievers like moderately difficult goals and quick feedback, and often make excellent individual salespeople — but not always good managers, because they prefer doing to delegating. McClelland's research suggested that effective managers in large organisations were higher in a socialised need for power — influence used for the organisation — than in achievement or affiliation.

==========

🎯 3. TWO TOOLS FOR WORK MOTIVATION

EXPECTANCY THEORY

Victor Vroom (1964) proposed that people put in effort when three things are true, and that motivation is roughly their product:

Motivation = Expectancy × Instrumentality × Valence
Expectancy:      "If I try, can I hit the target?"   (0–1)
Instrumentality: "If I hit it, will I get the reward?" (0–1)
Valence:         "Do I value that reward?"           (0–1)

Because the terms multiply, if any one is near zero, motivation collapses — however large the others are.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE 1 · THE IMPOSSIBLE TARGET

A rep values the festive-season bonus highly (valence 0.9). The company has always paid it when earned (instrumentality 0.9). Last year's target was a stretch; he rated his chances at 0.6. This year the target is raised 40%; he now rates his chances at 0.15.

Last year:  0.6  × 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.49
This year:  0.15 × 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.12

Motivation falls by about three-quarters,
with the same bonus on offer.

Raising the bonus won't fix it: even with valence at 1.0, 0.15 × 0.9 × 1.0 ≈ 0.14. The broken term is expectancy. Fix that — a reachable target, more support, or a stepped bonus that pays partially — and motivation returns. The same logic shows why delayed or disputed bonus payouts are so damaging: they cut instrumentality for every future scheme.

GOAL-SETTING THEORY

Edwin Locke and Gary Latham's decades of research produced one of the most robust findings in work psychology: specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy goals or "do your best" — provided people are committed to the goal, have the ability, and get feedback on progress. The effect is large and holds across many jobs and countries.

It comes with a warning. A 2009 paper called "Goals Gone Wild" documented the side effects of narrow, high-pressure targets: people neglect everything not measured, take excessive risks and are more likely to cheat. The best-known case is Wells Fargo, where aggressive cross-selling targets led employees to open millions of accounts customers hadn't asked for, exposed in 2016. In channel sales, the same pressure produces stock loading, fake billing and promised discounts the company never approved. Use specific, difficult goals — and watch the behaviour that produces the number, not only the number.

==========

🍽️ 4. BIOLOGICAL MOTIVES, BRIEFLY

Hunger shows how biology and environment combine. The hypothalamus (Part 1) and hormones signal hunger and fullness, but external cues — the time on the clock, the smell of food, portion size, eating with others — strongly influence when and how much people eat. The same pattern runs through most motives: a biological base, heavily shaped by habit and context.

==========

❤️ 5. WHAT AN EMOTION IS

An emotion has three parts: physiological arousal (heart rate, breathing, hormones), behavioural expression (face, voice, posture) and subjective experience (how it feels). The main theories disagree about the order:

• James–Lange (1880s): Event → body reacts → you feel the emotion — "We feel afraid because we tremble."
• Cannon–Bard (1920s): Event → body reaction and feeling at the same time — Different emotions share similar arousal, so arousal can't be the cause.
• Schachter–Singer (1962): Event → arousal → you look for a label → emotion — Emotion = arousal + interpretation.
• Lazarus (cognitive-mediational): Event → appraisal of what it means for you → emotion and arousal — How you interpret the event comes first.

The two-factor and appraisal views have the most practical use. In a 1974 study, men who met an attractive researcher on a high, swaying suspension bridge rated her as more attractive and were more likely to call her later than men who met her on a low, stable bridge — consistent with arousal from the bridge being relabelled as attraction. Arousal is easily misattributed. A manager walking into a review straight from a stressful call may read irritation into a rep's neutral comment. And because appraisal shapes emotion, the same event — a lost dealer — can produce despair or determination depending on how it's framed.

==========

🙂 6. READING EMOTIONS IN FACES

Paul Ekman's research from the 1960s found that six basic emotions — happiness, sadness, anger, fear, surprise and disgust — were recognised from facial expressions across many cultures, including isolated groups in Papua New Guinea. Later work complicated this. Recognition across cultures is well above chance but lower than within a culture, and some researchers, notably Lisa Feldman Barrett, argue that emotions are constructed by each brain from context rather than triggered as fixed universal programmes. Cultures also have different display rules — norms about which emotions to show, when and to whom. A dealer's polite smile in a hierarchical setting may tell you nothing about his satisfaction.

Two popular extensions fare poorly. The facial-feedback hypothesis says that making a facial expression intensifies the feeling. A famous 1988 study had people hold a pen in their teeth (forcing a smile) and found they rated cartoons funnier. A 2016 replication across 17 labs found no effect. A larger 2022 project found a small effect for deliberate smiling but not for the pen method — so the effect, if real, is small. And lie detection from faces and body language is close to useless: across hundreds of studies, people judge truth from lies correctly about 54% of the time, barely above the 50% you'd get by guessing. Trained police officers do little better, though they are more confident.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE 2 · "I CAN ALWAYS TELL WHEN A DEALER IS LYING"

A manager judges 100 claims from dealers, 50 true and 50 false, with the typical 54% accuracy.

Correct judgements:  54 of 100
By pure guessing:    50 of 100
Gain over guessing:   4 judgements in 100

Four extra correct calls in a hundred — and he will be confidently wrong in 46. Body language is not evidence. Check claims against records: invoices, stock counts, payment history.

==========

💼 7. EMOTIONS AT WORK

Sales and service jobs require emotional labour (Arlie Hochschild, 1983): managing your emotional display as part of the job — staying cheerful with an abusive customer. Surface acting, faking an emotion you don't feel, is consistently linked to exhaustion and burnout. Deep acting, trying to actually feel the required emotion, for example by seeing the situation from the customer's side, is less draining. Emotions also spread: emotional contagion means a manager's visible anxiety before a review travels through the whole team.

==========

🔁 8. HELD UP?

• Specific, difficult goals raise performance: Robust — Hundreds of studies — with known side effects when goals are narrow and extreme.
• Autonomy, competence and relatedness sustain motivation: Well supported — Consistent across work, education and health studies in many cultures.
• Needs are met in Maslow's strict order: Not supported — Needs are universal, but higher needs matter even when lower ones are unmet.
• Smiling makes you happier (facial feedback): Small at most — The pen study failed a 17-lab replication; a later project found a small effect for deliberate smiling.
• You can spot liars from body language or "microexpressions": No — Average accuracy is about 54%, barely above chance.
• Six basic emotions are universally recognised: Partly — Recognised above chance across cultures, but less accurately, and with real cultural differences.

==========

📝 SUMMARY

1️⃣ Motivation starts, directs and sustains behaviour; intrinsic and extrinsic sources usually mix.
2️⃣ Drive-reduction explains biological needs; arousal theory explains seeking challenge. Yerkes–Dodson: performance peaks at moderate arousal, lower for complex tasks.
3️⃣ Maslow's needs are universal but not strictly ordered. Self-determination theory: autonomy, competence and relatedness sustain motivation. McClelland: achievement, affiliation and power vary between people.
4️⃣ Expectancy theory: motivation = expectancy × instrumentality × valence. An impossible target zeroes it, whatever the bonus.
5️⃣ Goal-setting: specific, difficult goals with commitment and feedback work — but narrow, extreme targets breed corner-cutting and cheating.
6️⃣ Emotion = arousal + expression + experience. Theories differ on order; arousal is easily mislabelled and appraisal shapes the feeling.
7️⃣ Basic emotions are recognised across cultures above chance, shaped by display rules. Facial feedback is small at most; lie detection from faces is barely above chance.
8️⃣ Emotional labour: faking feelings (surface acting) drives burnout; emotions spread through teams.

➡️ NEXT: Psychology for Managers 9/12 — Stress and Health

==========

Sources: chapter structure follows Ciccarelli & White, Psychology, 4th ed. (Pearson), Ch. 9; text and figures are original. Tay & Diener, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2011. Deci & Ryan, self-determination theory. Vroom, Work and Motivation, 1964. Locke & Latham, American Psychologist, 2002. Ordóñez et al., "Goals Gone Wild", Academy of Management Perspectives, 2009. Dutton & Aron, 1974. Facial feedback: Wagenmakers et al., 2016; Coles et al., Nature Human Behaviour, 2022. Lie detection: Bond & DePaulo, Personality and Social Psychology Review, 2006. Hochschild, The Managed Heart, 1983. Worked-example figures are illustrative.

==========
