notes.body:
🧠 PSYCHOLOGY FOR MANAGERS, PART 9: STRESS AND HEALTH

==========

⚡ TL;DR

Stress is the body's emergency system left switched on. Cortisol suppresses parts of the immune system, and in one study a small wound took about 24% longer to heal in long-term caregivers.

Even good news is stressful: a promotion with a transfer scores well over a third of the way to the threshold the classic life-events scale calls high risk. Whether a demand feels like a challenge or a threat depends on the resources people believe they have.

The headline result: the most damaging jobs combine high demands with low control. Giving reps more say over how they hit a target can move a role from 'high strain' to 'active' without cutting the number. WHO defines burnout as unmanaged workplace stress, and its six drivers — workload, control, reward, community, fairness, values — are mostly in the manager's hands.

The chapter structure follows Ciccarelli & White, Psychology (4th ed.), Chapter 11. The text, examples and diagrams are original.

==========

😓 1. WHAT STRESS IS

Stress is the physical, emotional and behavioural response to events we see as threatening or challenging. The events themselves are stressors. Not all stress is harmful: eustress is the positive, energising kind that comes with a challenge you expect to meet; distress is the kind that wears you down. The same event — a big new account — can be either, depending on how it's appraised (section 4).

==========

🌪️ 2. WHERE STRESS COMES FROM

• Catastrophes — floods, earthquakes, pandemics. Unpredictable, large-scale, often shared.
• Major life changes — even positive ones. In 1967 Thomas Holmes and Richard Rahe built the Social Readjustment Rating Scale (SRRS), which scores 43 life events by how much adjustment they require: death of a spouse scores 100, divorce 73, marriage 50, being fired 47. People with high totals over a year showed somewhat higher rates of illness.
• Daily hassles — traffic, a broken printer, a dealer who won't pick up. Individually trivial, they add up, and in several studies predict health and mood better than major life events.
• Pressure, frustration (being blocked from a goal) and conflict between options. In an approach–avoidance conflict, one option has both pulls and pushes — a promotion that comes with a transfer away from family — and people tend to waver as the decision nears.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE 1 · THE "GOOD NEWS" STRESS SCORE

An ASM is promoted to RSM and moves from Kochi to Pune. Score the year using SRRS values:

Change in responsibilities at work   29
Outstanding personal achievement     28
Change in residence                  20
Change in living conditions          25
Change in work hours or conditions   20
Change in social activities          18
Spouse begins or stops work          26
                              Total 166

Every item is part of "good news", yet the total is substantial — about a third of the way to the 300 that Holmes and Rahe treated as high risk. The SRRS is a blunt tool, made in the 1960s for American adults, and it ignores how each person appraises events. But the point stands: transfers and promotions are stressful, and support during the first months — housing help, a buddy in the new region, a lighter first-quarter target — is not indulgence.

STRESS BUILT INTO JOBS

Two well-tested models explain why some jobs are more stressful than others with the same workload:

• Demand–control model (Robert Karasek, 1979): the most damaging jobs combine high demands with low control over how and when work is done. High demands with high control are "active" jobs — challenging but healthier.
• Effort–reward imbalance (Johannes Siegrist): stress rises when high effort meets low reward, where reward includes pay, but also recognition, job security and career prospects.

==========

🫀 3. WHAT STRESS DOES TO THE BODY

In the 1930s–50s Hans Selye described the general adaptation syndrome (GAS), the body's response to any prolonged stressor, in three stages:

1. Alarm — the sympathetic nervous system fires; adrenaline surges; resistance briefly drops, then rises.
2. Resistance — the body sustains a high level of arousal to cope, using up resources.
3. Exhaustion — if the stressor continues, resources run down; vulnerability to illness rises.

Two systems carry the response. The fast sympathetic–adrenal route releases adrenaline in seconds. The slower HPA axis — hypothalamus to pituitary to adrenal glands — releases cortisol, which raises blood sugar and suppresses non-urgent functions, including parts of the immune system. Useful for an afternoon; harmful for a year.

The effects are measurable. In studies by Janice Kiecolt-Glaser and colleagues, medical students' immune markers dropped during exam periods, and a small standardised wound healed about 24% more slowly (about nine days longer) in people caring for a relative with dementia than in matched controls. Long-term stress is also linked with high blood pressure and heart disease, partly directly and partly through what stressed people do — sleep less, eat worse, smoke and drink more, exercise less.

A famous correction: for decades stomach ulcers were blamed mainly on stress. In the 1980s Barry Marshall and Robin Warren showed most are caused by a bacterium, Helicobacter pylori, and treatable with antibiotics; they won the 2005 Nobel Prize. Stress may still worsen ulcers, but it isn't the main cause — a reminder that "it's just stress" can hide a treatable condition.

==========

🔍 4. IT DEPENDS HOW YOU SEE IT

Richard Lazarus's cognitive appraisal model says stress depends on two judgements. Primary appraisal: is this event irrelevant, a threat (possible harm) or a challenge (possible gain)? Secondary appraisal: do I have the resources to cope? A demanding new target appraised as a challenge you can meet produces energy; appraised as a threat you can't handle, it produces distress. Research on work stressors supports the distinction: "challenge" demands such as responsibility and time pressure tend to go with higher motivation, while "hindrance" demands such as red tape, role confusion and office politics go with lower performance and more strain.

This gives managers a cheap lever: secondary appraisal depends on perceived resources. Telling a rep what support exists — budget for a scheme, help from the key-account team, your time — changes how the same target lands.

==========

🧍 5. PERSONALITY AND STRESS

• Type A — the competitive, impatient, hostile pattern described by cardiologists Meyer Friedman and Ray Rosenman in the 1950s, and linked to heart disease. Later research found the overall Type A pattern was a weak predictor; the toxic ingredient is hostility — cynical mistrust and anger. Ambition and drive alone are not the problem.
• Hardiness (Suzanne Kobasa) — a combination of commitment (involvement in what you do), control (believing you can influence events) and challenge (seeing change as opportunity). Associated with better health under stress.
• Optimism — expecting good outcomes — is linked with better coping and health, partly because optimists take more active steps.

==========

🤝 6. SOCIAL AND CULTURAL FACTORS

Social support — people you can turn to for help, advice or company — is one of the strongest buffers against stress, and isolation is a health risk comparable to well-known physical ones in some large studies. Field sales is structurally isolating: reps spend most days alone on the road. Regular team contact, buddies in new regions and a manager who calls to ask how things are going, not only about numbers, are part of the job design. Moving between cultures brings acculturative stress — relevant to transfers between regions with different languages and food. Poverty and job insecurity are chronic stressors in their own right.

==========

🛟 7. COPING

Problem-focused coping deals with the stressor itself: planning, asking for help, negotiating a target. Emotion-focused coping manages the feelings: exercise, talking it through, reframing, relaxation. Problem-focused coping works best when the situation can be changed; emotion-focused coping helps when it can't. Avoidance — denial, drinking, withdrawing — gives short relief and long costs.

Among specific methods, regular physical exercise has some of the most consistent evidence for reducing stress and improving mood. Mindfulness meditation has moderate evidence: a 2014 review of trials found moderate improvements in anxiety, depression and pain, with smaller or unclear effects on other outcomes. It helps; it isn't a cure-all, and an app subscription isn't a substitute for fixing an impossible workload.

==========

🔥 8. BURNOUT

Christina Maslach defined burnout by three features: exhaustion, cynicism (detachment from the work and the people it serves) and reduced efficacy (feeling ineffective). Since 2019 the World Health Organization's ICD-11 has listed burnout as an occupational phenomenon resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed — not as a medical condition. The definition places the cause in the job.

Maslach and Michael Leiter identified six areas where mismatches between person and job drive burnout. They double as a manager's checklist:

• Workload: Too much, with no recovery — Realistic targets; protect days off
• Control: No say in how work is done — Let reps plan beats and schemes within limits
• Reward: Effort unrecognised — Timely pay-outs; specific recognition
• Community: Isolation or conflict — Regular team contact; deal with toxic behaviour
• Fairness: Favouritism, opaque decisions — Transparent target and territory allocation
• Values: Asked to act against one's ethics — No pressure to mislead dealers or load stock

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE 2 · MOVING A JOB OUT OF "HIGH STRAIN"

Score two rep roles on demands and control, 1 (low) to 5 (high), from a team survey (illustrative):

Demands  Control   Quadrant
Urban rep (today)      5        2      High strain
Urban rep (redesign)   5        4      Active
Rural rep              3        4      Low strain

The redesign kept the demands — same target — but raised control: reps choose their visit sequence, approve small schemes up to a limit, and set one day a week for admin. On the Karasek model that moves the role from the riskiest quadrant to the healthiest demanding one, without cutting the number.

==========

🔁 9. HELD UP?

• Chronic stress harms immunity and the heart: Supported — Consistent evidence from lab, field and long-term studies.
• Type A personality causes heart disease: Partly — The broad pattern is a weak predictor; hostility is the active ingredient.
• Ulcers are caused by stress: Mostly no — Mostly bacterial; stress may aggravate them.
• Mindfulness reduces stress: Moderately — Moderate effects on anxiety and depression in trials; not a fix for job design.
• High demands plus low control is especially harmful: Supported — Repeated in large studies of workers, though effect sizes vary.
• Burnout is a personal weakness: No — WHO defines it as a result of unmanaged workplace stress.

==========

📝 SUMMARY

1️⃣ Stress is the response to events appraised as threatening or challenging; eustress energises, distress wears down.
2️⃣ Stressors include catastrophes, life changes (scored by the SRRS; even promotions and transfers score highly), daily hassles, frustration and conflict.
3️⃣ Jobs combining high demands with low control, or high effort with low reward, are the most stressful.
4️⃣ Selye's GAS: alarm, resistance, exhaustion. Cortisol from the HPA axis suppresses immunity; chronic stress slows healing and is linked to heart disease.
5️⃣ Appraisal decides whether a demand feels like a threat or a challenge; perceived resources matter.
6️⃣ Hostility, not ambition, is the harmful part of Type A. Hardiness and optimism help.
7️⃣ Social support is a powerful buffer; field sales is isolating by design.
8️⃣ Coping: problem-focused when the situation can change, emotion-focused when it can't. Exercise has strong evidence, mindfulness moderate.
9️⃣ Burnout — exhaustion, cynicism, reduced efficacy — is an occupational phenomenon. Its six drivers (workload, control, reward, community, fairness, values) are mostly in the manager's hands.

➡️ NEXT: Psychology for Managers 10/12 — Social Psychology

==========

Sources: chapter structure follows Ciccarelli & White, Psychology, 4th ed. (Pearson), Ch. 11; text and figures are original. Holmes & Rahe, 1967. Karasek, Administrative Science Quarterly, 1979. Siegrist, 1996. Kiecolt-Glaser et al., The Lancet, 1995. Challenge and hindrance stressors: LePine, Podsakoff & LePine, Academy of Management Journal, 2005. Mindfulness: Goyal et al., JAMA Internal Medicine, 2014. Burnout: Maslach & Leiter; WHO ICD-11, 2019. Survey scores in worked example 2 are illustrative.

==========

🔗 The PDF has the diagrams, worked examples, practice problems, glossary and answer key. Coming next: Psychology for Managers 10/12 — Social Psychology

notes.body:
🧠 PSYCHOLOGY FOR MANAGERS, PART 10: SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY

==========

⚡ TL;DR

People go along with a wrong majority surprisingly often, but a single ally frees them to dissent. Groups drift toward agreement and extremes, so the leader should speak last and someone should argue the other side. Effort drops in groups unless individual contributions are visible.

Compliance techniques such as foot-in-the-door work, but modestly; used manipulatively, they burn the repeat relationship. In Milgram's study 65% obeyed to the maximum, and obedience fell when others refused. When judging a rep who missed target, the fundamental attribution error makes managers blame the person before checking the territory.

The headline result: contact between groups with equal status and shared goals reliably reduces prejudice — the design for any sales-force merger. And the bystander effect is real in the lab, but CCTV of real conflicts shows someone intervenes in about 9 of 10.

The chapter structure follows Ciccarelli & White, Psychology (4th ed.), Chapter 12. The text and examples are original.

==========

👥 1. CONFORMITY AND GROUPS

Conformity is changing your behaviour to match a group. In Solomon Asch's 1951 studies, a participant sat with a group asked to say which of three lines matched a reference line — an easy task, with near-perfect accuracy alone. But the others were actors who, on certain trials, unanimously gave the wrong answer. Across those trials, participants went along with the group about a third of the time, and roughly three-quarters conformed at least once. When just one other person gave the right answer, conformity dropped sharply.

People conform for two reasons: informational (the group may know something you don't) and normative (wanting to be accepted). Conformity tends to be higher in more collectivist cultures. The lesson about the lone ally is the most useful: a single dissenting voice frees others to speak.

GROUPTHINK AND POLARISATION

Groupthink (Irving Janis, 1972) is a group's tendency to value agreement over good decisions. Its warning signs: an illusion of invulnerability, dismissing warnings, pressure on dissenters, self-censorship, and an illusion that everyone agrees. It is most likely in close-knit groups with a directive leader under time pressure. Group polarisation is related: after discussion, groups tend to take a more extreme position in the direction they already leaned. A cautious team becomes more cautious; a bullish one more bullish.

Remedies: the leader speaks last; someone is assigned to argue against the plan; people write down their views before discussion; outsiders review big decisions.

FACILITATION AND LOAFING

The presence of others raises arousal. Social facilitation: we perform simple, well-practised tasks better with an audience, and complex or new tasks worse — Yerkes–Dodson again (Part 8). Social loafing: people put in less effort in a group when individual contributions aren't identifiable. In the 1880s Max Ringelmann found that people pulling on a rope together pulled less hard per person as the group grew; later studies with clapping and shouting found the same.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE 1 · PRICING SOCIAL LOAFING

Eight reps share a single team target with a shared bonus. Working alone, each would average ₹50 lakh a year. Suppose loafing cuts average effort by 20% when output isn't tracked individually (illustrative).

Potential:      8 × ₹50 lakh       = ₹400 lakh
With loafing:   8 × ₹50 × 0.80     = ₹320 lakh
Lost to loafing                    = ₹80 lakh

The fix is not to abolish team targets — they help cooperation — but to make each contribution visible: individual dashboards alongside the team number, clear ownership of accounts, and recognition that names people. Loafing shrinks when people believe their effort is identifiable and matters.

==========

🤝 2. COMPLIANCE: GETTING A YES

Compliance is changing behaviour in response to a direct request. Several techniques are well documented — and widely used in sales:

• Foot-in-the-door — a small request first makes a larger one more likely. In a 1966 study by Jonathan Freedman and Scott Fraser, homeowners asked to put a large, ugly "Drive Carefully" sign in their garden mostly refused (about 17% agreed). But among those who had, two weeks earlier, agreed to display a tiny sign, about 76% agreed.
• Door-in-the-face — a large request that's refused makes a smaller follow-up more likely, because the requester appears to have conceded. In a 1975 study, students asked to chaperone young offenders to a zoo for a day agreed about 17% of the time; asked first to mentor them for two years (refused), about half then agreed to the zoo trip.
• Lowball — get agreement, then raise the cost. People tend to stick with commitments even when the terms worsen.
• That's-not-all — add a bonus before the person has answered.

Robert Cialdini's book Influence (1984) grouped these into six principles: reciprocity (we return favours), commitment and consistency (we act in line with what we've already said or done), social proof (we follow what others like us do), authority, liking (we say yes to people we like and who are like us), and scarcity (we want what's limited).

A line to hold: these principles describe real tendencies, so they can be used honestly (showing genuine testimonials from nearby dealers, offering a real limited-period scheme) or manipulatively (fake scarcity, lowballing a dealer on credit terms). The manipulative uses work once and destroy the relationship that repeat business depends on.

==========

🎖️ 3. OBEDIENCE

Obedience is following the orders of an authority. In Stanley Milgram's 1963 study, 40 men were told they were helping study learning by giving a "learner" (an actor) electric shocks of increasing strength for wrong answers. As the learner protested, then screamed, then fell silent, an experimenter in a grey coat said "please continue". In the best-known version, 26 of 40 — 65% — went all the way to the maximum 450 volts. No shocks were real.

Variations showed what drives it. Obedience fell when the learner was in the same room, when the experimenter gave orders by phone, and dramatically when two other "teachers" refused. A partial replication by Jerry Burger in 2009, stopping at 150 volts for ethical reasons, found about 70% willing to continue past that point, close to Milgram's rate. Historians who studied Milgram's archives have raised real concerns — some participants doubted the set-up, and procedures varied more than reported — but the core finding that ordinary people defer heavily to authority has held.

The organisational lesson: when a senior person pushes, juniors comply with things they know are wrong — loading stock, misreporting, skipping safety steps — especially when the authority is close and dissent is isolated. Make dissent easy and safe, and make it normal for someone to say "no".

==========

📣 4. ATTITUDES AND PERSUASION

An attitude is an evaluation of a person, object or idea, with three components: affective (feelings), behavioural (tendencies to act) and cognitive (beliefs). Attitudes predict behaviour better when they are strong, specific and personally relevant.

TWO ROUTES TO PERSUASION

Richard Petty and John Cacioppo's elaboration likelihood model says persuasion travels two routes. On the central route, people think carefully about the arguments; strong arguments persuade and weak ones backfire. On the peripheral route, people respond to cues — the speaker's attractiveness or status, the number of arguments, the mood. Which route people take depends on their motivation and ability to think about the message. A contractor choosing paint for a ₹40 lakh hotel project is on the central route: give him data on coverage, durability and lifetime cost. A homeowner glancing at a hoarding is on the peripheral route: celebrity, colour and repetition do the work. Central-route persuasion takes more effort but produces attitudes that last and resist counter-arguments.

COGNITIVE DISSONANCE

Leon Festinger proposed that holding inconsistent beliefs, or acting against one's beliefs, creates discomfort — cognitive dissonance — that people reduce by changing a belief. In a 1959 study, students did a boring task and were then paid either $1 or $20 to tell the next participant it was fun. The $1 group later rated the task as more enjoyable. With $20, the lie was explained by the money; with $1, the only way to reduce dissonance was to believe the task was not so bad. Small incentives can change attitudes more than large ones.

The everyday business version is post-purchase dissonance: after a big purchase, customers worry they chose wrong. Reassurance — a follow-up call, a thank-you note listing what they got — reduces it and protects repeat business.

==========

🔎 5. JUDGING OTHERS: ATTRIBUTION

We constantly explain other people's behaviour. Attribution theory distinguishes internal (dispositional) explanations — something about the person — from external (situational) ones — something about the circumstances. The most important finding is the fundamental attribution error: when judging others, we overweight personality and underweight the situation. In a 1967 study, people read essays they knew had been assigned to writers, yet still judged the writers as believing what they'd written.

When judging ourselves we do the opposite. The actor–observer bias: I missed target because of the monsoon; you missed it because you're lazy. And the self-serving bias: successes are mine, failures are bad luck. In reviews, this is the mistake that does the most damage. Before concluding that a rep is the problem, check his territory, stock availability, competitor activity and dealer mix — and compare him with others facing the same conditions.

First impressions form within seconds and are sticky, through the primacy effect (Part 5) and confirmation bias (Part 6). Stereotypes — generalised beliefs about members of a group — are efficient shortcuts that become harmful when applied to individuals.

==========

🌉 6. PREJUDICE AND HOW TO REDUCE IT

Prejudice is a negative attitude toward people based on group membership; discrimination is acting on it. Henri Tajfel's minimal group experiments showed how little it takes: boys divided into groups on a trivial basis, such as preferring one painter over another, favoured their own group when sharing out rewards. Social identity theory explains this: our self-esteem is tied to groups we belong to, so we favour the in-group. In Muzafer Sherif's 1954 Robbers Cave study, two groups of boys at a summer camp became hostile when made to compete for prizes, and hostility eased when they had to cooperate on shared goals, such as fixing the camp's water supply. (Later analysis showed the researchers shaped events more than the original report admitted, but the pattern has support elsewhere.)

The best-supported remedy is intergroup contact. A 2006 meta-analysis of over 500 studies by Thomas Pettigrew and Linda Tropp found that contact between groups reliably reduces prejudice, especially with equal status, shared goals, cooperation and support from leaders. Elliot Aronson's jigsaw classroom, where each student holds a piece of information the group needs, applies the same idea. For a company merging two sales forces, or mixing head-office and field staff, the design is clear: mixed teams, a common target, equal status within the team, and visible backing from leadership.

==========

😊 7. LIKING

We like people we see often (proximity and the mere-exposure effect: familiarity breeds liking), people similar to us, people who like us back (reciprocity of liking), and — unfairly — attractive people. These are the mechanics of the "relationship" in relationship selling: regular visits, finding common ground and showing genuine interest in the dealer. They work because they are real, which is also why they can't be faked for long.

==========

🚨 8. HELPING AND THE BYSTANDER EFFECT

In 1964 Kitty Genovese was murdered in New York, and a newspaper reported that 38 neighbours watched and did nothing. The story prompted John Darley and Bibb Latané's research on the bystander effect: the more people present, the less likely any one of them is to help. In their 1968 study, a participant heard another student apparently having a seizure over an intercom. When participants believed they were the only listener, about 85% went to help before the fit ended; when they believed four others were also listening, only about 31% did. The main cause is diffusion of responsibility: everyone assumes someone else will act.

Two corrections. The Genovese story was badly exaggerated: far fewer people saw the attack, and at least one called the police; the newspaper later acknowledged the errors. And a 2020 study of CCTV footage of real public conflicts in three countries found that in about 9 of 10 cases at least one bystander intervened — and that more bystanders made intervention more likely, since it only takes one. The lab effect is real for each individual; in real groups, someone usually acts.

Diffusion of responsibility is common in organisations: a problem flagged in a group email of twenty people that nobody owns. Name an owner, not a group.

==========

🔁 9. HELD UP?

• Asch conformity: Holds — Replicated many times, though rates vary by era and culture.
• Milgram obedience: Mostly — Partial replication at similar rates; archival critiques about procedure and belief.
• Foot-in-the-door, door-in-the-face: Hold, modest — Meta-analyses find reliable but smaller effects than the classic studies.
• Cognitive dissonance: Mostly — A core finding; some classic paradigms have replicated weakly.
• Intergroup contact reduces prejudice: Strong — Hundreds of studies; strongest under the right conditions.
• Bystanders don't help: Lab yes, life less so — Individual likelihood drops in groups, but in real conflicts someone usually intervenes.
• The Implicit Association Test reveals who will discriminate: Weak — IAT scores predict individual behaviour poorly and are unstable on retest.

==========

📝 SUMMARY

1️⃣ Conformity: in Asch's studies, people went along with a wrong majority about a third of the time; one ally sharply reduced it.
2️⃣ Groupthink and polarisation distort group decisions; the leader speaking last and an assigned dissenter help. Social loafing shrinks when individual effort is visible.
3️⃣ Compliance: foot-in-the-door, door-in-the-face, lowball; Cialdini's six principles. Honest use builds relationships, manipulation burns them.
4️⃣ Obedience: 65% went to the maximum in Milgram's study; it falls when authority is distant and others refuse. Make dissent safe.
5️⃣ Persuasion: central route (arguments) for engaged audiences, peripheral route (cues) for disengaged ones. Cognitive dissonance changes attitudes; reassure customers after big purchases.
6️⃣ Attribution: the fundamental attribution error overweights personality. Check the situation before blaming the person.
7️⃣ Prejudice arises easily from group identity; contact with equal status and shared goals reduces it.
8️⃣ Liking grows with proximity, similarity and reciprocity.
9️⃣ Bystander effect: diffusion of responsibility lowers individual helping — name an owner. In real-world conflicts, someone usually helps.

➡️ NEXT: Psychology for Managers 11/12 — Personality

==========

Sources: chapter structure follows Ciccarelli & White, Psychology, 4th ed. (Pearson), Ch. 12; text and figures are original. Asch, 1951/1956. Janis, Victims of Groupthink, 1972. Freedman & Fraser, 1966. Cialdini et al., 1975; Cialdini, Influence, 1984. Milgram, 1963; Burger, American Psychologist, 2009. Festinger & Carlsmith, 1959. Petty & Cacioppo, 1986. Jones & Harris, 1967. Pettigrew & Tropp, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2006. Darley & Latané, 1968. Philpot et al., American Psychologist, 2020. IAT: Oswald et al., 2013. Worked-example figures are illustrative.

==========

notes.body:
🧠 PSYCHOLOGY FOR MANAGERS, PART 11: PERSONALITY

==========

⚡ TL;DR

Most of Freud is hard to test, but defence mechanisms such as rationalisation, projection and denial describe everyday work behaviour well. Self-efficacy and an internal locus of control predict effort, and self-efficacy can be built with small wins and good models.

The model researchers actually use is the Big Five: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism, measured as scores, not types. Roughly 40–50% of the variation is linked to genes, and the family home siblings share explains little.

The headline result: a 2022 re-analysis puts structured interviews (about 0.42) ahead of work samples (0.33) and ability tests (0.31) in predicting job performance, with unstructured interviews and conscientiousness at about 0.19. MBTI types are unstable: even 80% stability per letter gives only about a 41% chance of the same type on retest.

The chapter structure follows Ciccarelli & White, Psychology (4th ed.), Chapter 13. The text and examples are original.

==========

🛋️ 1. THE PSYCHODYNAMIC APPROACH

Sigmund Freud described a mind largely driven by the unconscious — wishes, fears and memories outside awareness. He split personality into three parts:

• The id — inborn drives seeking immediate gratification (the "pleasure principle").
• The superego — the internalised rules of parents and society; the conscience.
• The ego — the rational part that negotiates between the two and reality.

When the conflict produces anxiety, the ego uses defence mechanisms, which are the part of Freud most useful today because they describe everyday behaviour well:

• Denial: Refusing to accept reality — "The new competitor won't affect our dealers."
• Rationalisation: A plausible excuse for an unacceptable motive — "I didn't want that promotion anyway."
• Projection: Attributing your own feelings to others — A manager who resents the boss says the team resents him.
• Displacement: Redirecting feelings to a safer target — Shouted at by the RSM, a rep snaps at the distributor's staff.
• Sublimation: Channelling impulses into acceptable activity — Aggression into competitive sport.

Freud's theory of psychosexual stages has little scientific support, and much of his theory is hard to test. His followers — the neo-Freudians — moved away from sexual drives. Carl Jung added a collective unconscious and introduced the ideas of introversion and extraversion, which survive in modern personality science and, less reliably, in the MBTI (section 6). Alfred Adler emphasised striving to overcome feelings of inferiority, and birth order. Karen Horney stressed social and cultural forces and anxiety in relationships.

==========

🔄 2. THE BEHAVIOURAL AND SOCIAL-COGNITIVE APPROACH

Behaviourists saw personality as a set of learned responses (Part 4). Albert Bandura's social-cognitive view added thought: personality emerges from reciprocal determinism, a constant three-way interaction between a person's thinking, their behaviour and the environment. A confident rep seeks out tough accounts, wins some, and becomes more confident. Two concepts from this approach are among the most useful in management:

• Self-efficacy — belief in your ability to succeed at a specific task. It predicts effort and persistence and can be built, mainly through small successes, watching similar people succeed, and credible encouragement.
• Locus of control (Julian Rotter) — whether you believe outcomes are controlled by your actions (internal) or by luck and others (external). An internal locus is associated with more effort and better job outcomes.

==========

🌱 3. THE HUMANISTIC APPROACH

Carl Rogers focused on the self-concept — how people see themselves. Distress arises when the real self (who you are) and the ideal self (who you think you should be) are far apart. Growth needs unconditional positive regard: acceptance of the person, separate from approval of every action. Rogers's influence is strongest in counselling (Part 12) and in coaching: feedback that criticises a specific behaviour while making clear the person is valued is more likely to be heard than feedback that seems to judge who they are.

==========

🖐️ 4. THE TRAIT APPROACH AND THE BIG FIVE

Trait theorists describe personality as a set of stable dimensions on which people vary. Gordon Allport found thousands of trait words in the dictionary; Raymond Cattell used statistics to boil them down to 16 factors. Later research converged on five broad dimensions that appear across languages and cultures — the Big Five, or OCEAN:

• Openness to experience: Curious, imaginative, open to new ideas — Adapts to change; useful in creative and strategic roles.
• Conscientiousness: Organised, dependable, hard-working — The most consistent Big Five predictor of performance across nearly all jobs.
• Extraversion: Sociable, energetic, assertive — Helps somewhat in sales and management roles.
• Agreeableness: Cooperative, trusting, kind — Helps in teamwork and service; very high scores may struggle in tough negotiation.
• Neuroticism (low: emotional stability): Anxious, moody, easily stressed — High neuroticism predicts more stress and burnout.

The Big Five are dimensions, not types: most people score somewhere in the middle of each. They are moderately stable across adulthood, and change in predictable ways with age — people tend to become more conscientious and agreeable and less neurotic as they mature. Some researchers add a sixth factor, honesty–humility (the HEXACO model), which is particularly relevant to integrity at work.

A long-running debate, the person–situation debate, asked whether traits really predict behaviour, since people act differently across situations. The resolution: a trait predicts a single action poorly but predicts a person's average behaviour across many situations well. Situations matter too: a strong situation, such as a clear rule, reduces differences between people.

==========

🧬 5. BIOLOGY AND PERSONALITY

Twin and adoption studies, including the long-running Minnesota study of twins raised apart, find that roughly 40–50% of the variation in Big Five traits is linked to genetic differences. A surprising finding: the environment siblings share — same home, same parents — explains little of their personality differences. Most of the environmental influence is non-shared: different friends, experiences, roles and chance events. Temperament in infancy (Part 7) is an early, partly inherited root.

==========

📋 6. MEASURING PERSONALITY

• Interviews — unstructured interviews (a free-flowing conversation) are weak and prone to bias. Structured interviews, where every candidate gets the same job-related questions scored on a set rubric, are among the best predictors of performance (section 7).
• Projective tests — the person interprets an ambiguous image: the Rorschach inkblots, or the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT), which asks for stories about pictures. The idea is that people project their unconscious onto the image. Reliability and validity are weak for most uses.
• Personality inventories — standardised questionnaires. The MMPI is used clinically and has built-in scales to detect lying or random answering. The NEO-PI and similar instruments measure the Big Five and are the tools used in research.

THE BARNUM EFFECT

In 1949 psychologist Bertram Forer gave his students a "personalised" personality profile and asked them to rate its accuracy. They rated it about 4.3 out of 5. Everyone had received the same text, assembled from horoscopes: "You have a great need for other people to like and admire you… At times you are extroverted, affable, sociable, while at other times you are introverted, wary, reserved." The Barnum effect is our tendency to accept vague, flattering descriptions as uniquely accurate. It explains why people find almost any personality report convincing, which is why "it felt so accurate" is not evidence that a test works.

THE MBTI PROBLEM

The Myers–Briggs Type Indicator, built in the 1940s on Jung's ideas, sorts people into 16 types from four either/or choices (for example, introvert or extravert). It is enormously popular in companies. Its problems are well documented. Most traits are normally distributed, so most people are near the middle — and a forced either/or split puts people who barely differ into opposite types. Many people get a different type when they retake it after a few weeks. And type has little demonstrated power to predict job performance.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE 1 · WHY TYPE TESTS FLIP

Suppose a person sits near the middle on several MBTI scales, so on retest each of the four letters has an 80% chance of coming out the same (illustrative).

P(all four letters the same) = 0.8 × 0.8 × 0.8 × 0.8
                             = 0.8⁴ ≈ 0.41

Even with each letter fairly stable, there's only about a 41% chance of getting the same four-letter type. That is a mechanical result of cutting continuous traits into categories. The Big Five avoids it by reporting scores, not types. If your company uses MBTI for team-building conversations, fine; for hiring, promotion or team assignment, it is the wrong tool.

==========

📈 7. WHAT PREDICTS JOB PERFORMANCE

Validity in hiring is measured as the correlation (r, Part 0) between a selection method's scores and later job performance. In 1998 Frank Schmidt and John Hunter published an influential summary that put general mental ability (Part 6) near the top. A 2022 re-analysis by Paul Sackett and colleagues corrected a statistical over-adjustment in that work and revised many estimates downward. Approximate values from the 2022 analysis:

• Structured interview: ~0.42
• Work-sample test: ~0.33
• General mental ability test: ~0.31
• Conscientiousness: ~0.19
• Unstructured interview: ~0.19

Figures are rounded and vary across jobs; combining methods predicts better than any single one.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE 2 · WHAT R ACTUALLY BUYS YOU

The share of performance differences a predictor accounts for is roughly r²:

Structured interview:   0.42² ≈ 0.18  → about 18%
Conscientiousness:      0.19² ≈ 0.04  → about 4%
Unstructured interview: 0.19² ≈ 0.04  → about 4%

Two lessons. First, even the best single method leaves most of the variation in performance unexplained, so humility in hiring is warranted. Second, a structured interview accounts for roughly four times as much variance as an unstructured chat that takes the same hour. Moving from "tell me about yourself" to a fixed set of job-related questions with a scoring rubric is the cheapest improvement most hiring processes can make. (r² understates practical value somewhat — even modest correlations improve the average quality of hires noticeably — but the comparison between methods holds.)

==========

🔁 8. HELD UP?

• Personality has five broad dimensions: Robust — Replicated across languages and cultures; a sixth (honesty–humility) is well supported too.
• MBTI type predicts job fit: No — Types are unstable on retest and show little predictive validity.
• Birth order shapes personality: No — Large studies of tens of thousands of people find no meaningful effect on Big Five traits.
• Inkblot tests reveal hidden personality: Weak — Poor reliability and validity for most uses.
• Handwriting analysis predicts performance: No — Studies find no validity once the content of the writing is controlled.
• Conscientiousness predicts performance: Yes, modestly — Consistent across jobs, though smaller than once thought.

==========

📝 SUMMARY

1️⃣ Personality is a stable pattern of thinking, feeling and behaving, studied through four approaches.
2️⃣ Psychodynamic: id, ego, superego and the unconscious. Most of Freud is untestable, but defence mechanisms describe everyday behaviour well. Jung's introversion–extraversion survives.
3️⃣ Social-cognitive: reciprocal determinism; self-efficacy and internal locus of control predict effort and can be built.
4️⃣ Humanistic: Rogers's self-concept and unconditional positive regard — criticise behaviour, value the person.
5️⃣ Trait: the Big Five (openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism) are dimensions, moderately stable, and conscientiousness is the most consistent work predictor.
6️⃣ About 40–50% of trait variation is linked to genes; shared family environment explains little.
7️⃣ Structured interviews and inventories work; projective tests are weak. The Barnum effect makes any vague profile feel accurate. MBTI types are unstable — even 80% stability per letter gives only about a 41% chance of the same type.
8️⃣ Best predictors of job performance (2022): structured interviews (~0.42), work samples (~0.33), general mental ability (~0.31). Unstructured interviews and conscientiousness are about 0.19.

➡️ NEXT: Psychology for Managers 12/12 — Psychological Disorders and Therapies

==========

Sources: chapter structure follows Ciccarelli & White, Psychology, 4th ed. (Pearson), Ch. 13; text and figures are original. Big Five: McCrae & Costa; HEXACO: Ashton & Lee. Forer, 1949. MBTI reliability: Pittenger, 1993, and later reviews. Birth order: Rohrer, Egloff & Schmukle, PNAS, 2015. Selection validity: Schmidt & Hunter, Psychological Bulletin, 1998; Sackett et al., Journal of Applied Psychology, 2022. Worked example 1 uses illustrative probabilities.

==========

🔗 The PDF has the diagrams, worked examples, practice problems, glossary and answer key. Coming next: Psychology for Managers 12/12 — Psychological Disorders and Therapies

notes.summary: An overview of what counts as a psychological disorder, how common disorders are in India and worldwide, the main categories, and which treatments work, ending with what a manager should and shouldn't do when someone is struggling. Covers definitions and causes, DSM-5-TR and ICD-11, WHO and Indian prevalence estimates, anxiety, mood, psychotic and personality disorders, psychodynamic, person-centred, behaviour and cognitive therapies, cognitive distortions and the thought record, evidence on therapy and medication, and India's Mental Healthcare Act. The attached A4 PDF has the worked examples, practice problems, glossary and answer key.
notes.body:
🧠 PSYCHOLOGY FOR MANAGERS, PART 12: PSYCHOLOGICAL DISORDERS AND THERAPIES

==========

⚡ TL;DR

A disorder is a pattern that causes significant distress or impairment, beyond an expected reaction to events. Causes are biological, psychological and social combined; stress adds to an existing vulnerability.

About 1 in 8 people worldwide live with a mental disorder, and India's national survey put it at about 1 in 10 adults, with most untreated. In a team of forty, expect four or five, mostly invisible.

The headline result: treatment works. The average person in therapy ends up better off than about 75–80% of comparable untreated people, with CBT and exposure especially effective, and antidepressants beat placebo, modestly, in a 500-trial analysis. The manager's job is narrow: notice, ask, listen, point to help (Tele-MANAS 14416; emergencies 112) and adjust work — not diagnose.

The chapter structure follows Ciccarelli & White, Psychology (4th ed.), Chapters 14–15, at overview level. The text and examples are original.

==========

🧭 1. WHAT MAKES BEHAVIOUR A DISORDER

No single test separates "disordered" from "normal". Psychologists combine several criteria:

• Statistical rarity — unusual behaviour. But rarity alone isn't illness: exceptional talent is rare too.
• Violating social norms — but norms differ across cultures and change over time.
• Personal distress — the person suffers. Important, but some conditions don't cause distress to the person who has them.
• Impaired functioning — difficulty working, maintaining relationships or caring for oneself.

The working definition used today: a psychological disorder is a pattern of thoughts, feelings or behaviour that causes significant distress or impairs a person's ability to function, and is not simply an expected reaction to a situation (grief after a death, for example).

==========

🧬 2. WHAT CAUSES DISORDERS

Several models offer explanations. The biological model looks at genes, brain chemistry and brain structure. Psychological models look at learned behaviour, patterns of thinking and early experiences. The sociocultural model looks at poverty, discrimination, family and culture. Most clinicians now use the biopsychosocial model, which combines all three, and a vulnerability–stress (diathesis–stress) view: a person may carry a vulnerability — genetic or from early life — that becomes a disorder only when enough stress is added. That is why chronic workplace stress (Part 9) matters: it can be the added load that tips a vulnerable person into illness.

==========

🗂️ 3. HOW DISORDERS ARE CLASSIFIED

Two systems are used worldwide. The American Psychiatric Association's DSM-5-TR (2022) describes each disorder by its symptoms, duration and effects. The World Health Organization's ICD-11 (in effect from 2022) is the international standard, and the system used in India's public health records. Diagnosis enables treatment, research and insurance. It also carries a cost: labels can stick and stigmatise. Since 2019 ICD-11 has also listed burnout — as an occupational phenomenon, not a mental disorder (Part 9).

==========

🌍 4. HOW COMMON THEY ARE

The WHO's 2022 World Mental Health Report estimated that in 2019 about 970 million people — roughly 1 in 8 worldwide — were living with a mental disorder, most commonly anxiety and depression. In India, the National Mental Health Survey of 2015–16 estimated that about 1 in 10 adults had a current mental disorder, and that the large majority of people who needed treatment did not receive it — a treatment gap the survey put at roughly 70–90% depending on the disorder.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE 1 · WHAT PREVALENCE MEANS FOR ONE TEAM

Team size:                     40 people
At about 1 in 10 (India):       40 × 0.10 = 4
At about 1 in 8 (global):       40 × 0.125 = 5

Treatment gap of ~80%:          of 4, about 3 untreated

On average, four or five people in a team of forty, of whom perhaps three are not getting help. These are averages and the actual number varies, but the point holds: mental-health conditions in a team are normal, not exceptional, and most are invisible. The aim is not to identify them, but to make it easy for people to seek help and to adjust work while they do.

==========

📚 5. THE MAIN CATEGORIES

• Anxiety disorders: Excessive fear or worry: specific phobias, social anxiety, panic attacks, generalised anxiety — The most common group. Highly treatable.
• Obsessive–compulsive disorder: Intrusive, unwanted thoughts (obsessions) and repetitive acts to reduce the anxiety (compulsions) — Not the same as liking things tidy.
• Trauma-related (e.g. PTSD): Re-living a traumatic event, avoidance, feeling constantly on guard — Can follow accidents, assault, disasters.
• Depressive disorders: Persistent low mood or loss of interest, with changes in sleep, energy, appetite and concentration, for at least two weeks — Among the leading causes of disability worldwide.
• Bipolar disorder: Periods of depression alternating with mania: elevated mood, little need for sleep, racing ideas, risky decisions — Usually needs long-term medical treatment.
• Eating disorders: Serious disturbances in eating and in thoughts about food, weight and body — Can be life-threatening; specialist care needed.
• Schizophrenia: Positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, disorganised speech) and negative symptoms (flat emotion, withdrawal) — Affects fewer than 1 in 100 people. Not "split personality".
• Personality disorders: Long-standing, inflexible patterns that cause problems across situations, e.g. borderline or antisocial personality disorder — Distinct from ordinary personality differences (Part 11).
• Dissociative disorders: Disruptions in memory, identity or awareness — Dissociative identity disorder remains debated.

==========

🛋️ 6. PSYCHOLOGICAL THERAPIES

Therapies divide broadly into insight therapies, which aim at understanding, and action therapies, which aim at changing behaviour and thinking directly.

• Psychodynamic therapy — Freud's psychoanalysis explored the unconscious through free association and dream analysis, over years. Modern psychodynamic therapy is shorter and more focused on current relationships.
• Person-centred therapy (Carl Rogers) — the therapist offers empathy, genuineness and unconditional positive regard, and the client leads. Its core skills — reflective listening, not judging — are useful well beyond therapy.
• Behaviour therapy applies learning principles (Part 4). Exposure therapy confronts feared situations gradually and safely until the fear fades; systematic desensitisation pairs gradual exposure with relaxation. Exposure is among the most effective treatments for phobias, OCD and PTSD.
• Cognitive therapy (Aaron Beck) and rational emotive behaviour therapy (Albert Ellis) target distorted thinking. Combined with behavioural methods, this is cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), the most widely tested talking therapy, effective for depression, anxiety, insomnia and more.
• Group and family therapy treat problems in the context of relationships. Family involvement is particularly relevant in India, where care is often family-centred.

COGNITIVE DISTORTIONS

Beck identified recurring patterns of distorted thinking. They are worth knowing because everyone uses them under stress, and they show up constantly in sales reviews:

• All-or-nothing: "I missed target, so I'm a failure."
• Overgeneralisation: "I lost this dealer. I always lose the good ones."
• Catastrophising: "One bad quarter and I'll be fired."
• Mind reading: "The RSM thinks I'm useless."
• Personalisation: "The region missed because of me."

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE 2 · A THOUGHT RECORD

CBT's basic tool is a thought record: write the situation, the automatic thought, the evidence for and against, and a more balanced thought. A rep after a poor quarter:

Situation:   Q2 at 78% of target
Thought:     "I'm going to be fired."   (catastrophising)
Evidence for: the review is next week
Evidence against: Q1 was 104%; region at 85%;
             nobody fired for one quarter in 3 years
Balanced:    "Q2 was weak, partly the region.
             I need a plan for Q3 — not a resignation."

The thought changes from a catastrophe to a problem with a next step. This is a self-help technique for everyday stress, not a substitute for treatment — but managers who coach this way, asking "What's the evidence?", help people think more clearly under pressure.

DOES THERAPY WORK?

Yes. A 1977 meta-analysis by Mary Lee Smith and Gene Glass, and a larger follow-up in 1980, found that the average person in therapy was better off than about 75–80% of comparable untreated people. Many therapies perform similarly for many problems, which points to common factors — above all the therapeutic alliance, the working relationship between client and therapist. Some treatments are clearly better for specific problems: exposure for anxiety disorders, CBT for depression and insomnia. In India, where trained therapists are scarce, trials have shown that lay counsellors trained in simple structured therapies can deliver real benefits — one 2017 trial in Goa found a brief behavioural therapy delivered by lay counsellors reduced depression.

==========

💊 7. BIOMEDICAL TREATMENTS

Medications are prescribed by doctors, most often psychiatrists. Antipsychotics reduce the positive symptoms of schizophrenia. Antidepressants, most commonly SSRIs (Part 1), are used for depression and anxiety. Anti-anxiety medicines such as benzodiazepines act quickly but carry a risk of dependence, so are generally used short-term. Mood stabilisers such as lithium are used for bipolar disorder. A 2018 analysis of over 500 trials found all 21 antidepressants studied were more effective than placebo for acute depression in adults, though the average advantage was modest. Medication and CBT combined often work better than either alone. Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), now given under anaesthesia, remains an effective treatment for severe depression that hasn't responded to other treatments — far removed from its film image.

==========

🤲 8. WHAT A MANAGER SHOULD DO

India's Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 gives every person a right to access mental-health care and protection from discrimination, and it effectively decriminalised attempted suicide by presuming that a person who attempts it is under severe stress. The legal backdrop has moved toward treatment and away from blame. A manager's role is narrow and important:

▸ NOTICE, ASK, LISTEN, POINT, ADJUST

1. Notice changes that last for weeks: withdrawal, irritability, missed deadlines in someone usually reliable, visible exhaustion.
2. Ask privately and simply: "You haven't seemed yourself lately. How are you doing?"
3. Listen without diagnosing, fixing or comparing. Take it seriously.
4. Point to help: the company's employee assistance programme if there is one, a doctor, or Tele-MANAS (dial 14416), India's free, round-the-clock mental-health helpline. In an emergency, call 112.
5. Adjust work while they recover — flexible hours, lighter targets, fewer long drives — and keep what you've been told confidential.

If someone talks about not wanting to live, or about suicide, take it seriously, stay with them or make sure they are not alone, and connect them to help immediately — Tele-MANAS or emergency services.

==========

🔁 9. HELD UP?

• Psychotherapy works: Yes — Consistent across decades of meta-analyses; the alliance matters most.
• Depression is simply a "chemical imbalance": Oversimplified — A 2022 review found no consistent evidence for low serotonin as the cause. Antidepressants still help many people, by mechanisms not fully understood.
• Rosenhan's 1973 "sane in insane places" study proved psychiatric diagnosis is meaningless: Doubtful — Later investigation of the study's records raised serious questions about how it was carried out and reported.
• Venting anger (punching a pillow) gets it out of your system: No — Experiments find venting tends to increase later aggression.
• ECT is outdated and harmful: No — Under modern anaesthesia it is an effective treatment for severe, treatment-resistant depression.
• Lay counsellors can deliver effective therapy: Yes, for some conditions — Supported by trials in India and other low-resource settings.

📝 SUMMARY

1️⃣ A psychological disorder is a pattern of thought, feeling or behaviour causing significant distress or impairment, beyond an expected reaction to events.
2️⃣ Causes are biopsychosocial: vulnerability plus stress. Chronic work stress can be the added load.
3️⃣ Disorders are classified by DSM-5-TR and ICD-11. Labels help treatment but can stigmatise.
4️⃣ About 1 in 8 people worldwide live with a mental disorder; in India about 1 in 10 adults, with most untreated. In a team of 40, expect four or five.
5️⃣ Main groups: anxiety, OCD, trauma-related, depressive, bipolar, eating, schizophrenia, personality and dissociative disorders.
6️⃣ Therapies: psychodynamic, person-centred, behaviour therapy (exposure), cognitive therapy and CBT. Therapy works — the average client ends up better off than about 75–80% of untreated people — and the alliance matters most.
7️⃣ Medications (antipsychotics, antidepressants, anti-anxiety drugs, mood stabilisers) and ECT help specific conditions, often best combined with therapy.
8️⃣ Managers: notice, ask, listen, point to help (Tele-MANAS 14416; emergencies 112), adjust work — and don't diagnose.
